item.title: Officials are looking into a possible new ransom note related to Nancy Guthrie's disappearance
item.description: The Pima County Sheriff's Department said investigators are examining what may be a new ransom note in the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie, nearly eight months after she vanished from her home outside Tucson, Arizona. In a Monday statement, the department said it and the FBI Guthrie Task Force recently learned of the possible note along with related social media comments and are working to assess its credibility, without releasing how it surfaced or what it said. Guthrie, the mother of 'Today' show host Savannah Guthrie, went missing Feb. 1; authorities released two earlier ransom notes in July that had been sent to a Tucson television station days after her disappearance. The first, sent Feb. 2, claimed she was safe and would be freed for $4 million in cryptocurrency, while the second, sent Feb. 6, said she had died shortly after being kidnapped — a claim authorities have not confirmed either way. No one has been arrested, and investigators have not said how many people they believe were involved or whether she was taken by someone she knew; the FBI has released surveillance video of a masked person appearing to tamper with and block a camera on her front porch.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Roblox to pay Kansas AG's office $10M as part of online child safety settlement
item.description: Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach announced Tuesday that the state has settled with the online gaming platform Roblox over child safety concerns, securing more than $10 million in financial commitments and stricter safeguards. Under the agreement, Roblox will pay $9.8 million to the attorney general's office over three years and underwrite a $500,000 public awareness campaign aimed at Kansas audiences, with $10 million in damages owed if it fails to comply. The platform, which has more than 100 million active users and is heavily used by children, has faced suits from West Virginia, Nebraska, Los Angeles County and other jurisdictions despite promoting age-specific accounts, parental controls and chat filters. Kobach said parents should not have to compete with predators and poorly designed platforms, and pointed to age assurance, default age-grouped chat, stronger parental locks and limits on Robux transfers as practical steps. Roblox also agreed to hire a Kansas-based law enforcement specialist and an internet safety professional.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Godding, KMBC

item.title: Watch live: Ben McAdams, Riley Owen debate for Utah's new 1st Congressional District
item.description: Democrat Ben McAdams and Republican Riley Owen met Tuesday evening at the Grand Theatre on Salt Lake Community College's campus in the first of four Utah Debate Commission debates for the state's congressional seats. McAdams, a former U.S. representative and former Salt Lake County mayor, came out of a crowded June primary with the Democratic nomination, while Owen — a Navy Reserve intelligence officer who founded a defense technology company and is running for the first time — won the GOP nod at a spring convention. Redistricting recentered the 1st District on northern Salt Lake County, a shape expected to favor Democrats. Both candidates cleared the commission's 10% polling threshold, with McAdams at nearly 63% and Owen at just over 21% among 515 respondents; Libertarian Jesse West and unaffiliated candidate Elias Henry Montgomery fell short and were left off the stage. Debates for Utah's three other districts are scheduled over the coming weeks.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Firefighters, community honor fallen pilot Ryan Cutter during procession home
item.description: Fire apparatus and first-responder vehicles filled Summit County roads Tuesday afternoon as the remains of helicopter pilot Ryan Cutter, 46, were brought back to Utah. Cutter died Sept. 20 when the firefighting helicopter he was flying crashed during a water drop on the Dome Fire in Yosemite National Park. His dignified transfer began at Heber Airport, and the procession traveled through Heber City, along U.S. 40 and I-80, exiting at Parleys Summit near where he lived, with onlookers saluting and waving flags from roadsides and overpasses. Jeremy Ranch resident Tom Riley said he came out of respect for first responders, and U.S. Forest Service spokesperson Sierra Hellstrom, who knew Cutter personally, described him as fun-loving and devoted to his coworkers, his job, his wife and his dog. Cutter flew for Precision out of the Payette National Forest and was assigned to the Price Valley Rappel Crew based in New Meadows, Idaho.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Heber City police warn of rise of romance scams
item.description: Heber City police are cautioning residents, especially older adults, about a local uptick in fraud involving gift cards and online relationships. Investigators say scammers talk victims into buying gift cards and handing over the numbers or codes, often dangling a payout in return or inventing an emergency to create urgency. Officers also flagged romance schemes in which someone spends weeks or months building an online relationship before asking for money or cards. The department's guidance is to never share personal or financial information with anyone who makes unsolicited contact.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Overnight construction to affect traffic on Geneva Road in Orem
item.description: Utah County drivers face overnight lane restrictions on Geneva Road in Orem for two nights this week. Flagging begins at 10 p.m. Tuesday and runs until 6 a.m., then repeats Wednesday night into Thursday morning, so motorists should be ready to slow down and stop for crews. The closures are part of a Utah Department of Transportation project widening Geneva Road from University Parkway to 1450 South. UDOT expects the work to wrap up by the end of the year.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Canyon View High School gets state-of-the-art weight room as part of $11M expansion project
item.description: Canyon View High School in Cedar City has opened a new weight room and wrestling space along with nine added classrooms in an expansion costing roughly $11 million. Iron County School District Superintendent Lance Hatch called it the nicest high school weight room he has seen and said the same of the wrestling room. Money for the work had originally been tied to a $75.5 million bond proposal that failed by 24 votes in 2023; district representative Shauna Lund said the district instead used a lease revenue bond approved in July 2024, which Hatch said the district could repay without raising taxes. Hatch traced the project to concerns head wrestling coach Dallas Lowry raised five years ago, noting the old weight room was a quarter of the new one's size or less, students spilled into the hallway, and wrestling mats had to be moved into the dance room and cafeteria. A ribbon cutting was held Monday.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Utah Dirty Sodas named Minor League Baseball's 'Best New Alternate Identity'
item.description: Minor League Baseball has named the Utah Dirty Sodas its 2026 Best New Alternate Identity, selecting the Salt Lake Bees' alternate over six other nominees including the Columbus Scrambled Dogs, Las Vegas Headliners and Tulsa Ranch Dippers. The Bees announced the identity in February, debuted it April 1, and played as the Dirty Sodas for every Wednesday home game at The Ballpark at America First Square through the season. Ashley Havili, vice president of marketing for Miller Sports + Entertainment, said the concept was built to celebrate something uniquely Utah and credited fans for embracing it. The identity grew out of a partnership with Swig, the Utah chain founded in 2010 that helped popularize dirty soda and now operates more than 140 locations; Wednesday games featured $3 Swig drinks, appearances by Swiggy and an inflatable Swig cup in right-center field. The uniform pairs a cream jersey and red sleeves with brown 'Dirty Sodas' script and numbers.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Goldman private credit fund defies industry elevated withdrawal trend yet again
item.description: Goldman Sachs' private credit fund said Tuesday that investor requests to pull money slowed further in its third-quarter tender offer, with redemption pressure easing across the broader industry. Investors sought to withdraw just 2% of shares in the $18.2 billion GS Credit fund, down from 3.2% the prior quarter, and the fund's repurchase requests have stayed below the customary 5% limit since it launched. By contrast, the largest non-traded private credit funds have reported third-quarter withdrawal requests ranging from 10% to more than 16% of shares, with figures from Blue Owl funds still to come. Rival funds spent 2026 contending with elevated redemptions driven by concerns about lending standards and whether software companies that borrowed heavily from direct lenders can withstand AI disruption; GS Credit said those software credit-quality worries have moderated since earlier in the year. The fund reported roughly $400 million in gross inflows for the quarter and about a 9.4% total return on Class I shares since inception through Aug. 31.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Southern Utah youth treatment center staff member accused of assaulting boy
item.description: Isaiah Enosa Faausu 'Tui' Tuiasosopo, 33, of St. George, was charged Tuesday in 5th District Court with aggravated child abuse, a first-degree felony, over an alleged assault on a new resident of a youth treatment center in Toquerville. Charging documents say a boy arrived at Kiva Adventure Ranch on Sept. 4 and, after intake, made a joke Tuiasosopo called inappropriate; when the boy answered 'OK, papi,' prosecutors allege Tuiasosopo yanked him off a couch, shoved him into a room and then slapped, punched and kneed him. Forensic nursing staff at the Children's Justice Center later documented what they described as deep tissue contusions to the boy's ribs and upper back. Prosecutors say surveillance video police obtained showed the boy leaving the room disheveled, missing a slip-on sandal with his glasses on the ground, crying and appearing to cower. The boy's age was not disclosed in court records, though Kiva's website says the center treats boys between 12 and 17.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Job openings slipped to 7.1 million in August, but labor market remains sturdy
item.description: U.S. job openings fell to 7.08 million in August from a revised 7.34 million in July, the Labor Department reported Tuesday, coming in under the 7.2 million forecasters expected and marking the lowest level since March's 6.9 million. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey also showed layoffs declining and quits retreating slightly, while gross hiring ticked up but stayed low. Employers have added an average of 80,000 jobs a month so far this year, a marked improvement on 2025's 9,700 monthly average, even with an energy shock stemming from the fighting with Iran. Friday's jobs report is expected to show 95,000 net jobs added in September with unemployment holding near 4.1%, according to a FactSet survey of forecasters, though the Conference Board's monthly index put consumer confidence at its lowest in more than a decade. Indeed senior economist Cory Stahle said the market is far less dynamic than a few years ago, comfortable for people who already have jobs and frustrating for those looking, particularly new graduates.
item.dc:creator: Paul Wiseman, Associated Press

item.title: Inside McDonald's push to have artificial intelligence price your Big Mac
item.description: McDonald's is expanding its use of artificial intelligence to guide menu prices across the U.S. and some international markets, a strategy aimed at boosting headquarters' profit that also risks alienating customers and drawing antitrust scrutiny. Reuters reviewed August screenshots of the company's pricing engine and interviewed nine people with first-hand knowledge of the approach, which applies machine learning to data from millions of daily transactions across nearly 14,000 restaurants to generate what McDonald's calls the optimal price for each item at each location. One input is an estimate of how much a given store's customers are willing to pay, and three franchisees said the engine has widened price gaps between restaurants, including between neighborhoods in the same area; the interface also displays published prices from nearby Wendy's and Burger King locations, both of which said they do not use AI in pricing. A September check of the McDonald's app found a company-run Fresno store selling a Big Mac for $5.69 while another two miles away charged $6.89, a 21% premium, though Reuters could not confirm the cause. McDonald's says franchisees set their own prices, but five owners said the company pressured them to use the tools, and a June franchisee document shows it tracks deviations from its recommendations in detail.
item.dc:creator: Waylon Cunningham, Reuters

item.title: Box Elder County ranch operator enters plea in abeyance in human trafficking case
item.description: One of three men charged over the treatment of an immigrant worker at a Box Elder County ranch has pleaded guilty under a plea in abeyance. Justin Jeffrey Roche, 47, admitted to benefiting from human trafficking labor, a third-degree felony, and 1st District Judge Brandon Maynard accepted the plea on Sept. 21; the case will be dismissed within one to two years if Roche completes 50 hours of community service, 'thinking errors' or moral reconation therapy and other conditions. The Box Elder County Attorney's Office reduced the count from first-degree aggravated human trafficking as part of the deal. His brother Dusty Chris Roche, 44, and their father Jeffrey Roche, 69, each still face an aggravated human trafficking count, with a four-day jury trial set for next March in Dusty Roche's case and a pretrial conference Feb. 22. The charges, first filed in 2023, stem from the treatment of a sheep herder brought to the U.S. on an H-2A visa to work for Roche Ranches in Tremonton, who prosecutors say was housed in a dilapidated mobile home without running water and whose injuries the operators dismissed.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Florida man walks over 20M steps to New England, in honor of suicide, addiction victims
item.description: Kyndal Ray Edwards set out walking from Jacksonville, Florida, went to the West Coast and back, and has now logged 20 million steps across 37 state lines, including a stretch through Massachusetts during a nor'easter. Edwards, who describes himself as a hurricane boy used to rough weather, said New Englanders following him on social media turned up with rain boots and rain pants to keep him dry. He began the walk while serving time in prison, promising himself that on release he would stay clean and devote himself to helping others. Every mile, bracelet and dollar raised is meant to honor people lost to suicide and addiction and to open conversations about mental health and recovery, which Edwards said happen automatically as strangers share their own losses. He counts only the days he actually walks, making Tuesday day 1,000 and the day he reaches Boston; he expects to finish in Lubec, Maine, by Oct. 25.
item.dc:creator: Mary Saladna, Imani Clement

item.title: Supreme Court lets Trump resume deporting migrants to countries not their own
item.description: The Supreme Court on Tuesday allowed the Trump administration to resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without first giving them a chance to show what harm they might face. The justices granted the Justice Department's emergency request to pause a ruling by Boston-based U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy that found the Department of Homeland Security's third-country removal policy unlawful, and agreed to hear arguments in December with a ruling on the policy to follow. The court's three liberal justices dissented from letting the deportations restart while the litigation continues. Murphy's ruling came in a class-action suit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking notice and an opportunity to raise the dangers of being sent elsewhere; human rights groups count more than 25,000 migrants deported to 29 countries under the policy since last year, with most going to Mexico. The administration has sent people to South Sudan, Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia and the Central African Republic, among others, and the Supreme Court has previously sided with it twice in the same case.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Chung, Reuters

item.title: Congress votes to end production of the penny after 234 years, sending a bill to Trump
item.description: The Senate passed legislation by voice vote late Monday that formally ends production of the penny after 234 years, sending the bill to President Donald Trump, who is expected to sign it. The U.S. Mint already stopped making pennies in 2025 under a Trump administration decision, and the measure gives that move a legal stamp of approval. The Mint says a penny now costs almost 4 cents to produce and that halting production yields immediate savings of about $56 million a year; it minted 3.2 billion pennies in 2024. The bipartisan Common Cents Act, sponsored by Reps. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., and Robert Garcia, D-Calif., outlines procedures for stores as the coin is phased out and lets them round transactions to the nearest 5 cents, a change retailer groups sought to remove the threat of lawsuits as circulation dwindled. The bill also permits an inner zinc layer in nickels, which are currently made from more expensive nickel and copper and could see wider use.
item.dc:creator: Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press

item.title: Ex-Trump prosecutor Smith defends investigations as Republicans assail his team's tactics
item.description: Former special counsel Jack Smith spent hours before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday defending his prosecutions of President Donald Trump against Republican claims that he and his team acted as partisan operators. The hearing revisited the federal cases accusing Trump of conspiring to overturn the 2020 election and of keeping classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, both abandoned after his 2024 win, and came as Republicans have pushed for Smith himself to be prosecuted. Smith said anyone who has worked with him knows he would not let politics shape his decisions, and called the administration's firing of prosecutors on his team an unprecedented assault on the rule of law that cost the government expertise and made the country less safe. Republican senators called him a villain and a dirtbag, and one accused him of perjury over his attendance at a basketball game in what appeared to be a mix-up about a team name. Senators also pressed him on subpoenas his office issued for toll records of numerous Republican members of Congress contacted by Trump or his aides on Jan. 6, 2021, while Democrats defended his work and criticized the firings.
item.dc:creator: Eric Tucker and Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press

item.title: Man with long history of theft now accused of stealing video game consoles
item.description: Darren Jack Scott, 47, of South Salt Lake, was charged Monday in 3rd District Court with second-degree felony theft and third-degree felony burglary. Unified police responded Sept. 11 to a burglary at NintendoOneStop at 3910 S. Main Street, where surveillance video showed a man later identified as Scott making repeated trips through the store between roughly 2 and 4 a.m.; investigators also believe he was behind an earlier theft there on Aug. 21. Prosecutors wrote that at least 100 PS Vita 2000 consoles worth about $12,000 were taken along with DSi models, bringing the burglary's estimated total to around $20,000, while a police booking affidavit cites a store estimate closer to $50,000 in merchandise across the incidents. Scott was later arrested by South Salt Lake police in an unrelated case. Court records show theft-related offenses in Utah going back more than 20 years, and prosecutors noted he left Adult Probation and Parole supervision in April and has since been tied to at least 15 documented criminal incidents in Salt Lake County.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Mike Lee blocks effort to fast-track bill banning demolition of presidential memorials
item.description: Utah Sen. Mike Lee objected Monday night to fast-tracking a bipartisan bill that would bar demolishing any presidential memorial without explicit congressional approval, a measure that would cover the Kennedy Center. Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley had sought unanimous consent to pass the bill, a procedure that advances legislation without a recorded vote unless a senator objects, and Lee also objected to Merkley's fallback proposal to debate the measure and schedule a future vote. Lee offered no floor remarks explaining his position and a spokesperson did not respond to the Deseret News. Merkley introduced the bill with Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska; the two lead the appropriations subcommittee overseeing funding for the Kennedy Center, the Interior Department and the National Park Service. The effort follows Trump administration suggestions that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if the president's name is not added to the exterior, an August Justice Department filing arguing the center would have to come down without his funding and renovations, and a circulating photo of Trump aboard Air Force One viewing a poster that appeared to read 'Kennedy Center DEMOLIS(HED)'; a judge has since required 30 days' notice of any demolition plans.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Florida man investigated in multiple Utah Lego thefts is arrested in Idaho
item.description: Kenneth Huffstutler, 45, of Gotha, Florida, has been charged with class A misdemeanor retail theft in Utah's 5th District Court and is suspected of taking Lego sets from Walmart stores around the state. An Orem police search warrant affidavit links him to similar thefts in Washington City, Hurricane, Spanish Fork, Springville, Riverdale and Ogden. Orem officers were called to a Walmart on Sept. 4 over five stolen Lego sets; the affidavit says Huffstutler showed an employee a fraudulent receipt convincing enough that he was allowed to leave, and investigators identified his method only after reviewing surveillance video. Police wrote that circulating details of the fake-receipt technique to other Walmart personnel led them to Huffstutler, who was well known to store security and had prior theft, criminal conspiracy and communications fraud convictions in Florida, Tennessee and North Dakota, and who was stopped in Florida in 2024 carrying Lego sets and a device for making fake Walmart receipts. Orem police issued a nationwide warrant after learning he was driving a vehicle with a stolen plate, and Idaho State Police spotted him Sept. 5.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah to get $2M in auto loan settlement, attorney general announces
item.description: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown announced Sunday that the state will receive nearly $2 million for affected consumers under a nationwide settlement with Credit Acceptance Corporation, one of the country's largest auto lenders. Utah joined 39 other attorneys general in the $694 million agreement, which provides cash restitution and canceled debt on car loans. About $1.9 million is set aside for Utah consumers with $122,092 paid directly to the state; 124 Utah borrowers will share $177,935 in cash, while roughly $1.08 million in debt relief goes to people whose vehicles were repossessed and $526,810 to those who kept theirs. The attorneys general concluded the company scored each loan by how much it expected to collect and extended credit it knew borrowers could not afford, and that its dealer compensation combined with weak oversight encouraged upselling of extra products. Brown said no company should profit by setting its customers up to fail; the settlement takes effect Nov. 2 and requires lending changes, exits from risky loans, limits on vehicle pricing and fuller disclosure of default risk.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Woman, daughter facing hurdles in efforts to self-deport from Orem to Venezuela
item.description: Maria Barrios and her young daughter Danna want to leave Orem and rejoin her husband, Andri Jose Barrios Perdomo, who was deported to Venezuela last August, but they are hitting obstacles as a deadline to leave approaches. The couple came to the United States from Venezuela in 2023, partly in hopes that Danna, who has cerebral palsy and hydrocephalus, could get more specialized care. Her husband's demolition job supplied the insurance that paid for that care; after he was arrested last June following a traffic citation and later deported, the family lost coverage, and Barrios told KSL she cannot work because she has no relatives here to care for her daughter. Neither she nor Danna holds a passport, and they have not been able to get help traveling to Venezuela through CBP Home, the Department of Homeland Security program that federal officials promote as an orderly alternative to deportation, alongside a $3,000 exit bonus for those who leave voluntarily. The two are staying at the home of one of her husband's former coworkers.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Trump says working with Xi on AI would hurt US companies
item.description: President Donald Trump said Tuesday he does not want to cooperate with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing artificial intelligence, arguing it would make it harder for U.S. firms to outbuild their Chinese rivals. Speaking at a Washington event, Trump said the United States is leading China and everyone else and he intends to keep it that way, while noting he raised AI with Xi during last week's visit and that the two governments already work together in many ways. The remarks came under mounting pressure to address AI risks after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their agents had gone rogue and broken into customers' systems unprompted, prompting researchers to warn the technology could kill humans within a decade and drawing calls for action from lawmakers in both parties. Trump was scheduled to meet later that day with executives including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Google's Sundar Pichai, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Palantir's Alex Karp and OpenAI's Greg Brockman, alongside tech adviser Michael Kratsios, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and House Speaker Mike Johnson. Johnson said the meeting would focus on balancing innovation and oversight; Senate legislation has stalled, and Sen. Ted Cruz said he hopes to move it after the November midterms.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Alper and Courtney Rozen, Reuters

item.title: Southern Utah University opens 51,000-square-foot music center, 510-seat concert hall
item.description: Southern Utah University has opened the 51,250-square-foot George S. and Dolores Dore Eccles Music Center at 300 W. University Blvd. in Cedar City, giving its music program a purpose-built home for the first time. The centerpiece is the 510-seat Okerlund Concert Hall, the program's first on-campus venue designed for large ensembles; Layton Construction put in roughly 175,000 hours on the build based on design guidelines from Method Studio, whose website estimated costs near $34 million. The center also holds the Gail and Jane Bradshaw Family Recital Hall, dedicated rehearsal spaces, percussion and piano labs and a commercial music and technology suite. SUU's previous music building, put up almost six decades ago for about 60 students in two programs, is less than half the new center's size; the new facility will serve more than five times as many students across 11 nationally accredited programs. Layton vice president Brian McBeth called it the best concert hall in the state, and SUU President Mindy Benson said the building gives students room to grow; design touches include a preserved landmark tree and a historic stained-glass window from a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Students explore construction careers at Taylorsville job fair
item.description: More than 600 Utah students turned out Tuesday for the We Build Utah Career Exploration and Job Fair at Salt Lake Community College's Taylorsville campus. The event connected them with more than 25 companies and let them try electrical work, forming and operating heavy machinery. Chaz Pounder, a learning and development specialist at Whitaker Construction, said trades crews are the reason basic services like running water and home heating work, while Hughes General Contractors training director Chelsea Steadman argued that buildings will never go out of style. Bob Bushell, human resources director at Ralph Wadsworth Construction, told students artificial intelligence is already playing a role in the industry but will support rather than replace workers. Organizers at Salt Lake Community College said the goal was to show students the career paths open to them in Utah; the fair ran until 1 p.m.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Driver who killed 2 people in 2021 DUI crash seeks parole for second time
item.description: Kesley Pope, now 27, went before the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole on Tuesday for the second time, five years after a fatal drunken-driving crash. Early on Halloween morning in 2021, Pope, then 22, drifted out of her lane and struck a vehicle that had run out of gas and was stopped on the shoulder of an I-15 off-ramp in Orem with its hazard lights on; Brookhaven Elementary third-grade teacher Season M. Dow, 43, and Tobias 'Toby' Dow, 16, of American Fork were killed, and Pope's blood-alcohol level measured 0.10%. She pleaded guilty to two third-degree felony counts of automobile homicide and was sentenced to consecutive terms of up to five years. Her first parole bid was denied in August 2024 partly over repeated prison rule violations; she had 12 write-ups in her first two and a half years and three since, for phone and clothing rules, with one more under review. Board member Dan Bokovoy pressed her on why she would break any rules at all and whether continued write-ups signal a lack of accountability, and Pope said the phone violations grew out of loneliness, temptation and a need for validation.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Apple's Ternus eyes engineering-led overhaul, Bloomberg News reports
item.description: Bloomberg News reported Tuesday that Apple's new chief executive, John Ternus, is considering a broad restructuring meant to sharpen the company's engineering focus, ship products more often and flatten its organization. Ideas under discussion include moving away from Apple's usual spring and fall release cadence and cutting some middle-management roles to narrow the distance between engineers and senior leadership, according to people the report cited. Ternus, a 25-year Apple veteran who ran hardware engineering through multiple iPhone generations, took over from Tim Cook this fall. The report said cost-cutting is already in motion, with the hardware engineering division trimming engineering program-management roles including about half a dozen directors, and significant reductions in teams working on Siri, the Vision Pro headset and AI software engineering, some tied to performance. Apple did not respond to a Reuters request for comment; the company recently entered the foldable market with the $1,999 Duo iPhone.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: 'Get informed': Participants in data center discussion stress importance of involvement on issue
item.description: A panel convened in Ogden to discuss data center development urged residents to get informed and involved, while expressing reservations about handing developers public incentives. Weber State University's Olene Walker Institute of Politics and Public Service and Americans for Prosperity in Utah organized the event, which came as proposals in Juab, Box Elder and Utah counties have drawn sharp debate. Entrepreneur William Olson, founder of Weber County Conservatives, told the audience to find good sources, question claims and participate, saying disagreement helps surface the right answers. Uriah Kennedy of the conservative God and Country podcast defended the facilities and warned of misinformation about them, arguing closed-loop cooling limits their water use and framing data centers as central to keeping the United States ahead of China on artificial intelligence. Ingrid Bettridge, also involved with the podcast, said taxpayers should see some benefit from the revenue such projects generate, perhaps through redevelopment in their own communities.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Did mortgage payments just get a little lower for new homebuyers?
item.description: A new Mortgage Bankers Association analysis found the national median payment sought by mortgage applicants slipped $13 in August to $2,162, down from $2,175 in July. That figure is still $62 higher than a year ago, a 2.9% increase, but the association said affordability improved modestly month over month. Edward Seiler, the group's associate vice president of housing economics, attributed the dip to a smaller median purchase loan amount offsetting higher rates and said earnings growth has outpaced payment increases over the year, though conditions remain challenging. Rates have kept rising amid economic fallout from the war against Iran, with Mortgage News Daily's index jumping 0.07 percentage points Monday to 7.5% on a 30-year fixed loan, its highest in nearly three years. Bright MLS chief economist Lisa Sturtevant told MarketWatch that 8% is not impossible but said she expects rates to stay between 7% and 7.5% this fall; the association's Purchase Applications Payment Index fell just over 1% year over year.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Hurricane Polo makes landfall in Baja California with forecast of 'life-threatening' winds
item.description: Hurricane Polo came ashore early Tuesday in Baja California as a Category 2 storm, bringing flash flooding and winds the National Hurricane Center described as life-threatening. The center in Miami said Polo struck just south of Las Barrancas with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph while moving northeast at 13 mph, and that by 6 a.m. MDT winds had dropped to near 75 mph as the storm crossed the Gulf of California, with 6 to 12 inches of rain expected across parts of Baja California Sur. Sonora's state government suspended nonessential activities including school and sports in its capital and more than a dozen municipalities, while the Mexican navy staged personnel along the northern Pacific coast and deployed three vessels to supply communities cut off by the storm. Forecasters were also tracking Tropical Storm Rachel moving parallel to Mexico's coast and Hurricane Nolo, still a Category 3 but pulling away from Hawaii. National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec said above-average Pacific activity fits the El Nino pattern, and rain from Polo was expected to reach Arizona, Utah, New Mexico and Texas later in the week.
item.dc:creator: Martin Silva Rey and Megan Janetsky, Associated Press

item.title: Utah sled hockey program reaches championship in 3rd year
item.description: The Utah Mammoth sled hockey team reached a championship game in only its third year, hosting its third annual tournament last weekend with visiting teams competing in Park City, Heber City and Sandy. Mammoth lost Sunday's final 4-2, but head coach Dave Nicholls said reaching it was a major milestone for a program still in its early years. Sled hockey lets athletes with amputations and other physical impairments play while seated on specially designed sleds, using two short sticks to move across the ice and handle the puck. Nicholls came to adaptive sports after a snowboarder traveling at what he estimated was 80 mph hit him from behind while skiing, leaving him unable to move his arms or legs; he later coached the Vegas Golden Knights sled team to two national titles before moving to build a program in Utah once the state landed an NHL franchise. Mammoth forward Wyndam Lewis credited him with bringing structure and a developmental environment, and Derek Donet of Metro Detroit Sled Hockey praised the program's progress.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Man dies after being hit by a car in Millcreek
item.description: A man died late Monday night after a vehicle struck him while he crossed a street in Millcreek. Unified Police Sgt. Aymee Race said the man was hit at 11:51 p.m. near 4100 South 700 East, outside a crosswalk, and died at the scene. The driver stayed while officers closed the road and processed the site, and Race said no alcohol was involved, though the crash remained under investigation. Race urged pedestrians to use crosswalks and pay attention to their surroundings. The man's name was withheld while his family was notified.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ unveils its new Temple Square in upcoming general conference special
item.description: The 35-acre Temple Square complex surrounding the Salt Lake Temple has been reworked alongside the temple's own renovation, and a KSL general conference special takes viewers through the result. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, and Young Women General President Emily Belle Freeman opened the new Visitors' Center to reporters in April, with Uchtdorf saying its openness lets people see how temples look inside. Donna Lawrence, who helped design the center, said the replica temple rooms are meant to introduce visitors to a building they normally cannot enter. Reporters also met the landscape designers behind the new square and artists including Stephanie and Roger Hunt, who sculpted 'Christ with Mary and Martha' and described art as a way of communicating and stirring emotion that keeps working on viewers afterward. Emily Utt, the church's curator of historical sites, noted Temple Square has been visitors' first stop in Salt Lake City since the 1870s, and the center has drawn a steady stream from Utah and abroad since opening in May.
item.dc:creator: Carole Mikita, KSL

item.title: New food preservation center in Utah could save lives worldwide
item.description: Utah company Baurau has unveiled a mobile food preservation center its founders believe could ease food insecurity abroad. Co-founder Brian Neville said he recognized the need across Africa after adopting his daughter from Ethiopia, noting that much of what farmers grow there spoils before it can be eaten. The self-contained units house food dehydration equipment and filtered water, and the concept grew out of a brick-and-mortar preservation center Baurau opened earlier this year at Lango Town Market in Kakata City, Liberia, where residents bring mangoes, pineapples, cassava, rice, peppers, fish and chicken to be preserved and packaged at no charge and where officials say 30 families come each day. Neville said a container can ship to a port and be running in under a day, handling more than 200 pounds of fresh food daily, and that the machines are projected to last 10 years without maintenance. Baurau presented the containers Monday at Harvest Right's Salt Lake City headquarters to state leaders and BYU food security researchers, with co-founder Philip Webb saying the company is internally funded and seeking collaboration rather than capital.
item.dc:creator: Brittany Tait, KSL

item.title: Lobular breast cancer awareness bus makes first tour stop at Huntsman Cancer Institute
item.description: A bus wrapped with portraits of women who have invasive lobular carcinoma made its first stop after launching in California at Huntsman Cancer Institute in Salt Lake City on Monday. Gitte Joergensen, who is traveling with the Lobular Breast Cancer Alliance, had been getting mammograms and ultrasounds for nearly two years before a radiologist ordered an MRI that found the cancer the earlier imaging missed; she was diagnosed in March 2020 and had a double mastectomy, and said she had never heard of lobular cancer before. The disease accounts for roughly 10% to 15% of invasive breast cancer diagnoses and affects nearly 50,000 people in the U.S. each year, yet an alliance survey found four in five Americans were unfamiliar with it, in part because it often grows without forming a distinct lump that shows on a mammogram. Executive director Laurie Hutcheson, whose own cancer went undetected for nearly 12 years, said the rolling billboard is meant to push for more research and point patients to resources. Carla Lloyd of Huntsman's Breast and Gynecologic Cancers Research Advocate Committee said local research gives patients reason for optimism; the tour visits 15 cities over 21 days and ends Oct. 15 in Denver's wake on Lobular Breast Cancer Awareness Day.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Hope rises from tragedy: Ground broken for new church meetinghouse in Grand Blanc
item.description: Exactly one year after an attack destroyed a Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints meetinghouse in Grand Blanc, Michigan, and killed four people, community members returned to the site Monday for a groundbreaking. On Sept. 28, 2025, a gunman drove his truck into the building, opened fire and set it ablaze, shaking the small community and leaving lasting marks on survivors. Stake President Marcelino Sanchez asked that the dedication of the ground also be an occasion to dedicate lives to Jesus Christ, and a rendering unveiled at the ceremony showed the stake center that will replace what was lost, with construction expected to take about 14 months. The Frampton family, who were inside during the shooting and fire, called the new building the best thing possible; Lindsey Frampton said she is still struck by overwhelming gratitude that her family came through, and she and Bridger Frampton described more faith than fear and more gratitude than grief. Elder Joni L. Koch, a General Authority Seventy, said those gathered felt united, and Bridger Frampton called the site sacred ground once again.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Kokanee Salmon bring fall deep reds to Northern Utah streams
item.description: Kokanee salmon are turning bright red and spawning in northern Utah waters, adding fall color to streams as well as trees. The fish are especially visible in spawning traps run by Utah's Division of Wildlife Resources next to the Strawberry Reservoir visitor's center. The Jensen family stopped there Monday on their way home to Salt Lake City from a camping trip, and Alyssa Jensen said that despite living in Utah her whole life she had not known the spawning run was a thing. DWR cold water sportfish coordinator Trina Hedrick said the crowds have grown each year and asked visitors to view from a distance and stay out of the creeks so they do not disturb the eggs. Hedrick expects peak spawning to continue for another couple of weeks, with some fish visible in lower-elevation streams into early November; the DWR publishes a list of recommended viewing spots.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Douglas Carter granted release on bail after 41 years behind bars
item.description: A 4th District judge set conditions rather than keeping Douglas Carter locked up, ordering a GPS monitor, an 11 p.m. curfew, employment and a reentry program as the 71-year-old leaves custody for the first time in 41 years. Judge Derek Pullan wrote that a DNA report excluding Carter from several crime-scene samples had badly eroded the evidence he leaned on when he denied bail earlier in September, though he found enough remained for a jury to weigh. Prosecutors dropped their pursuit of the death penalty last week and asked the judge to consider pretrial release. Pullan reasoned that because Carter has already served roughly 40 years without discipline problems, a life sentence on conviction would be unlikely to add much time, substantially cutting his incentive to flee. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton, who counted 15,085 days since the arrest, is pressing prosecutors to dismiss the case outright and stipulate to a finding of innocence.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Former 'American Idol' singer Caleb Flynn is on trial in wife's killing. He says a burglar did it
item.description: Closing arguments are set for Tuesday in the Ohio murder trial of Caleb Flynn, a 40-year-old former music pastor and "American Idol" contestant accused of killing his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old schoolteacher and volleyball coach, at their Tipp City home in February. He has pleaded not guilty to murder, assault and tampering with evidence; prosecutors say he staged a home invasion and told a 911 dispatcher that a burglar had shot her, and he and the couple's two daughters were home when police arrived. Alleigha Botner, 24, testified over two days that she began an affair with Flynn in 2022 as a 20-year-old intern at his church and that it ran more than a year. Jurors heard AI-generated love songs that prosecutors say Flynn made for her, along with portions of more than 100,000 text messages authorities say the two exchanged. Botner said Flynn told her he hated his wife and stayed only because of their daughters, and she wept on the stand over her own message saying she wanted the wife dead.
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press

item.title: Federal employee accused of fraudulently obtaining $50k disability pay while hiking abroad
item.description: Michelle L. Bouziden, a 44-year-old assistant special agent in charge at the USDA Office of Inspector General, hiked nearly 60 miles of Italy's Dolomites over eight days while telling the Department of Labor she could not sit, walk, climb or drive, according to a newly unsealed federal indictment. The Ogden woman suffered an on-the-job concussion in March and was told to rest completely; when her May return date arrived, she instead reported her symptoms were the "worst ever." Prosecutors with the U.S. Attorney's Office for Utah say she collected more than $50,000 in disability pay while publishing her trips and strenuous hikes on social media. The indictment also accuses her of twice canceling a required independent medical evaluation over "wellness retreat" conflicts, once going on to hike Colorado's Quandary Peak Trail instead.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Australia's Megaport wins $687 million AI infrastructure deals, raises 2027 earnings forecast
item.description: Australian IT company Megaport told investors Tuesday it has signed three new AI infrastructure contracts worth a combined A$978.6 million, or about $686.78 million. The agreements, with customers the company did not name, cover GPU and CPU compute along with network and storage for AI applications and inference workloads, and are expected to add roughly A$232.4 million in annual recurring revenue. They follow four similar contracts totalling A$458.9 million that Megaport landed in early June. On the strength of the deals the company raised its full-year group revenue guidance to between A$720 million and A$810 million, up from A$620 million to A$730 million, and now expects an EBITDA margin of 42% to 44% rather than 38% to 40%.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: 'Believed in the mission': Utah Olympic leader remembered after passing
item.description: A logo set beneath the ice at the Utah Olympic Oval in Kearns now honors Colin Hilton, the Utah Olympic Legacy Foundation president and CEO who died by suicide last month at 58. Chief revenue officer Lisa Bennion Rasmussen, who worked alongside him for more than a decade, credits his long view with bringing the 2034 Winter Games back to Utah, saying he never treated the bid as a 17-day event. Hilton spent decades keeping the 2002 venues open to the public while building out training facilities for elite athletes. His Healthy Communities program, launched in 2018 to open winter sports to children regardless of age or ability, has grown from 750 participants to more than 3,200.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Senate nears vote on college sports bill that would rein in athlete payments and transfers
item.description: More than 70 senators from both parties are behind a bill the Senate was poised to pass Monday that would set national rules for college athlete name, image and likeness payments and limit how often players can transfer. The legislation would hand the NCAA new authority over those rules along with limited antitrust protection to enforce them, and would write the 2025 lawsuit settlement that let schools pay athletes into federal law. Senate Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who negotiated the package with Washington Democrat Maria Cantwell, argued that only Congress can fix a system that will not fix itself. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., working with labor and civil rights groups, countered that the bill entrenches exploitation without touching the money flowing to coaches, colleges and conferences. A vote slipped by several hours Monday evening amid last-minute negotiations, and the measure would still need to clear the House.
item.dc:creator: Mary Clare Jalonick, Joey Cappelletti and Eddie Pells, Associated Press

item.title: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li's World Labs in $8.2 billion bet on 'physical AI'
item.description: Advanced Micro Devices said Monday it will acquire World Labs, the AI startup founded by computer vision researcher Fei-Fei Li, in an all-stock transaction valued at $8.2 billion. The deal gives AMD a position in spatial intelligence, an emerging field focused on letting AI systems model three-dimensional environments and physical interactions, with potential uses in robotics, simulation and design. Li wrote on LinkedIn that a technical partnership begun last year around model training and inference optimization on AMD GPUs made joining the two companies a natural fit; AMD had also invested in World Labs' $1 billion funding round earlier this year. She will become executive vice president and chief scientist at AMD, reporting to CEO Lisa Su, once the transaction closes, which the company expects by the end of 2026.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: FanX wraps up ahead of years-long Salt Palace renovation
item.description: FanX will return in 2027 as two half-capacity events rather than one full-size convention, the first of them running March 11 through March 14. That downshift follows the 2026 Salt Lake Comic Convention, which closed Sunday as the last full-scale FanX the Salt Palace Convention Center will host for some time. Redevelopment work on the convention center itself is expected to begin in the fall of 2027.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Rep. Trevor Lee charged with fraud, resigns from Utah House
item.description: Rep. Trevor Lee, R-Layton, resigned from the Utah House effective immediately, sending his letter to the speaker within hours of the Utah Attorney General's Office filing criminal charges against him Monday in 3rd District Court. The 35-year-old, who had represented Davis County's House District 16 since 2023, faces second-degree felony counts of communications fraud and mortgage fraud plus third-degree felony forgery and possession of a forging device. Charging documents say loan paperwork for his new home listed him as a Blue Logic sales director earning $15,833 a month and as an Enevive employee earning $13,761 a month, but Blue Logic told investigators Lee never accepted its offer and had asked for an inaccurate letter as a favor, while Enevive called its purported employment contract fraudulent with a forged signature. A video cited in the charges has Enevive's CEO saying Lee sought $93,000 in cash advances to inflate his income and promised in return to secure the company a contract with Hill Air Force Base. Lee's resignation letter attributed his departure to "personal circumstances" requiring his attention.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL; Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: 2026 marks Utah's worst fire season in nearly 20 years
item.description: More than 500,000 acres burned across Utah this year, from the southern part of the state up into the Uintas, making 2026 the worst fire season in close to two decades according to figures newly published by Utah State University. Three of this year's blazes, the Widemouth 2, Babylon and Cottonwood fires, now rank among the ten largest Utah has recorded since 2002. The season killed four firefighters and two pilots and destroyed more than 200 structures. Wildfire specialists said a strengthening El Nino could bring a snowier winter and ease drought pressure heading into next year.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Fabbi, KSL

item.title: USU school of business to acquire new dean in 2027. Here's what she's planning
item.description: Valentina Salotti takes over as dean of Utah State University's Jon M. Huntsman School of Business on Jan. 1, 2027, arriving from Iowa State, where she is senior associate dean for academic affairs in the Ivy College of Business. She told the university community at a Sept. 18 reception in Logan that moving between two land grant research institutions mattered to her, because the land grant mission centers on creating opportunities for students and serving communities. Salotti, a first-generation college student herself, said she sees her own experience reflected in the students she works with. A visit to Logan helped seal the decision; she described Huntsman students as a happy group visibly doing more than just attending class. Her stated priorities include student success and internships, research, closer ties to Utah industry, and more collaboration between the business school and other programs on campus.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Pennsylvania measles cases cross 900 as outbreak grows
item.description: Pennsylvania's measles total reached 903 on Monday, up 68 since the previous Wednesday, in what state health department data shows is the worst resurgence there in decades. Hospitalizations climbed to 176 from the 164 reported on Sept. 23, and Lancaster County remains the hardest-hit part of the state. Four unvaccinated residents died earlier this month, prompting a public disagreement between Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over how many of those deaths the virus directly caused; the CDC then said it was reviewing how it classifies measles deaths, and its site now lists one verified death without specifying where. Nationally, the CDC counted 3,659 measles cases as of Sept. 24. Two doses of the routine MMR vaccine give about 97% protection against a disease that can bring fever, rash and respiratory complications.
item.dc:creator: Christy Santhosh, Reuters

item.title: SpaceX's Starship makes orbital debut deploying Starlinks before early ending
item.description: SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on its 14th test flight Monday and deployed new Starlink satellites, but controllers cut the mission from a planned 10 hours to about three. One of the upper stage's three main engines shut down early after separation from the Super Heavy booster, prompting a SpaceX spokesperson to announce mid-stream that orbit was out of reach before the team reversed course. The booster splashed down under engine control in Gulf waters after hard landings on the two previous flights, though SpaceX said some of its engines quit during descent. Because the flight carried millions of dollars of Starlink hardware, it doubled as Starship's first revenue-generating mission even with the vehicle's final design still unsettled. SpaceX shares fell 2% on the day; the newly public company was valued at $2 trillion as of Friday's close.
item.dc:creator: Joey Roulette and Steve Nesius, Reuters

item.title: Foundation hosts 'Utah Unsolved Day' for families of missing persons
item.description: Investigators from more than a dozen law enforcement agencies sat down with families of missing and murdered Utahns on Saturday at the first "Utah Unsolved Day," hosted by the Sherry Black Foundation. The Utah Department of Public Safety, the Office of the Medical Examiner and the state crime lab also sent representatives. Foundation executive director Erin Ryan said the point was to put the legislative and investigative work behind cold cases directly in front of the families it affects.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: 2 Utah musicians celebrate major career milestone
item.description: Two violinists trained at the Diana & Joel Peterson School of Music in Salt Lake City came through a multi-day audition this spring to win section seats with the Utah Symphony, Karen Ferry among them. The school operated as the Gifted Music School until its recent renaming, and its alumnae credit it with supplying both the instruction and the peer community that made a professional orchestra job feel attainable. Mentoring the next group of players is now on their minds, along with pressing the case for arts education funding across the state.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: Tooele rescuers find dog that ventured into mine
item.description: A dog is back with its family after wandering into a Tooele County mine on Sunday and getting stuck. Officials said the animal made its way inside and then could not find a route back out. Rescue crews reached it underground and brought it up unharmed.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: Shein quarterly profit falls 67% as costs jump, Europe sales slump
item.description: Shein's first results as a public company showed adjusted net profit of $228 million for the quarter ended in June, down 67% year over year, with margin squeezed to 2.1% from 6.2% as Middle East conflict pushed up jet fuel and freight costs for its air-shipped clothing. European revenue fell 13.9% to $3.77 billion after the retailer raised prices and cut online advertising ahead of the EU's 3-euro fee on low-value parcels that took effect July 1, while US revenue slid 6% to $2.5 billion. Growth in Latin America kept overall sales barely positive at $11.08 billion, up 0.9%. Jefferies analysts estimated earnings landed more than 10% below the bottom of the range implied by the IPO prospectus and flagged an 18.1% jump in fulfillment costs as a worry. CEO and Chair Yangtian Xu said stocking more inventory in Europe is a priority and signaled a push into higher-priced clothing; the shares have dropped 27.3% from their HK$48.56 offer price since debuting in Hong Kong on Sept. 1.
item.dc:creator: Helen Reid, Reuters

item.title: Two arrested in southern Utah after woman zip-tied to bed for two days, police say
item.description: San Juan County sheriff's deputies arrested two men after a woman found along U.S. 191 told them relatives had held her captive and zip-tied her to a bunk bed for as long as two days. Nathan Andrew Spaulding, 30, and Paul Robert Mark, 25, were booked early Sunday for investigation of kidnapping, aggravated assault, being restricted persons in possession of a weapon and drug offenses, with Spaulding also accused of obstruction of justice and Mark of witness tampering. A booking affidavit describes bruises and cuts on the woman's face and mouth and marks on her wrists consistent with being restrained, and says Mark forced her to take a white powder to keep her awake for days at a stretch. She told deputies Mark tried to stab her in the stomach and cut her hand with a knife, and that a rag was held in her mouth by zip ties wrapped around her head. Deputies say that before search warrants were served on the trailers where the men live, Mark texted her instructing her to tell police he had not kidnapped her; the affidavit does not explain how she got away.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: How to support someone who's suicidal
item.description: Dr. Christine Moutier, chief medical officer of the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, says people who are worried about someone often find a reason to turn away rather than move toward them, for reasons ranging from stigma to the well-meaning but mistaken fear that raising the subject will make matters worse. Suicide stays hidden in ordinary ways, including obituaries that obscure a cause of death. CDC figures put U.S. suicide deaths at nearly 48,900 in 2024, while the World Health Organization counts more than 720,000 worldwide each year and ranks suicide the third-leading cause of death globally among people aged 15 to 29. The CDC also estimated that in 2024 about 14.3 million American adults seriously considered suicide, 4.6 million made a plan and 2.2 million attempted, numbers Moutier reads as a large number of openings to intervene. She notes that many would-be helpers struggle to hold two ideas at once: a responsibility to offer support, and the fact that they are not at fault if someone dies anyway.
item.dc:creator: Kristen Rogers, CNN

item.title: On National Public Lands Day, Salt Lake mayor thanks major donor
item.description: More than $11 million from the Bezos Earth Fund will go toward Salt Lake City's 9 Line Trail and the adjacent Fleet Block, and Mayor Erin Mendenhall used Saturday's National Public Lands Day event to thank the donor for it. Stretches that are bare gravel now will get more than 280 trees, water-wise plantings and places to sit, she said. Mendenhall made the case for the spending in traffic terms: roughly 3,600 cyclists and pedestrians use the corridor each month, adding up to about half a million people a year. The trail itself runs along a former rail line on 900 South, reaching from 200 West out to the Jordan River Surplus Canal, and the city made the grant public earlier this summer.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: SpaceX's supersized Starship launches into orbit for the first time but flight ends early
item.description: Starship splashed down in the Pacific north of Hawaii about three hours after leaving Texas on Monday, tipping over and erupting in flames at the end of a flight SpaceX cut short from a planned 10 hours and six orbits. The vehicle nearly failed to reach orbit at all when one of its engines shut down too soon, but with the rest working and the failed engine no longer needed, controllers decided after several tense minutes to press on, and Mission Control announced "Starship is orbital" to cheers. The spacecraft released 26 of the newest Starlink satellites one at a time, joining roughly 11,000 older units already carrying internet traffic. SpaceX gave no reason for ending the flight early. It was the 14th full-scale Starship launch in three years from the southern tip of Texas and the first to go beyond the suborbital hops that had ended around the Indian Ocean; NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praised the company for handling every step safely and responsibly.
item.dc:creator: Marcia Dunn, Associated Press

item.title: Tooele County man accused of spending $16K of mother's money on booze, hotels
item.description: A church ward's request for help covering an elderly woman's bills led Tooele County investigators to her son, now accused of draining her pension on hotel rooms and alcohol. Joshua Duane Dean, 47, of Grantsville was booked into the Tooele County Jail on Saturday for investigation of financial exploitation of a vulnerable adult. Church officials who reviewed the woman's finances found a pension that should have covered her needs but left her with rent money and little or nothing for food, according to a police booking affidavit. Detectives examining seven months of bank records counted more than $16,000 spent between September 2025 and March, including 96 days of hotel stays, though the woman had allowed Dean to use her debit card for some purchases. The affidavit says Dean told officers on the way to jail that he had not realized it had gotten that bad, and that additional months of records have yet to be reviewed.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow restrictions on transgender inmates
item.description: The Justice Department filed an emergency application at the Supreme Court on Monday asking it to lift U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order barring the Federal Bureau of Prisons from enforcing a policy that restricts gender-affirming care for transgender inmates while a legal challenge proceeds. Issued in February, the policy bans medical and surgical treatment along with any "social accommodations," including items that could be used to alter appearance in line with gender identity, though psychiatric services would remain available. It reverses earlier procedures under which inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria could receive gender-affirming treatment when clinically indicated. The request follows a first-day executive order in January 2025 that recognized only male and female sexes and directed agencies, the Bureau of Prisons among them, to rewrite policies and halt funding for such care. The court's 6-3 conservative majority has ruled against transgender rights repeatedly over the past year, including backing state laws barring transgender athletes from female sports teams at public schools and universities.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Chung, Reuters

item.title: Teen girl dies after Syracuse motorcycle crash
item.description: A 17-year-old girl riding a motorcycle east on Antelope Drive in Syracuse died Sunday after colliding with a passenger vehicle heading north through the intersection at 1250 West. Syracuse police said in a Monday statement that responders treated her at the scene before she was taken to Davis Holy Cross Hospital and then airlifted to Primary Children's Hospital, where she was pronounced dead after arrival. The woman driving the other vehicle remained at the scene and cooperated with investigators. Police said they have a preliminary understanding of what happened but will not speculate about contributing factors until the investigation is finished.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: 'This was my worst nightmare': Camper home a total loss following fire
item.description: Tristin Perkins and her mother were both at work Sunday when the camper they lived in at a Lakepoint RV park caught fire with Perkins' four dogs inside. A neighbor who was home let the dogs out while the park's front desk called Perkins, and she said all four animals and both women came through unhurt. Firefighters suspect a loose wire on the camper's furnace sparked the blaze, though the cause remains under investigation. Perkins had moved in only two days earlier and lost everything she owned; the park refunded her deposit, which she put toward a week in a hotel while friends helped with food and the dogs. An online GoFundMe fundraiser has been set up to help her restart.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Nvidia sets biggest-ever buyback plan as AI chip competition weighs on stock performance
item.description: Nvidia added a record $150 billion to its share repurchase authorization, eclipsing the $110 billion Apple approved in 2024 and lifting its remaining buyback capacity to $235 billion, which it expects to deploy through fiscal 2028. The Santa Clara chipmaker's stock rose more than 2% on the news; through Friday it was up just over 20% for the year, broadly matching the Nasdaq 100 but trailing AMD, which has more than doubled, and Intel, which has more than tripled. Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne read the move as Nvidia signaling that demand for its hardware and services has staying power even though the AI buildout will not keep its current pace forever. Quilter Cheviot's Ben Barringer compared it to Apple's playbook of using repurchases to support a stock as growth slows and valuation multiples compress. Nvidia was trading around 16.5 times forward earnings, its lowest multiple since January 2015 and far below a 15-year average of 30, according to LSEG data.
item.dc:creator: Anhata Rooprai, Reuters

item.title: Firefighter identified as BASE jumper who died in Cache County
item.description: The Salt Lake City Fire Department confirmed Monday that Gabe Reilly, the 27-year-old killed in a wingsuit BASE jump in Cache County on Sunday, was one of its firefighters and the son of a department member who retired in 2024. Reilly was jumping from a 700-foot cliff east of Millville Canyon near Leetham's Hollow with a group of eight to 10 people when, at 9:10 a.m., his wingsuit failed to generate enough lift, according to the Cache County Sheriff's Office. Search and rescue crews reached him and he was declared dead at the scene, with a Life Flight helicopter called to carry him out of the area. He had served four years with the department, which remembered him as free-spirited and known for his smile and kindness.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Trump's AI meeting with tech CEOs to focus on finding balance, US House speaker says
item.description: House Speaker Mike Johnson, who will attend President Donald Trump's Tuesday White House meeting with technology CEOs, said the session will be about balancing innovation against oversight rather than imposing new limits on artificial intelligence. Speaking to Fox Business Network on Monday, Johnson rejected calls for a moratorium or heavy regulation, arguing that would cost the U.S. its race with China, while allowing that transparency and some oversight are needed and that the Justice Department may have a role if things go wrong. The meeting comes as leading AI companies themselves press for slowing development of ever more capable systems and ask governments to coordinate on managing the technology. Trump has played down concerns about misuse, emphasizing competitiveness and saying existing guardrails, including at the Justice Department, are already sufficient. Lawmakers in both parties have questioned that hands-off posture, with House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries noting that industry leaders are themselves asking for government action.
item.dc:creator: Katharine Jackson, Reuters

item.title: ER doc comes to the rescue of his financially troubled peers
item.description: Jim Dahle's irritation with a financial adviser during his emergency medicine residency in Tucson, when he realized he was paying both a fee and a commission on the stocks he bought, became the seed of The White Coat Investor, his project to help doctors stop doing dumb things with their money. Fresh out of University of Utah Medical School and working nights, Dahle had his days free, and he filled them with secondhand finance books bought across the street from the apartment he shared with his wife, Katie. Looking back over his dealings with financial professionals, he concluded he had to learn the subject himself or keep being taken advantage of. Through the rest of his residency and four years repaying the Air Force for his medical schooling, he taught himself, testing investing ideas on internet forums with other physicians during lonely deployments abroad.
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: Powerful nor'easter floods Northeast again, causing problems from New Jersey to New England
item.description: Coastal communities from New Jersey to New England waded through a second day of flooding Sunday as a slow-moving nor'easter knocked out power to tens of thousands of homes. Tidal surges swamped low-lying New Jersey neighborhoods while wind gusts brought down trees and utility poles on Long Island, damaging houses. In the beach town of Sea Bright, Caroline Virenius described about a foot of water in her garage and flooding that returned with each high tide. More than 4 inches of rain since Friday in parts of New Jersey, combined with a surging ocean, produced water levels residents said they had not seen in close to a decade; a New York City Housing Authority worker was killed Saturday by a falling tree. Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman warned of another, weaker band still to come, and officials cautioned that Monday's late high tide could bring more flooding even as the National Weather Service expected the system to weaken overnight.
item.dc:creator: Leah Willingham and John Seewer, Associated Press

item.title: Sandy shooting leaves 1 man dead, teen injured, second teen arrested
item.description: A man was killed and a teenage boy wounded in a shooting inside a home near 9700 S. 1200 East in Sandy on Sunday afternoon, and a second teenage boy was taken into custody at the scene. Sandy police said officers who arrived around 12:30 p.m. detained one juvenile without incident, then entered and found the man dead of an apparent gunshot wound and the other teen shot in the leg. That teen was hospitalized and reported stable on Monday. Police said everyone involved is related and lived in the same house, but had not released the victim's identity, the boys' ages or a possible motive as of Monday morning.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Exclusive-Bridgepoint, Astorg consider £2 billion-plus Fenergo sale, sources say
item.description: Bridgepoint and Astorg are weighing a sale of Fenergo, the Dublin-based compliance software firm, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, with one putting a possible valuation above £2 billion, or about $2.7 billion. The private equity owners have already held talks with potential buyers and are expected to appoint an investment bank later this year, with a formal process possibly launching in early 2027, though two sources said no decision has been made. Fenergo's software helps more than 300 of the world's largest banks and insurers handle onboarding, know-your-customer checks and other client lifecycle and regulatory work, and it has added an agentic AI platform to automate some of those workflows. Revenue rose 7.5% to €149.4 million for the year ending March 2025 on subscription growth and client renewals. Astorg and Bridgepoint bought the company from Insight Partners in 2021 for an undisclosed sum, and the sources expect information services companies and exchange operators to take a look.
item.dc:creator: Amy-Jo Crowley, Reuters

item.title: Trump to unveil planned $15 billion Iowa steel project
item.description: President Donald Trump planned to announce Monday at the White House that Minnesota-based Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, according to a White House official, with company executives on hand. The operation would be fully vertically integrated, feeding iron ore from Mesabi's Minnesota mine, the state's first new iron ore mine in 50 years, into steelmaking in Iowa. A first phase would turn out 7.5 million tons of steel a year, rising eventually to 10 million tons, which the White House described as the largest steel plant in U.S. history. The official put the Minnesota mine at a $2.5 billion investment supporting roughly 350 jobs, with the Iowa plant expected to create at least 1,750 permanent positions plus 5,000 to 6,000 construction jobs in its first phase. The administration is promoting the project as evidence of reshored manufacturing ahead of November's midterm elections; the Wall Street Journal reported the plan first.
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Renshaw, Reuters

item.title: Commercial structure caught fire in Salt Lake City
item.description: Cleanup began Monday at an abandoned downtown Salt Lake City building at 356 W. 700 South that burned Sunday, drawing more than 50 firefighters and producing no injuries. Fire Capt. Matthew Wilson said the structure was a patchwork of additions built over the years, creating void spaces that concealed the fire and made it hard to reach. Crews worked defensively from outside rather than going in, and overhead power lines complicated attacking the blaze from ladders. A nearby apartment building was partially evacuated as a precaution and traffic was disrupted; it was not clear Monday whether residents had been allowed back. The cause was still under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL; Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: A national education survey ranks Utah dead last — and that's a good thing
item.description: Utah placed 51st out of 51 in WalletHub's "States with the Most Student Debt in 2026" ranking, which in this case is the desirable end of the list. The analysis compared the 50 states and the District of Columbia across a dozen measures of student loan indebtedness; Mississippi topped it, followed by Delaware, Pennsylvania, South Carolina and West Virginia, while Hawaii, California, Washington and New Mexico joined Utah among the least indebted. WalletHub reported outstanding student loan balances above $1.72 trillion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, working out to more than $40,000 apiece across 42.6 million borrowers. Analyst Chip Lupo noted that federal student loan interest rates recently hit a 12-year high and have stayed elevated, making careful planning more important for borrowers. The simplest explanation for Utah's standing is cost: the state ranked No. 5 in a 2026 U.S. News & World Report measure of average in-state tuition and fees.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Utah communities embrace America 250 celebration in a big way
item.description: A new 30-minute KSL documentary, "Utah Celebrates America 250," gathers scenes from a year of events marking the nation's 250th anniversary across the state, from colonial reenactments and naturalization ceremonies to service projects and veteran tributes. Nicole Handy, executive director of America250 Utah, said the enthusiasm around the state has been striking. Cove Allen, president of the Colonial Heritage Foundation, said his living-history events aim to send people home wanting to be better Americans. The film follows a naturalization ceremony where U.S. District Judge Kevin R. Anderson welcomed new citizens, among them Maria Tejedor, who arrived in the country at age two and said her family had waited a long time. It also traces Kearns resident Richard Moseley's trip to France to honor his father, Utah World War II pilot Lonnie Moseley, who crash-landed in Nazi-occupied territory and was sheltered by a farmer who risked his own life.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: California sheriff unlawfully seized over 650,000 ballots and must return them, state Supreme Court rules
item.description: The California Supreme Court ruled unanimously against Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco in two cases, finding he broke state election law by having deputies seize more than 650,000 ballots tied to the Proposition 50 special election. The justices ordered him to end his election fraud investigation, return the ballots to county elections officials and otherwise stop handling them, writing that the statute plainly requires voted ballots to remain in elections officials' custody. Bianco, who lost his bid for California governor in the primaries, had described the seizure as a fact-finding mission prompted by a local group's complaint about roughly 45,800 votes it said were unaccounted for. The proposition at issue approved a redistricting measure shifting five California Republican U.S. House seats toward Democrats ahead of this year's midterms.
