Attorney General Rob Bonta, whose directives the court said Bianco ignored, was among the challengers, along with UCLA's Voting Rights Project, whose lawsuit produced the ruling, and Riverside leaders who petitioned for the ballots' return.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Rodriguez, Chelsea Hylton, KOVR

item.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo
item.description: Hurricane Nolo pulled away from the Hawaiian Islands on Sunday with maximum sustained winds near 105 mph, but high-wind and high-surf advisories stayed in force on parts of the Big Island through the evening. Forecasters warned the storm's outer bands could still bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with up to 20 inches of rain possible in places. National Hurricane Center director Michael Brennan urged residents to stay off the roads, citing downed trees and power lines as much as the water. More than 120 National Guard members were activated on the island out of roughly 400 statewide under the governor's emergency proclamation, and President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration opening FEMA assistance to a community still recovering from Hurricane Lala. Meanwhile, Mexico's Baja Peninsula braced for Category 3 Hurricane Polo, with 125 mph winds, to arrive Monday after it raked the country's southwest coast.
item.dc:creator: Eugene Garcia and Gregory Bull, Associated Press

item.title: The Campus Cup is back — and UVU and BYU are already battling for it
item.description: Utah's Campus Cup, a statewide contest launched in 2012 by then-Lt. Gov. Greg Bell, is running again, with schools scoring points for voter registrations submitted through their own links and for promoting registration on campus. Turnout among voters aged 18 to 24 was the lowest of any age group in the last presidential election at 47.7%, the gap the competition was built to close. Utah Valley University won in 2024 with more than 2,500 registrations, ahead of BYU's 2,000-plus, then Utah State, Weber State, Southern Utah and Salt Lake Community College. Justin Jones, executive director of UVU's nonpartisan Gary R. Herbert Institute, said the aim is broader student engagement, whether that means registering, voting, supporting a campaign or taking an internship, and that government works better with more young voices in it. BYU voter registration specialist Courtney Rockwood framed voting as students' first look into adulthood and their first real say in their own communities.
item.dc:creator: Reagan Campbell, Deseret News

item.title: Cutting these types of foods may ease depression symptoms
item.description: A UC San Francisco pilot study published this week in JAMA Psychiatry found that people with depression who cut back on ultra-processed foods showed moderate to large improvements across three measures of depression, with anxiety scores improving modestly as well. Participants reduced their intake of such foods by more than 85%, according to a university news release; the NIH-funded work involved just 20 people. Senior author Dr. Andrew Krystal, a professor in UCSF's psychiatry and neurology departments, said the main achievement was establishing that a larger trial is workable, and the university plans to enroll a much bigger group in 2028. Ultra-processed foods, a category stretching from cookies and chips to hot dogs, white bread and frozen meals, make up a large share of the typical American diet and drew a clear thumbs-down in the federal government's new dietary guidelines.
item.dc:creator: Lois M. Collins, Deseret News

item.title: Donation, support of administration, keep Alzheimer's drug crusade alive at University of Utah
item.description: Two unexpected developments have revived University of Utah neuroscientist Donna Cross's effort to move a repurposed cancer drug toward human trials for Alzheimer's and other brain diseases. Cross has shown that Paclitaxel reverses brain injury in mice, but when the mouse trials ended two years ago she had no money to fund a next stage. A man in the Northwest who came across coverage of her research while scrolling the news, which traveled as far as the UK's Daily Mirror, contacted her and gave $450,000 with no conditions; his wife has Alzheimer's, and Cross's own motivation traces to her grandmother's dementia. Separately, a senior University of Utah administrator offered to advocate for institutional support, drawing on her own history: 17 years ago, while living with multiple sclerosis, she was treated for breast cancer with a drug cocktail that included Paclitaxel and came out of it free of both conditions. She has stayed free of MS ever since and believes the Paclitaxel is the reason.
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: AI is changing how Americans choose snacks, says Conagra
item.description: Shoppers are increasingly putting the question of what to eat to an AI assistant, and they tend to ask for an attribute — more protein, more fiber — rather than a brand, Conagra Brands told Reuters. The company behind Slim Jim and Hunt's commissioned research firm Circana to work through more than 53 million transactions spanning 17,000 products in a US snacking market worth $198.2 billion a year and expanding about 1.4 times as fast as food overall. Bob Nolan, Conagra's senior vice president of growth science, argued that the six years since the pandemic have reshaped American eating habits more than the preceding half-century, with weight-loss drugs and the White House's "Make America Healthy Again" push accelerating the move toward nutrient-dense options. That shift has come at the expense of cookies and salty snacks, which Nolan said are under pressure. Younger buyers, Gen Z in particular, are separately driving demand for sweet-and-spicy, tangy and briny flavors.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Marrow, Reuters

item.title: Man hospitalized after falling while hiking Mount Timpanogos
item.description: A man in his 30s was flown to a hospital Sunday after falling on Mount Timpanogos. The Utah County Sheriff's Office, which reported the accident on Facebook, placed the fall at about 12:30 p.m. and said he suffered multiple injuries. KSL published the account as preliminary.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: BASE jumper dies after wingsuit failure in Cache County
item.description: A 27-year-old man died Sunday morning in Cache County when his wingsuit failed to generate enough lift during a BASE jump, according to the Cache County Sheriff's Office. He was jumping from a 700-foot cliff east of Millville Canyon, near Leetham's Hollow outside Hyrum, as part of a group of eight to 10 jumpers, and the sheriff's office placed the accident at 9:10 a.m. Cache County Search and Rescue reached the site, and a Life Flight helicopter was brought in to remove him from the terrain. The sheriff's office thanked the county fire and search-and-rescue crews along with the Life Flight and Department of Public Safety aircrews, and offered condolences to the man's family. Investigators characterized him as an experienced jumper.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Agency says sea turtle eggs laid on California beaches are a first for the US West Coast
item.description: Lifeguards patrolling a southern California beach at night assumed the turtle struggling in the sand was ill; it was in fact laying eggs, in what the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's West Coast Fisheries division calls the first recorded natural nesting by any sea turtle species on the US West Coast. The first nest turned up near Seal Beach on Sept. 16, and a second — possibly from the same olive ridley — appeared three days later near the Huntington Beach Pier in Orange County. Both sites have been fenced off, and NOAA puts incubation at 45 to 60 days. Olive ridleys are the smallest sea turtles, topping out around 100 pounds, and are usually found in tropical Pacific, Indian and Atlantic waters. Trevor McDonald, marine safety chief for the Huntington Beach Fire Department, said the discovery has the department excited, while onlookers expressed hope the nests survive tides, storms and the beach's heavy event schedule.
item.dc:creator: Eugene Garcia and Ed White, Associated Press

item.title: Scientists map gene activity in brain's prefrontal cortex
item.description: Nine studies published Wednesday in Nature and other journals chart gene activity across the prefrontal cortex, the region behind the forehead that governs planning, decision-making and emotional regulation. Researchers profiled the nuclei of more than 6.3 million cells — neurons, immune cells, vascular cells and support cells — taken from 1,494 deceased donors ranging from infancy to age 108 and spanning varied genetic ancestries, some with no diagnosed brain condition and others with Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Dr. Panos Roussos of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who helped lead the work, said the value of the map is in narrowing the search for treatment targets by showing which cell populations are vulnerable and which biological processes track with preserved function. The data suggest heavy molecular change through development, a plateau beginning around age 24, and renewed change late in life concentrated in immune and support cells — though Roussos cautioned that the brain does not stop developing on a particular birthday. The work came out of the PsychAD consortium with funding from the National Institute on Aging.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: 'We love this building': Constant care preserves Salt Lake Tabernacle's craftsmanship and sound
item.description: The Salt Lake Tabernacle's domed roof and oval floor plan were an acoustic solution rather than a stylistic one, designed so crowds could hear a speaker before amplification existed. Emily Utt, historic sites curator for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, traces the structure to Brigham Young's 1847 call for a shared gathering place; an open-air bowery came first, then an 1857 building that let crews rehearse techniques before the current tabernacle hosted its first meeting in 1867 and was dedicated in 1875. Builders drew sandstone from Red Butte Canyon and timber from City Creek Canyon, and painted pine columns to imitate red marble — work Utt reads as evidence that pioneer tradesmen wanted the building to be beautiful, not merely functional. The room's sound is now inseparable from the Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square and an organ of more than 11,600 pipes, and Utt goes so far as to call the building the choir's 361st member. Daily pin-drop demonstrations, a practice dating to the 1870s, still draw thousands of visitors.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Tornado sparks preparedness reminder for Davis County families
item.description: A tornado that crossed Davis County last week sent local families to Saturday's Davis County Emergency Preparedness Fair at Western Sports Park in Farmington. Centerville resident Luke Ruoti, who filmed the funnel cloud with his son Cooper, said the experience showed him how little the family had planned for a storm of a kind that rarely reaches northern Utah. The free event gathered emergency managers, public safety agencies and other organizations around demonstrations on earthquakes, severe weather, wildfire, flooding, home safety, sanitation and assembling supply kits. Cooper's interest ran more to the parked emergency helicopter, while his father said the presentations raised hazards the family had not considered. Centerville Emergency Manager Louisa McDonald urged residents to plan for emergencies that begin inside the house, not only the ones nature delivers.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: B'Nai Israel Temple religious legacy lives on in Salt Lake Art Museum
item.description: The building at 249 S. 400 East in Salt Lake City has been a synagogue, a restaurant, a furniture showroom and, since July 24, the Salt Lake Art Museum — whose opening exhibit is about the congregation that built it. Utah's Jewish community traces to Fanny Brooks, who passed through in 1854 and settled with her family a decade later; Congregation B'nai Israel formed in 1873, split in 1885 into Reform and Orthodox branches, and dedicated the 400 East building in July 1891, using it for more than 80 years. The congregation merged into Congregation Kol Ami in 1970 and sold the building in 1976, after which Henriksen Butler occupied it and added an accessible entrance at the rear that spared the original staircases. Tour guide Kevin Earl, who researches the city's historic churches, said the exposed trusses and nearly all the windows survive, the exception being a skylight panel replaced after a workman dropped a wrench through it during restoration. Kol Ami now meets at 2425 E. Heritage Way, and Earl argues the valley's mix of synagogues, mosques and Buddhist and Hindu temples is what gives the state's religious history its texture.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: 6 dead after explosion destroys building in Athens
item.description: Six people died when a two-story residential building collapsed in Plaka, the tourist district beneath the Acropolis in central Athens, the Greek fire brigade announced Saturday. Four of the dead were American citizens, according to US officials; two American couples had been staying in one apartment and an elderly couple lived in another. Fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis said crews working with rescue dogs, cameras and sensors recovered the bodies from the rubble. Athens' mayor pointed to gas infrastructure as the likely cause, and residents had reported smelling gas beforehand; the fire brigade's crime investigation unit was at the scene. The blast scattered debris and glass as far as three blocks, damaging nearby homes, shops and vehicles, and US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle posted on X that she was deeply saddened by the American deaths.
item.dc:creator: Angeliki Koutantou, Reuters

item.title: Utah voters across faiths embrace Dallin H. Oaks' call for political compromise, poll finds
item.description: A Y2 Analytics and Public Wisdom survey of 547 Utahns found broad agreement across religious lines with the argument President Dallin H. Oaks made in "Faith, Freedom, and the Common Good," delivered Sept. 16 to a capacity crowd of 4,000 at the Washington National Cathedral. More than nine in ten respondents completely or mostly agreed that a person can be moral while holding different political priorities, and nearly 90% agreed that commitment to God requires treating others fairly, a view active Latter-day Saints endorsed more emphatically than Utahns with no religious affiliation. Support was softer but still substantial on compromise itself: 79% agreed that finding compromises produces better outcomes for political and religious interests, and 74% rejected the idea that compromise weakens the integrity of religious belief. Utahns split more evenly on whether the Constitution and Bill of Rights are divinely inspired, with 69% of active Latter-day Saints saying they are. Oaks, president of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and recognized by secular scholars for his "civic theology," argued that the Constitution compels peacemaking as its route to freedom, unity and fairness for all.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Hurricane Nolo expected to unleash powerful winds, flash flooding on Hawaii
item.description: Hurricane Nolo was moving slowly about 145 miles south of the Big Island on Saturday with sustained winds of 105 mph, threatening flash flooding and extreme surf across Hawaii through the weekend. Forecasters expect as much as 20 inches of rain on parts of the Big Island, with heavy rainfall on the other islands and a risk of mudslides. National Hurricane Center director Michael Brennan warned residents to stay out of both the flooding and the wind, which could bring down trees and power lines. President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration Friday, allowing FEMA to coordinate federal assistance, and the governor's emergency proclamation activated hundreds of Hawaii National Guard members. The storm arrives while the Big Island is still recovering from August's Hurricane Lala, which shifted roughly 100 homes off their foundations; the nonprofit CORE has been air-shipping camp stoves and hygiene supplies from Oahu to a relief hub running since that storm.
item.dc:creator: Eugene Garcia, Associated Press

item.title: At UN, Russia and Germany's top diplomats hold first talks since 2022
item.description: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met Saturday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, their countries' first such talks since before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Relations have been frozen since the invasion and worsened after an August drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Lavrov made little effort to suggest a thaw, telling reporters he had heard nothing from Wadephul that Berlin had not already published and that his counterpart could simply have phoned and said "read my statement." Wadephul pressed for progress on restarting Black Sea grain exports, which along with energy shipments have been badly curtailed by attacks on vessels and port infrastructure. Lavrov said Russia has discussed safe navigation proposals with India, Egypt and Turkey, possibly as bilateral arrangements, and blamed Ukraine for the attacks on shipping; Ukraine says it is open to agreements and holds Russia responsible for the war's consequences.
item.dc:creator: Antoni Slodkowski and Tom Balmforth, Reuters

item.title: Salt Lake City seeks creative funding options as Liberty Park upgrades could cost $41M
item.description: Salt Lake City's Department of Public Lands has priced a three-phase vision plan for Liberty Park at $36.3 million to $40.9 million, a figure that will likely force the city to hunt for funding beyond its usual sources. Foot traffic studies put daily weekday visits near 7,000 and weekend days close to 11,000 at the park, which approaches its 150th birthday in the next few years. Staff briefed the City Council on Tuesday, about two years after beginning a cultural landscape report and vision plan shaped by feedback from more than 1,000 residents. Associate landscape architect Kathryn Sonntag said the plan leans toward enhancing what already exists: new riparian planting and a birdwatching boardwalk at the pond, a formal path replacing one visitors wore in themselves, new trees to succeed the aging canopy, and a replacement greenhouse. Council Vice Chairwoman Erika Carlsen said the park's popularity is precisely what will require additional money and support to sustain.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Health officials to urge caution around kratom, other substances after Mississippi student deaths
item.description: Two University of Mississippi student deaths have put kratom in front of Utah health officials, who are urging caution even though no cause of death has been released and kratom was only noted as present at both scenes. Online warnings circulating among students, including a post from the unaffiliated BarstoolUtes account, raised alarm about cychlorphine, a synthetic opioid that can turn up in tablets and gummies. Dr. Brandon Forsyth of the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food, who tests emerging substances, said neither he nor the Salt Lake County Health Department has evidence cychlorphine has reached Utah, though it could be added to nearly any product. Kratom itself remains easy to buy at gas stations and smoke shops; recent state legislation restricts sales to whole-leaf products for those 21 and older and bans synthetic or enhanced versions, but Forsyth cautioned that banned stock may still be on shelves. He said the substance acts as both stimulant and sedative, with opioid effects strong enough at high doses to cause unconsciousness or shallow breathing.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist flown to hospital after crash near Layton
item.description: A 24-year-old motorcyclist was airlifted with serious injuries Friday after colliding with a car on state Route 193 near the U.S. 89 intersection outside Layton. Layton Police Lt. Clint Bobrowski said he was notified of the crash at 6:10 p.m., though the exact time it occurred was not clear. Investigators said the man was riding east when traffic ahead slowed abruptly; he braked hard, swerved into oncoming lanes and hit a westbound car. Police did not say whether he was wearing a helmet. The car's driver stayed at the scene and did not appear to be impaired.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Bountiful honors former QB, lightening strike victim
item.description: Bountiful High honored former quarterback Steve Matheson before Friday night's football game, playing a video about his life as his family walked onto the field. Matheson, who quarterbacked the Redhawks' 2002 state championship team, died Aug. 29 in Florida: he had extended a work trip to visit a childhood friend, and the two were returning from the water during a sudden storm when they stopped to help stranded boaters and he was struck by lightning. The school also gave him its Distinguished Alumni Forever Brave Award. His wife, Abbie Matheson, said the tribute helped her and their four children see how widely he was felt beyond the family, and described a husband who was always looking for someone to serve. What struck her most, she said, was how quickly he could connect with people.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: A crop you've probably never heard of is taking off in Idaho
item.description: Teff, an Ethiopian warm-season grass grown for grain or livestock forage, has quietly become a significant Idaho crop, with BoiseDev reporting in 2022 that the state ranked second worldwide in grain production. It reached the Boise area in the 1980s, and Wayne Carlson founded Maskal Teff in 1986 to grow it for injera, the fermented flatbread central to Ethiopian cooking. The University of Idaho's Aberdeen research center began growing it in the east of the state in 2018, mainly as forage. Researcher Joseph Sagers told EastIdahoNews.com that Idaho's July and August conditions suit the crop, which tolerates drought better than competing forages but has no frost tolerance at all. Its appeal to farmers is higher protein than oats, triticale, winter wheat or forage barley, plus a short season that lets it go in a month later than other crops, though that same short window makes some growers wary.
item.dc:creator: Rett Nelson, EastIdahoNews.com

item.title: Vast crowd greets pope with 'Leo' chants at France tour's biggest event
item.description: An outdoor Mass on the Champs-Elysees drew an estimated 700,000 people Saturday, the largest event of Pope Leo's four-day visit to France. Crowds filled 1.4 miles of central Paris between the Place de la Concorde and the Arc de Triomphe, chanting his name as his open-top popemobile stopped repeatedly so he could bless children and people with disabilities handed forward by volunteers, with more than 600,000 registered in advance. Leo, the first U.S. pope, is using the three-city trip to rebuild the Church's standing in France after abuse scandals. Speaking Friday at UNESCO headquarters he said the UN and other multilateral bodies are in crisis, and he again urged caution on artificial intelligence, warning French leaders of a future in which "a paradise of machines" takes control. Attendee Geraldine Pambou, 42, said she wanted him to keep speaking for peace; his criticism of the Iran war drew a rebuke from Trump earlier this year.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee and Elizabeth Pineau, Reuters

item.title: 7UP 'ghost sign' in Cedar City sparks memories of wedding proposal 50 years ago
item.description: Demolition of the Best Western Town & Country Hotel in Cedar City, clearing the way for a new Maverik gas station, uncovered a painted 7UP advertisement that had been hidden for some 40 years. For Gloria Bratton the reappearance brought back the autumn of 1974, when she was working at Lin's grocery and Richard Bratton picked her up for a lunch break at Hugh's Cafe and proposed in the parking lot with the sign in view. She said the location was incidental, not planned, and that it mattered to her because she has no photographs of the engagement. The Cedar City Historic Preservation Commission dates the painting to around the 1960s and says it stood visible roughly 20 years before the hotel went up beside it. The Brattons married in 1975.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Monzo in talks on sale to Nubank at about £10 billion valuation, Sky News reports
item.description: Sky News reported Saturday that Nubank, the Sao Paulo-based digital bank listed in New York with a market value near $65.5 billion, has opened early talks about a combination with British rival Monzo that would value the UK firm between £8 billion and £10 billion. A source close to the process told the outlet that an acquisition is one of two routes Monzo's board is weighing. The alternative is a fresh funding round at more than £8 billion, with the money going toward expansion into mainland Europe. Monzo's latest annual report shows pretax profit of £87.3 million for the year to March 31, up from £60.5 million, on revenue of £1.7 billion against £1.2 billion a year earlier. An employee share sale in October 2024, whose buyers included Singapore's GIC and StepStone Group, had valued the company at £4.5 billion.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Grieving West Haven family thanks community for support in loss of 6-year-old daughter
item.description: Six-year-old Mollie Korth was struck by a car outside her West Haven home Wednesday night and died the next day, and her family is publicly thanking the neighbors who have surrounded them since. Her uncle, Chad Parks, described a large group of neighborhood children and parents gathering Thursday at a home decorated in teal and pink, Mollie's favorite colors. In a statement Parks read on the family's behalf, the relatives extended sympathy to the young driver and that family, saying they knew they were suffering too. Parks remembered a girl known for her energy who was close to her 11-year-old brother Daxton, sharing scooter rides and backyard soccer with him.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Utah County agrees to pay $1.8M for defense of man charged with capital murder, settling lawsuit
item.description: Utah County will spend $1.8 million defending Michael Jayne, roughly nine times the amount it first budgeted, under a settlement announced Friday. Jayne, charged with aggravated murder in the death of Santaquin Police Sgt. Bill Hooser, sued in April without a lawyer, arguing that a $200,000 cap on attorney fees plus $140,000 for other costs could not fund a death penalty defense; he pointed to the $1 million initially approved for Tyler Robinson, accused of killing Charlie Kirk. Judge Jill Parish appointed attorney Neal Hamilton and a Colorado civil rights firm to represent him, then called the cap "flat out per se unreasonable" at a July hearing and told both sides to settle. Elizabeth Wang, a partner at the firm, said the county's contracts violated American Bar Association guidance, which she noted bars fee caps outright. The deal covers money already spent and leaves room for Jayne's lawyers to seek more.
item.dc:creator: Amy Donaldson and Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Learning about the renovation work you don't see beneath Salt Lake Temple
item.description: Almost none of the Salt Lake Temple's seven-year renovation will be visible to the public, because the largest piece of it sits underground. Project manager Georges Bonnet told KSL that crews grouted the original pioneer foundation, then built a new seismic foundation under the building and set it on 98 base isolators weighing roughly 18,000 pounds apiece, each able to travel five feet in any direction during a quake. The 2020 Magna earthquake, Bonnet said, confirmed the need for the work. Reinforcing the towers and upper walls meant pulling about 6,000 stones off the building to reach the columns behind them. Original features were restored rather than swapped out, including the temple's Tiffany glass, which was removed, repaired and reinstalled.
item.dc:creator: Deanie Wimmer, KSL

item.title: Volition moves proposed Spanish Fork data center location after resident concerns
item.description: Volition is relocating its proposed Spanish Fork data center to the 440,000-square-foot Stockman Flats building off state Route 77 in the west of the city, abandoning the Canyon Logistics site where neighbors had objected for months over noise, water use and proximity to homes. CEO Jeff Chavez said the company believed it could resolve those objections through design but wanted a path that would sit better with the city, and that a narrowing window prompted the decision now: "if there was time for us to make a shift right now, is that the last window for us to do this?" The move follows a City Council vote earlier in the week approving a Title 15 amendment that cleared a route for the proposal through the development process. Resident Teresa Wood, who lives near the original site, said she was caught off guard and struggled to process two months of pressure ending so abruptly. Wood added that her objection was never to data centers generally but to putting this one so close to housing.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Man charged with killing 2 in shooting outside funeral in Salt Lake claims he acted in self defense
item.description: Third District Judge Kristine Johnson found that John Vea Uasike Jr. has made a prima facie self-defense claim in the January shooting outside a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse at 660 N. Redwood Road, clearing the first phase of a justification hearing. The finding raises what prosecutors must prove to avoid dismissal and means a jury would be instructed on self-defense at any trial. Uasike, 31, of Elverta, California, appeared Friday in a wheelchair, which his attorney Rudy Bautista attributed to wounds from the shooting; he faces two murder counts and two counts of firing a gun causing serious injury, plus second-degree felony charges. Sione Vatuvei, 38, and Vaea Tulikihihifo, 46, were killed and six other men were hospitalized in the Jan. 7 incident. Uasike's brother Thomas Tai testified that he was shot before his brother returned fire, and that the confrontation began when a man he did not know approached the group aggressively as they walked to their vehicle.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Trump rejects Iranian peace proposal, WSJ reports
item.description: The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that President Donald Trump has turned down an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and stop regional fighting within seven days, and has told aides he expects to restart bombing after November's congressional elections. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said at the UN on Friday that Tehran passed the plan to Washington through Qatari mediators and that everything was ready if the U.S. was serious. Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strait and end hostilities on all fronts including Lebanon, while the U.S. would lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen funds and waive oil sanctions, after which broader talks could begin. A U.S. official described the mediated discussions to Reuters as positive and constructive, though the Journal reported Trump was privately doubtful Iran would meet his terms, and Reuters could not independently confirm the account. The war began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes and has killed thousands over seven months while disrupting one of the world's most important shipping lanes.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland and Parisa Hafezi, Reuters

item.title: Delta Center upgrades unveiled that will add 1,500 full-view seats for Utah Mammoth games
item.description: Smith Entertainment Group showed off a rebuilt upper north end at the Delta Center on Friday, a 143-day project that adds more than 1,500 seats with a full view of the ice without spoiling sight lines for Jazz games. The work addresses the basic problem of adapting an arena built for basketball into a permanent home for both an NBA and an NHL team. SEG Real Estate president Jim Olson said the lower bowl was fixed last year and the upper south end comes next, with the goal that every seat eventually sees the whole sheet. Two new Sky Lounges suspended over the sidelines add 200 seats each, and six Utah restaurants join the concourse lineup this season, including Cafe Rio, R&R BBQ and Apollo Burger, bringing the arena's local total to 18. Fans get their first look at the preseason game Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Utah truckers fear cost of diesel fuel may run them out of business
item.description: Diesel hit $6.60 a gallon in Utah on Thursday, an all-time state high according to AAA and well above the $3.73 recorded a year earlier. The increase traces largely to the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, which has complicated tanker movement through the Strait of Hormuz, compounded by Russian reports that strikes on its refining infrastructure have cut oil exports. Utah trucking company owner Jamal Goldsmith told KSL that revenue is being consumed by fuel and other operating costs, leaving almost nothing behind, and that a driver he met at a rest area doubted he could continue much longer. Goldsmith said he expects to decide the fate of his own company by the end of November.
item.dc:creator: Devyn Latorre, KSL

item.title: Judge temporarily blocks Utah's new age verification law in Pornhub lawsuit
item.description: U.S. District Judge David Barlow issued a preliminary injunction Thursday against part of a Utah law that would have made adult websites liable when Utah users evade age verification through VPNs or similar tools. Aylo Freesites Ltd., owner of Pornhub and RedTube, sued in April arguing the provision would require it to pin down the location of every user worldwide and expose it to liability if even one slipped through. Barlow agreed the amended statute "essentially imposes strict liability" on such companies for determining user location and said Aylo was likely to win on the merits; his order pauses the location provisions while the case proceeds. The Utah Department of Commerce had already agreed last month to hold off enforcement, with Aylo continuing to block Utah access in the meantime. Utah's original 2023 age verification law prompted Pornhub to cut off the state entirely, and lawmakers expanded it this year.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Honduran man, twice removed from the US, charged with drug trafficking in Salt Lake
item.description: Francisco Rodriguez Raudales, 32, faces federal drug trafficking and immigration charges in Salt Lake City after a sting operation on Sept. 9. According to the U.S. Attorney's Office for Utah, undercover officers met with him and he produced a bag holding more than 4,500 grams of fentanyl-laced pills. Charges were filed the following day. The Honduran national had previously been removed from the United States twice, in 2012 and again in 2023, and is now charged with possession of fentanyl with intent to distribute and reentry of a previously removed alien. A jury trial is expected in early November.
item.dc:creator: Allison Stuart, KSL

item.title: General conference special programming
item.description: KSL has published its broadcast schedule for the semiannual general conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, held Oct. 3-4. The station fills the gaps between the four conference sessions across the two days with its own special programming. Viewers can watch on KSL, KSL.com or the KSL+ app, and listen on KSL NewsRadio. The article lists the specific programs scheduled around each session.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: USU gets $1.6M federal grant to expand digital mental health support for dementia caregivers
item.description: A Utah State University team has won a $1.6 million Department of Defense grant to build out online mental health tools for people caring for a family member with dementia, a group that includes active-duty service members, military spouses and veterans. Roughly 7 million Americans have dementia, a figure projected to double by 2060, and more than 11 million provide unpaid care. Beth Fauth, a USU professor who directs the state-funded Alzheimer's Disease and Dementia Research Center, is leading the project, which adapts Acceptance and Commitment Therapy from years of prior clinical work. Fauth argued that conventional caregiver programs and support groups teach disease management well but rarely build skills for handling the emotional toll. The grant funds an evaluation of whether a self-guided online tool can improve caregivers' emotional health, physical health behaviors and relationships, with a shortened version available to the person with dementia when they are able to take part.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Leaders urge society to seek 'wisdom of the indigenous people' during Native American Day
item.description: Native American Day fell on Friday in California and Nevada, and Native residents of Utah marked it alongside them even though Utah sets aside no comparable date despite having eight sovereign tribal nations. The observance began in 1968 when California tribal leaders and then-Gov. Ronald Reagan designated the fourth Friday in September as California Indian Day; it was later renamed, and states including Wyoming, Nevada, Arizona, Delaware, South Dakota and Oklahoma now hold similar observances. Shelby Chapoose, cultural resource manager for the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah, said Southern Paiute bands run from the Kanosh and Koosharem in the north through Nevada, Arizona and California, and that language, tradition and ceremony rather than state lines define the connection among them. She described the separations imposed on the tribe as a product of colonization and Manifest Destiny fitting Native people into a government narrative. Darren Parry, former chairman of the Shoshone Nation, welcomed any day that prompts recognition but said a single calendar date cannot answer for centuries of erasure.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Chile seizes more than 200 fossils of extinct mollusks
item.description: Chilean customs officers have confiscated over 200 ammonite fossils that entered the country in a shipping container declared as holding chains, pendants and glass household ornaments. The National Customs Directorate said Friday that the fossils, roughly 110 million years old, were packed in cardboard boxes and wrapped in Madagascan newspapers and magazines, though the container itself was shipped from China. Ammonites were marine mollusks related to modern octopuses and squid, wiped out in the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction that ended the non-avian dinosaurs about 66 million years ago. Specialists from the San Antonio Museum of Natural History verified the specimens as authentic. Chile has asked Madagascar to confirm where they came from and whether it intends to seek their return.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Lowe's enters the drone delivery service space
item.description: Drone delivery is reaching a home improvement chain for the first time: Lowe's has teamed with DoorDash and Wing, Alphabet's drone subsidiary, to fly orders to customers. The pilot is confined to North Carolina for now, and the limits are tight — nothing over 2.5 pounds, nothing farther than five miles from a participating store. Within that envelope the company says some orders land within 20 minutes. Lowe's is aiming the service at trade professionals as much as weekend do-it-yourselfers.
item.dc:creator: Travis Richards, KSL

item.title: FDA panel endorses first-of-a-kind cancer blood test from Grail
item.description: An FDA advisory panel voted 7-2 with one abstention that Grail Inc.'s Galleri blood test offers more potential benefit than risk, the first time a federal advisory group has backed a multi-cancer early detection test. Galleri does not diagnose cancer; a single blood draw looks for a DNA signal suggesting one of a long list of tumors, and anyone with a positive result needs follow-up care. The panel had already voted that the test appears safe and effective for people 50 and older, but members raised numerous questions about how well the technology performs and pressed for more study. Dr. Victor van Berkel of UofL Physicians said his yes vote was "perhaps hopeful rather than an accurate one," while arguing that catching early-stage cancers not covered by current screening would carry real benefit. The FDA is not bound by the advice and is expected to decide within a few months.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Perrone and Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press

item.title: Only a few more weeks to see 'Harry Potter and the Cursed Child' in Salt Lake City
item.description: Salt Lake City's run of "Harry Potter and the Cursed Child" ends Oct. 11, leaving a few weeks of performances at the Eccles Theatre. The stage story is set a generation past the books: Harry's son Albus lands in Slytherin, strikes up a friendship with Draco Malfoy's son, and the pair set out to rewrite history and save Cedric Diggory. Forbes has called the production one of the decade's defining pop culture events.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: 12-year-olds with smartphones are more likely to develop eating disorders by 14
item.description: A study published Friday in JAMA Network Open found that children who own a smartphone at 12 are more likely to show eating disorder symptoms by 14 than peers without one, drawing on a survey of nearly 9,000 US adolescents. Lead author Dr. Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at UC San Francisco, said a phone puts a world of appearance-focused content in a child's pocket and that parents should weigh not just whether to give a phone but when. Nagata's lab had previously linked screen time to binge eating, but most prior work measured how much time children spend on devices rather than the age they start. Roughly 22% of children and adolescents worldwide show signs of disordered eating by research estimates, with the line between that and a diagnosed eating disorder turning on severity and diagnostic criteria. Screen and social media use has also been associated with depression, lower self-worth and substance experimentation.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Schupak, CNN

item.title: Idaho officials will memorialize lives lost during mass shooting in Twin Falls
item.description: Twin Falls, Idaho, will build a permanent memorial to the Aug. 1 mass shooting at a local In-N-Out drive-thru, where a gunman killed three people, among them a man from Salt Lake City. City leaders announced the plan this week, framing it as recognition not only of those killed but of everyone the attack touched, and as somewhere people can go to grieve. Fundraising is underway, and officials said the design and location will be worked out together with victims' families, survivors and first responders.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: Former treasurer of Utah Scottish Association accused of stealing from group
item.description: The Utah Scottish Association says its former treasurer drained roughly $100,000 from the nonprofit over four years, a loss the group warned on social media Thursday could affect what it can pay its vendors. Jared Hunt, 57, of Ogden, now faces a single count of felony theft by deception. Salt Lake City detectives have so far documented about $80,000 in purchases Hunt allegedly made for himself with association money, a figure that could still grow because investigators did not examine 2026 transactions. The association said it deeply regrets the breach of public trust.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Endangered Utah bird species to get a boost. Here's how to watch its population soar
item.description: Four more California condors will be released into the wild Saturday at Vermilion Cliffs National Monument just south of the Utah-Arizona line, the 30th annual release run jointly by the Bureau of Land Management and The Peregrine Fund. The zoo-hatched birds join a flock of nearly 100 that trails only California's in wild population size. Robert Bate, who manages the monument for the bureau, framed the releases as proof that public lands can sustain the species. Condors fell to as few as 22 worldwide in the 1980s because of lead poisoning and other pressures; the global count now stands at 607, with 392 living wild. The Arizona-Utah flock has struggled recently, losing 34 birds in 2023 amid an avian flu outbreak, 25 in 2024 and eight last year, with lead poisoning and at least two illegal killings in Utah still a problem.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Blackstone-backed insurance underwriter The Fidelis Partnership files for US IPO
item.description: TFP Group, the specialty insurance underwriter known as The Fidelis Partnership, filed Friday for a US initial public offering. The Hamilton, Bermuda-based firm was founded by industry veteran Richard Brindle and became a standalone business in 2023 when Fidelis Insurance split into two entities; it underwrites across more than 150 business lines. TFP reported $127.5 million in net income on $407.5 million of revenue for the six months ending June 30, up from $74.5 million on $365.9 million a year earlier. Backers include Blackstone, with which TFP launched a Lloyd's of London syndicate last year, along with Alfa Insurance, Capital Z Partners and Travelers. Morgan Stanley, Barclays and J.P. Morgan are among the underwriters for the NYSE listing under "TFP," which comes after a slow September that saw only four companies go public.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Pope Leo warns in France that UN risks becoming 'charade'
item.description: Speaking Friday at UNESCO headquarters in Paris, Pope Leo said the United Nations and other multilateral bodies face a crisis of effectiveness and warned that international dialogue risks turning into a "charade" rather than a search for common ground. The first US pope, who took office in May 2025, also condemned leaders who invoke the law when it serves them and disregard it when it restrains them, treating justice as a commodity to be bought and sold, though he named no one. His remarks landed while a tense UN General Assembly was underway in New York. Leo had already drawn President Donald Trump's anger earlier in the year with his criticism of the Iran war. The France visit is also aimed at repairing the church's standing there after abuse scandals.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee and Elizabeth Pineau, Reuters

item.title: International Pentecostal conference to bring thousands to Salt Lake City
item.description: The United Pentecostal Church International will hold its four-day annual General Conference at the Salt Palace Convention Center, running Tuesday through Friday. Communications director Jonathan Mohr said past conferences have drawn 8,000 to 10,000 people and that attendance is open to anyone, not only Pentecostals. General superintendent David K. Bernard described the gathering as a chance for ministers to connect, conduct denominational business and collaborate across the fellowship. The organization counts more than six million constituents across 203 countries, though most attendees will come from North America. Utah has hosted the conference six times, most recently in 2004, and Mohr said the city's hotel supply and the size of the Salt Palace drove the choice.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Senate approves mental health legislation for pilots, air traffic controllers
item.description: The Senate unanimously approved bipartisan legislation late Thursday to modernize mental health rules for pilots and air traffic controllers, aiming to encourage earlier disclosure and treatment. Sens. John Hoeven and Tammy Duckworth sponsored the measure, which targets a long-standing problem: commercial pilots often hide conditions out of fear that admitting to therapy or medication could cost them their licenses, leaving risks unaddressed. A companion bill also passed requires the FAA to publish accessible guidance on approved medications so pilots and controllers do not unknowingly jeopardize their careers. The issue gained urgency after an off-duty Alaska Airlines pilot was charged in late 2023 with trying to shut down a jet's engines mid-flight and later told police he was having a nervous breakdown. Both bills still need House passage.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson, Reuters

item.title: Immigration crackdown hits Kansas, disrupts beef processing
item.description: Immigration agents spread across southwest Kansas this week, a region dense with feedlots and slaughterhouses, and the operation immediately rippled through the beef industry. Community organizers and three livestock producer groups said fear of arrest kept much of the largely immigrant workforce home, slowing processing plants and backing up cattle. Kathleen Alonso, a volunteer from Liberal, called the week chaotic and said agents were stopping Brown people and not others. Organizers and local officials reported ICE officers questioning motorists about citizenship around Dodge City, Liberal and Garden City and patrolling near meat plants and a large dairy, with dozens believed detained though no firm count was available. Industry and union officials warned the crackdown could push already record-high beef prices higher, cutting against the administration's stated aim of controlling beef costs; DHS, ICE and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
item.dc:creator: Tom Polansek, Reuters

item.title: Listening to loud music on a Singapore bus? It'll cost you
item.description: Blasting music on a Singapore bus can now cost a passenger real money. The Land Transport Authority set penalties of up to 500 Singapore dollars, around $390, for behavior it classifies as causing annoyance — a category covering loud audio, feet on seats, littering, and eating or drinking onboard. Conduct that endangers other riders or soils a bus or transit infrastructure carries a far steeper ceiling of 5,000 SGD, roughly $3,900. The authority justified the rules by calling public transport a shared space in which every commuter bears some responsibility for keeping the ride pleasant.
item.dc:creator: Lex Harvey, CNN

item.title: Man on the run for 10 years arrested in child exploitation sting
item.description: Lam Xuan Nguyen, 36, was arrested Thursday in an FBI child exploitation operation after a decade as a fugitive. Court records show he was convicted in 2016 in 4th District Court on three counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, a second-degree felony, but skipped his presentencing appointment and a warrant was issued. A police booking affidavit says the FBI's Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force learned in June of someone discussing abusing a boy under 13 online, and that Nguyen arranged a meeting in Utah and was taken into custody on arrival. He was carrying what police described as an apparent fake New York driver's license under another name, and fingerprints confirmed his identity. He was booked into the Salt Lake County Jail for investigation of attempted sodomy on a child, enticing a minor and forgery.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Nor'easter expected to disrupt travel, flood basements, knock out power along East Coast
item.description: A powerful nor'easter is set to lash the coast from Maine to Washington, D.C., through the weekend with heavy rain, flooding, strong gusts and rip currents. The timing is awkward: world leaders are departing New York after the UN General Assembly just as the FAA warns that wind could snarl operations at all three major New York-area airports. American, JetBlue and United are waiving change fees on Northeast flights from Friday through Sunday. Forecasters at the National Weather Service expect gusts near 55 mph, enough to make driving hazardous, while New York City officials flagged the risk of basement flooding and power outages. Amtrak said Northeast rail service could be disrupted as well.
item.dc:creator: Maria Tsvetkova and Michelle Nichols, Reuters

item.title: Xi says he'll see Trump again soon as he wraps up US visit with a look at the Constitution
item.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping closed out his three-day Washington state visit Friday by announcing two more meetings with President Donald Trump before the end of the year, doubling their 2026 face-to-face count. Trump took Xi to the National Archives to see the Constitution and Bill of Rights. Critics in the US called the visit heavy on ceremony and thin on results, with no breakthroughs on trade or AI safety; the main concrete outcome was extending the trade truce only until January, agreed as Xi landed. Trump said the two discussed the war in Iran. Scott Lincicome of the Cato Institute dismissed the summit as sound and fury signifying nothing, and former trade official Jeff Moon of China Moon Strategies argued that resultless summits let Beijing run out the clock on Trump's second term.
item.dc:creator: Michelle L. Price and Fu Ting, Associated Press

item.title: New Mexico jury finds Facebook liable of deceiving users about privacy protections
item.description: A Santa Fe jury found Facebook liable Friday for deceiving users about privacy protections, capping a two-week trial over the Cambridge Analytica breach. The case centered on a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to the consulting firm, whose clients included Donald Trump's 2016 campaign. Jurors concluded the failure to protect user data affected New Mexico's entire population of more than two million people and separately found the company misled the public about its investigations of data brokers, amounting to over two million violations. The judge will set the penalty; state attorneys are asking for the $5,000 statutory maximum per violation. New Mexico is the only state still pursuing these claims, because Meta's August multistate child-safety settlement of up to $18 billion also released it from future Cambridge Analytica liability, and the state separately won $942 million from Meta this year over protections for minors.
item.dc:creator: Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press

item.title: Cheetah cubs at Prague Zoo doing well after period of strong storms, mother's illness
item.description: Five cheetah cubs born June 18 at the Prague Zoo are healthy after a rough start, the zoo said Friday. The quintuplets, four males and a female, arrived in an outdoor enclosure just as strong storms moved over Prague. Curator Pavel Brandl said their mother, Daenerys, protected them from torrential rain and licked the water out of their fur despite being a first-time mother, care he called exemplary, and then came down with an intestinal infection in August. Brandl cautioned it may take a year to know whether the cubs clear the critical post-birth window, noting cheetah infant mortality runs high in the wild from predators and illnesses such as pneumonia. Scientists consider every cub significant to a species facing extinction.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Man sentenced to prison for kidnapping, raping 12-year-old and stealing a car
item.description: Aiden Dramore Larsen, 20, of Moroni, was sentenced Aug. 26 by 6th District Judge Robert Van Dyke to six years to life for rape of a child, plus concurrent one-to-15-year terms for child kidnapping and vehicle theft. Larsen pleaded guilty June 3 under a deal that dropped a second rape-of-a-child count, 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor and an enticing charge, with both sides recommending concurrent sentences. The 12-year-old victim's mother told the court in a July hearing that Larsen "stole her light" and that her daughter still does not feel safe and needs prolonged therapy. Charging documents say the Sanpete County Sheriff's Office reported the girl missing on Oct. 13, 2025, and a trooper near Richfield spotted a matching vehicle. Larsen fled onto I-70 at more than 100 mph, and the chase ended after police spiked his tires and the car went through fences at a Sevier RV park.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Independent review of UVU and Charlie Kirk shooting finds ways security could be better
item.description: An outside review released Friday concluded that no Utah Valley University employee acted in bad faith or with willful disregard for safety around the Sept. 10, 2025, shooting that killed Charlie Kirk on campus, while still identifying places security could improve. The review team of legal and law enforcement experts conducted more than 70 interviews and went through thousands of pages of university policies, training records and communications. It found UVU had a substantial base of policies, emergency procedures and public safety resources but did not always apply or document them consistently. Kirk was shot shortly after beginning a Turning Point USA event in the Fountain Courtyard, allegedly from the roof of the nearby Losee Center. Tyler Robinson has been bound over on all charges including aggravated murder, prosecutors intend to seek the death penalty, and Judge Tony Graf hopes to set trial dates at an Oct. 23 hearing.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Meta bolsters Muse safety warning after security vulnerability found, The Information reports
item.description: Meta is strengthening a safety warning inside Muse, its new personal AI agent, after an outside researcher reported a vulnerability through the company's bug bounty program, The Information reported Friday. According to an internal Meta incident report the outlet reviewed, the previously undisclosed flaw could have let an attacker reach a user's dedicated virtual machine, a private cloud account holding emails, files and other sensitive data. Meta initially rated it a "SEV-2," the third-highest level on its five-point severity scale, typically reserved for incidents with significant impact. Muse launched earlier this month to handle tasks like shopping, travel booking, email and payments, and has topped the free-app charts in the US and Canada, with Sensor Tower estimating about 2.8 million downloads in two weeks. Meta did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: K-9 handler helps families of Indigenous missing persons near Four Corners
item.description: Bernadine Beyale, who founded 4Corners K-9 Search and Rescue in New Mexico, has increasingly taken on the roles of advocate and de facto investigator for families of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons around the Four Corners. She told KSL that families are usually left to run most of the searching themselves, especially where circumstances look suspicious, and that she never expected to become the person called in the middle of the night. Beyale invited KSL onto Navajo Nation land in far southeastern Utah to meet two families still without answers. Among them is the family of Ryan Tom, last seen June 11, 2022, near an old windmill on a remote hillside in the Red Mesa area. His aunt Rosina Brown said the account that he simply wandered off does not fit, since he left his phone behind in June heat wearing flip-flops.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: ADARx Pharmaceuticals shares soar in Nasdaq debut after upsized IPO
item.description: ADARx Pharmaceuticals opened at $22.10 on Friday, 30% above its $17 IPO price, after the San Diego gene therapy developer raised $446.3 million in an upsized offering. The company sold 26.3 million shares at the top of its range, up from a planned 21.9 million. AbbVie agreed to put up to $100 million into a concurrent private placement that would leave it with roughly 4.9% post-IPO. IPOX research associate Lukas Muehlbauer told Reuters that AbbVie's backing supplied external validation alongside a Phase 3 lead drug with top-line data due by the end of 2027, and that investors remain selective, favoring mature clinical assets and adequate cash runway. Founded in 2019, ADARx targets immunity, kidney, cardiovascular and neurological diseases; biotech has been a bright spot in an otherwise thin IPO market, with City Therapeutics and Iambic Therapeutics filing this week.
item.dc:creator: Pragyan Kalita, Reuters

item.title: Crypto exchange Bitget pauses withdrawals after $350 million stolen in hack
item.description: Bitget halted customer withdrawals after roughly $351.6 million in cryptocurrency was stolen from some of its wallets, CEO Gracy Chen said. The Seychelles-based exchange noticed unauthorized transfers Thursday and suspended withdrawals; Chen said in a statement on X and in emailed comments to Reuters that all user funds are safe, the loss is covered by Bitget's own funds, and the suspension is a precaution rather than a sign of a shortfall. Bitget claims more than 120 million users, making it one of the largest exchanges globally. Crypto platforms have absorbed repeated thefts, including the $1.5 billion taken from Bybit last year in a hack the FBI attributed to North Korean actors, an accusation Pyongyang routinely denies. Authorities note that stolen crypto can be moved across borders quickly without touching the mainstream financial system.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Howcroft, Reuters

item.title: Supreme Court restores Trump's mass voter verification system
item.description: The Supreme Court on Friday let the Trump administration resume using an expanded immigration database to check the citizenship of registered voters, granting the Justice Department's request to lift a judge's order that had stopped state officials from running those checks against federal records using Social Security numbers and other data. The majority reasoned that the challengers likely lose because federal law expressly lets the Department of Homeland Security request citizenship and immigration information from other agencies, including the Social Security Administration. The court's three liberal justices dissented from the 6-3 conservative majority's order, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warning of harm to lawful voters ahead of the midterms. DHS redesigned the underlying SAVE database last year. The order is one of several recent moves expanding federal involvement in elections, even though the Constitution leaves election administration primarily to the states.
item.dc:creator: John Kruzel, Reuters

item.title: Church outlines more of its transportations plans for Salt Lake Temple open house
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints laid out more of how it intends to move 22,000 daily visitors to the Salt Lake Temple open house running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027. Juan Becerra, the church's government and community relations manager, told a Fairpark Community Council meeting that two secured lots at Redwood Road hold more than 1,700 stalls, with coach buses making roughly eight-minute runs to a drop-off on 200 West. Entry to the grounds will run 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, with shuttles operating later and starting at 9 a.m. on Sundays. The plan also sets aside a bicycle valet near West Temple and South Temple on the former Salt Lake Plaza Hotel site, plus separate areas for tour buses and rideshare drop-offs. More than a million tickets have already been claimed.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams and Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Hurricane Nolo threatening Hawaii with heavy rain as Polo churns near Mexico
item.description: Hawaii's Big Island braced Friday for what the National Hurricane Center warned could be catastrophic, life-threatening flooding from Hurricane Nolo, which sat about 220 miles to the south with 85 mph winds and was moving northeast. Forecasters expected 15 to 30 inches of rain, tropical storm conditions reaching land by evening and strengthening into a major hurricane Saturday, with the heaviest rain falling on the same southeastern ground soaked by Hurricane Lala in August. Though a direct hit was not forecast, Maui and the other islands could also see dangerous rainfall and mudslides. The governor issued an emergency proclamation activating more than 230 National Guard members, schools closed for the week, and Hawaiian Electric pulled crews back from Kauai restoration work following Hurricane Lowell. Mexico meanwhile remained under threat from Hurricane Polo, heading toward the Baja Peninsula.
item.dc:creator: Eugene Garcia, Associated Press

item.title: Utah, feds finalize $60M settlement over 22,000 acres near Great Salt Lake
item.description: Utah and the federal government have settled a decades-old dispute over land along the Great Salt Lake, with the state dropping its claim to 22,311 surface acres near the Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge in Corinne in exchange for $60 million earmarked for lake projects. The acreage folds into the refuge, which the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service manages. Gov. Spencer Cox said the deal converts a long-running fight into money that goes straight back into the lake, crediting federal and legislative partners. House Speaker Mike Schultz said in March that the two sides had agreed on a land line roughly five years ago but never on a price, and that the state had earlier been offered only $15 million. Lawmakers passed a resolution on the final day of the session clearing the way for terms that quadrupled that offer while confirming the land is federal.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Many groups are trying to save the Great Salt Lake. Here's how they can better collaborate
item.description: The Great Salt Lake Alliance and the Great Salt Lake Commissioner's Office released a joint report Wednesday collecting dozens of suggestions for how Utah could run its lake-rescue work better. The recommendations came out of a summer brainstorming session involving representatives from nearly 50 organizations, who converged on the need for tighter coordination and broader access to data and information. Participants also pointed to building project-implementation capacity, continuing to test new approaches, and strengthening public understanding. The report lays out three next steps: more solutions-focused education, better access to decision-supporting information, and folding the findings into state planning. Great Salt Lake commissioner Hannah Freeze said the input feeds the ongoing update of the Great Salt Lake Strategic Plan, which comes as the lake's southern arm sits at 4,189.7 feet and its northern arm at 4,189.6 feet.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Utah Fits All report sparks debate over scholarship use
item.description: A legislative report from Odyssey, the program manager for the Utah Fits All Scholarship Program, details how 14,522 students spent $94.7 million during the 2025-26 school year, split between 6,953 home-based students and 7,569 in private schools. The program, created by HB215 in the 2023 General Session, is in its third year. Rep. John Arthur, D-Holladay, a teacher and Utah's 2021 Teacher of the Year, told KSL he was frustrated by line items including $468,665 on headphones, $1.2 million on 3D printers and $909,050 on internet service. Arthur said he had to run a DonorsChoose drive to buy headphones for his own classroom while teachers statewide cover pencils and tissues. Utah Education Fits All executive director Robyn Bagley described the scholarship as an option for families seeking something other than public schools.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: AI messaging scam costs Italy's top bank Intesa millions, sources say
item.description: Fraudsters impersonating senior executives with AI took 95 million euros, about $108 million, from Fideuram, the private banking arm of Italy's largest lender Intesa Sanpaolo, according to two sources familiar with the matter. The scheme began in February when then-Fideuram chairman Paolo Molesini received what appeared to be a WhatsApp message from Intesa Sanpaolo CEO Carlo Messina asking for urgent help with an overseas transaction, followed by a call that seemed to come from a senior partner at a prominent law firm, a voice the sources said was AI-generated. Molesini had his finance department arrange a series of transfers to accounts largely in China and Hong Kong. Fideuram spotted irregularities quickly and alerted banks and authorities in several countries, and cooperation among Chinese, Portuguese and Italian authorities recovered roughly 53 million euros. About 36 million euros remains untraced after moving through overseas accounts and being converted into cryptocurrency; Corriere della Sera first reported the case, and both Intesa Sanpaolo and Fideuram declined to comment.
item.dc:creator: Emilio Parodi, Reuters

item.title: Man accused of sexually abusing young girl in Vernal
item.description: Kaden Lavar Potter, 19, was booked into the Uintah County Jail on Thursday for investigation of three counts of rape, four counts of object rape of a child, two counts of sodomy on a child, aggravated kidnapping, three counts of enticing a minor and three counts of sexual exploitation of a minor. A police booking affidavit says Vernal police began investigating in August a report that Potter repeatedly abused a girl between 12 and 14 years old between March and July. Police say Potter told them on Aug. 20 that the girl had claimed to be 18, but investigators cite a separate Vernal police report showing officers told him her real age back in April. Detectives served a search warrant on Aug. 27 on a camper belonging to Potter where some of the alleged crimes took place and collected evidence. Police say there may be additional victims.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah community honors those impacted by recent flooding in Tibet and Nepal
item.description: Members of Utah's Tibetan community held a vigil Wednesday night in Salt Lake City for those killed and still missing in the late-August flash flooding and mudslides across Tibet and Nepal. Utah Tibetan Association president Pema Chagzoetsand told KSL the gathering was not only a memorial but a way to keep the missing and the ongoing suffering from being forgotten, saying the disaster has not drawn enough attention. Confirmed deaths stand at 1,500, with nearly 7,000 people still unaccounted for, and recovery work continues a month on. Organizers picked Wednesday deliberately, as it is the traditional Tibetan day of prayer and remembrance. One attendee said the point was staying connected to a place thousands of miles away.
item.dc:creator: Allison Stuart, KSL

item.title: Nearly $10K later, here's what a Latter-day Saint writer learned after year of online sports betting
item.description: Atlantic staff writer McKay Coppins spoke at Utah Valley University on Thursday about the year he spent betting roughly $10,000 of his publication's money on sports as a reporting assignment. Coppins, a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, described gambling crowding out his mental life, from gambling podcasts in the shower to four football games split-screened on Sundays with a fifth on his phone, and his wife catching him checking DraftKings at church. He said he routinely stayed up past midnight hunting his next bet. The assignment landed against a steep national rise: Americans wagered about $4.9 billion legally in 2017, and by last year that figure reached roughly $160 billion, with more than 90% placed online, according to a JAMA Internal Medicine study. Coppins argued the saturation is inescapable, pointing to Shaquille O'Neal and Kevin Hart promoting DraftKings and Charles Barkley pitching FanDuel.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Mountain Trails Foundation announces seasonal, temporary trail closures
item.description: Bonanza Flat's trails near Park City go offline for the season Oct. 1, giving riders and hikers roughly one more week of access. The Mountain Trails Foundation said on Facebook that the annual shutdown is about wildlife, which needs the area undisturbed heading into winter. The closure is seasonal rather than permanent, and the terrain reopens later this year for winter recreation.
item.dc:creator: Allison Stuart, KSL

item.title: USU researchers add weather sensors to study why Peter Sinks gets so cold
item.description: Utah State University researchers are wiring Peter Sinks with additional sensors to work out why the limestone basin becomes the coldest spot in Utah nearly every winter. Sitting at 8,164 feet, the bowl-shaped sink recorded 69.3 degrees below zero on Feb. 1, 1985, the second-lowest reading ever taken in the lower 48 behind only Roger's Pass, Montana. Visiting Hungarian scholar Andras Dobos and USU graduate research assistant Timothy Wright said the two long-standing stations at the rim and floor produced plenty of data but only a partial picture. The team has now installed about 16 measurement points along the slope between rim and floor and in the nearby Lower Sink and Middle Sink basins. Wright noted the deepest part of the basin is not always where the coldest air settles.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Miracle and uncertainty: Families respond to removal of death penalty in 1985 case
item.description: Prosecutors have withdrawn their intent to seek the death penalty against Doug Carter, 71, and said they will not oppose bail, 41 years after the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen in Provo. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton said he delivered the news at the Utah County Jail, where Carter asked whether it was really true after so many reversals. New Utah State Crime Lab testing found none of Carter's DNA on evidence from the scene. Judge Derek Pullan had denied bail only a week earlier citing flight risk and set a new trial for July 2027; his 2022 ruling vacating the conviction over police and prosecutor misconduct was upheld by the Utah Supreme Court in 2025. Carter's daughter-in-law Melissa Anger called the news wonderful but said the family still doubts justice will be served.
item.dc:creator: Amy Donaldson and Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Airbus identifies A321neo quality issue, says no safety risk
item.description: More than 500 A321neo jets could be touched by a manufacturing flaw Airbus disclosed Thursday, a figure first reported by The Air Current. The planemaker described the problem as weakening protection against corrosion within the fuselage structure, but classified it as a matter of build quality rather than flight safety, so airlines have no reason to ground anything. Airbus said it has already traced where the defect originated, walled it off, and has a fix on hand.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Drug developer City Therapeutics files for US IPO as biotech listings surge
item.description: City Therapeutics filed Thursday for a U.S. initial public offering, joining a run of biotech companies lining up for the fall listing window. Founded in 2023 and based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the company is developing RNA-based drugs for rare diseases; its lead candidate, CITY-FXI, is in an early-stage trial for thrombosis. It has raised roughly $238.8 million since inception from investors including ARCH Venture Partners, Fidelity Management & Research, Invus and Viking Global Investors. Goldman Sachs, Jefferies, Stifel and Oppenheimer are underwriting the offering, and the company plans to trade on the Nasdaq under the symbol "CTY." Biotech has been a recurring theme in this year's IPO market, though fall listings have struggled as rising bond yields and worries about the AI trade dampen risk appetite.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Elementary school teacher accused of giving inappropriate 'hugs' charged with abuse
item.description: Eric Christoffersen, 40, of Kearns, was charged Thursday in 3rd District Court with three counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child, a first-degree felony. Granite School District listed him as a teacher at Arcadia Elementary in Taylorsville; he had been on leave since April, when the allegations surfaced, and the district fired him Thursday after learning charges would be filed. The investigation began when district police took a report from an 11-year-old girl who said Christoffersen would ask for hugs and then touch other parts of her body. Charging documents describe her account of him picking her up, spinning her by the arms and sliding his hand from her back down as he set her down, which she believed he passed off as accidental. A second student also told investigators she and other classmates were touched inappropriately.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 8 sailors in Lincoln carrier group attempted suicide on extended deployment, Navy leader says
item.description: Eight sailors attempted suicide while deployed with the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during a record-setting uninterrupted stretch at sea supporting the Iran war, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao disclosed in a letter dated Tuesday. Cao was responding to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., who asked last month about the crew after reports of stress, poor mental health and shortages of food and hygiene supplies drew national attention. Experts told the Associated Press that eight attempts among a 6,000-sailor strike group over 10 months is actually a low figure; the Navy reported 356 attempts servicewide in 2024, out of more than 1,500 across all active duty personnel. Dr. Harold Kudler, a retired VA psychiatrist and former national lead for VA mental health services, said the raw number is not the best gauge of shipboard conditions absent further detail. He added that something clearly happened to alarm families and reverberate through the military, and that it needs to be understood so it is not repeated.
item.dc:creator: Ben Finley and Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press

item.title: Members of the public can report visa fraud or abuse with new online tool
item.description: Sham marriages, invented job offers and doctored paperwork are among the abuses the State Department now wants ordinary people to flag through a newly launched reporting channel. The Online Visa Fraud Tip Portal is open to anyone willing to submit information for the department to review. Officials offered no detail on how submissions will be vetted, saying only that they are pursuing accountability by pulling visas and handing fraud cases off to law enforcement.
item.dc:creator: Travis Richards, KSL

item.title: Enoch community creating 'healing garden' 3 years after murder of 7 family members
item.description: Residents of Enoch in Iron County are building a dedicated "healing garden" three and a half years after a murder-suicide that killed eight members of one family. On Jan. 4, 2023, Michael Haight killed his wife, Tausha Haight, 40; her mother, Gail Earl, 78; and the couple's five children — Macie, 17; Briley, 12; Sienna, 7; Ammon, 7; and Gavin, 4 — before taking his own life, in a case that drew worldwide attention.
