Amy Neilson, an Enoch resident and mental health counselor, said the killings left local children questioning whether their own parents could do the same, unsettling homes that should feel safe. Cindy Baldwin, a close friend and neighbor who lived two doors away and shared a fenced backyard with the family, described the depth of the loss for her family and the community. She said her children could still see the slide off the Haights' deck afterward, and that working through that has been part of their own healing.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: State prisons on lockdown following attack on corrections officer
item.description: Both of Utah's state prisons were placed on lockdown Thursday after an inmate assaulted a corrections officer at the Central Utah Correctional Facility in Gunnison. A Department of Corrections spokesman said the attack happened between 9 and 10 a.m. inside one of the prison's housing units; the officer was taken to a local hospital and described as stable. The lockdown covers both the Gunnison facility, which houses only male inmates, and the Utah State Correctional Facility in Salt Lake City, and will remain in place until the investigation is complete. Corrections Commissioner Jared Garcia said the department has zero tolerance for such attacks and praised staff for acting quickly, saying the officer is expected to fully recover. The department did not immediately release details about those involved.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Anthropic signs $11.6 billion cloud deal with Akamai, gets warrant for up to 5% stake
item.description: Anthropic has agreed to spend $11.6 billion on cloud services from Akamai Technologies over seven years, and secured a warrant that could give it a stake of up to 5% in Akamai. The contract could grow by another $9 billion, bringing the potential total to roughly $20 billion; about 2% of the warrant is tied to the initial commitment and the remaining 3% would vest on that expansion. The warrant covers roughly 7.7 million Akamai shares at an exercise price of $111.33. Akamai expects the arrangement to require about $5.5 billion in total capital expenditure and plans to raise its 2026 capital spending by about $1.7 billion to pre-purchase components, including memory. Akamai shares rose 16% in extended trading Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Witness, deputy fought to save 6-year-old who died after impact from vehicle
item.description: A 6-year-old girl struck by a vehicle Wednesday night in West Haven died early Thursday, and neighbors described the effort to save her. Weber County Sheriff's Office Lt. Charles Creager said a deputy happened to be in the area and responded immediately. Jody Taylor, who lives a few houses from the crash site, said she called 911 while her friend and the deputy performed CPR until additional medical help arrived; she also went to the girl's mother, who was on the sidewalk in distress. Creager said the driver stayed at the scene and cooperated, and Taylor described him as young and devastated. The Weber Metro CRASH team is investigating and reconstructing the scene near 2550 South and 2700 West.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Costco beats quarterly sales estimates on resilient demand for essentials
item.description: Costco Wholesale reported fourth-quarter revenue of $95.72 billion, topping the $94.86 billion Wall Street expected according to LSEG data. Adjusted earnings came in at $6.60 per share against estimates of $6.53, helped by a 15-cent-per-share benefit from tariff refunds under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The company said demand held up for essentials as inflation-squeezed shoppers drove foot traffic to its warehouses. Consolidating trips and buying in bulk has pushed up average basket size. TD Cowen analyst Oliver Chen noted that Costco's gas stations, which typically price below market, have also drawn price-sensitive customers as the Iran war lifts fuel costs.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Senate rejects Democratic-led resolution to curb Trump's Iran war powers
item.description: The Senate narrowly rejected a Democratic-led resolution Thursday that would have required President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or seek congressional authorization, voting 50-49 largely along party lines. Four Republicans — Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — backed it, with Tillis, who leaves the Senate in January, supporting a war powers resolution for the first time. Democrat John Fetterman of Pennsylvania voted against. The measure, which the House passed in July, was largely symbolic, as the administration has not changed course after previous war powers votes. Democrats pushed the vote to put Republicans on record ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms on a conflict that has driven up food and fuel prices and drew just 34% approval in a Reuters/Ipsos poll this week; the vote came two days after Trump told the U.N. he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic."
item.dc:creator: Patricia Zengerle, Reuters

item.title: More than 20 mining claims filed in San Juan County on former Bears Ears land
item.description: Conservation groups say 23 mining claims have been filed in San Juan County on land stripped from Bears Ears National Monument since protections lapsed Sept. 11 following Trump administration modifications to the monument and other federal lands. The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance reports that Kimmerle Mining, a Moab-based prospecting company, filed 20 of them, near Lockhart Basin and the previously reclaimed Easy Peasy Mine. Charlie Luke, the Wilderness Society's Utah director, said 16 claims went in immediately after the mining ban lifted and called the activity proof that the threat is real rather than hypothetical. He argued special interests should not be allowed to profit from Bears Ears at the expense of future generations. Tribal leaders and conservation organizations are renewing calls to restore the monument's original boundaries.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Alaska Air expects Boeing 737 MAX 10 certification this month
item.description: Alaska Air expects the Federal Aviation Administration to certify Boeing's 737 MAX 10 by the end of September and plans to take its first delivery next spring, Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on Thursday. The airline aims to put the jet into passenger service between April and mid-May, though Berry said it must still finish certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the aircraft itself is approved, a process taking a few months. He called the timeline "sporting" but said the carrier is not panicking yet. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said last week that certification was coming very soon, with flight testing complete and final documentation in progress; the MAX 10 made up about 31% of Boeing's undelivered 737 orders at the end of June. Alaska now expects 22 MAX 10 deliveries in 2027 and 30 in 2028, part of a January order — the largest in its history — covering 105 of the jets plus rights to 35 more.
item.dc:creator: Dan Catchpole and Rajesh Kumar Singh, Reuters

item.title: Kevin O'Leary, Fox News seek dismissal of defamation lawsuit stemming from data center debate
item.description: Kevin O'Leary and Fox News have both asked a federal court to throw out a defamation suit tied to the fight over a proposed Box Elder County data center. Alliance for a Better Utah, Elevate Strategies and leaders Joshua Kanter and Gabrielle Finlayson sued July 15 in U.S. District Court in Salt Lake City, alleging O'Leary defamed them by suggesting they had ties to China during the public debate. O'Leary, who is behind the data center proposal, filed his response Monday arguing that his remarks came on opinion programming during an eight-week political fight in which both sides traded accusations, and that no reasonable viewer would take them as factual reporting. The comments at issue were made in a May 11 interview with Fox host Maria Bartiromo. Fox News argued in its own motion that the complaint fails to show the malice a defamation claim requires.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: At UN, Netanyahu defends Israel as delegates storm out
item.description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a combative defense of his country's regional actions at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday as dozens of delegates walked out in protest, prompting him to call them "moral cowards." Facing growing international isolation and an election he could lose, he used the address to attack New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has called him a war criminal and described him this week as the architect of a genocide against Palestinians. Netanyahu told Mamdani he could not be silenced and falsely accused him of supporting Hamas. He also accused Western European leaders of giving in to what he called antisemitic mobs and said Qatar and Turkey were spreading lies about Israel. It was his first visit to New York since Mamdani took office in January; Mamdani, who campaigned on arresting Netanyahu but later said he lacked the legal authority, did not immediately respond to Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Antoni Slodkowski and John Irish, Reuters

item.title: What is Utah's worst road? KSL drivers share their #1 suggestion
item.description: KSL asked its social media audience to name Utah's worst road and got dozens of replies, with one answer standing out: Pioneer Crossing in Lehi. Drivers pointed to a mix of heavy congestion, shifting construction and curving lanes on what has become a main route from Eagle Mountain to Interstate 15. Saratoga Springs resident Amy Cielowski said she leaves for work two hours early because of it, Dallin Liddle said the constantly moving lane markings make it dangerous, and Sean Anderson said he would rather detour through Lehi Main Street. UDOT spokesperson John Gleason said the agency is aware of the problem and recently expanded the road, increasing capacity by 50%. Crews are now installing traffic arms for new FLEX lanes that will switch direction for morning and evening rush hours.
item.dc:creator: Brian Carlson, KSL

item.title: Police officers in Indianapolis are accused of abusing Flock camera system
item.description: Misuse of license-plate surveillance technology has drawn criminal charges against five people tied to the Indianapolis police department — four serving officers and one who has since left. All five face fraud and misconduct counts, and one of them is additionally charged with stalking for allegedly running the Flock system to locate women he wanted to approach. Investigators say a different officer queried his former wife's vehicle upwards of 950 times over half a year. The department has sidelined the four still on the force, and its chief wants them dismissed.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: New polling reveals Utahn's opinions on data centers in their neighborhoods
item.description: Two-thirds of Utahns surveyed — 67% — would rather leave their neighborhoods unchanged than accept a data center nearby, according to polling by the Deseret News with the Hinckley Institute of Politics. The national picture ran the same direction: close to 60% ranked shielding their communities from such facilities above the goal of outpacing China, while just 26% treated the buildout as a competitive necessity and 15% had no firm view. Respondents weighed in even on projects that came packaged with promises of jobs and local economic growth.
item.dc:creator: Curtis Booker, KSL

item.title: A new candidate emerges in Utah this election season: El Niño
item.description: Ski Utah has turned hopes for a big snow year into a mock campaign, planting a sign outside Deer Valley Resort this month reading "Vote Super El Niño 2026-2027." The nonprofit, which markets the state's ski and snowboard resorts, plans to make the yard signs generally available next week. President and CEO Nathan Rafferty framed it as the one race all of Utah can agree on, whatever divides the state the rest of the year. The push follows a record-low snowpack during the La Niña-influenced 2025-2026 winter; the National Weather Service Climate Prediction Center reported earlier this month that there is better than a 90% chance of a very strong El Niño event this fall and winter. Forecasters note the pattern usually pushes the Pacific jet stream toward the Southwest, though Utah typically sits between the two regimes and sees a near-even mix of above-normal, normal and below-normal precipitation either way.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: FDA nominee Overton says all vaccines safe as senators press on shots, abortion, vaping
item.description: Dr. Heidi Overton, President Donald Trump's nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, told senators at a contentious confirmation hearing Thursday that every vaccine on the market is safe and effective and that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is not lethal. The health committee's Republican chairman, Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician, pressed her on the point and criticized her for standing behind Trump as he signed an executive order splitting the childhood vaccine schedule into more doses, saying the order rested on "zero scientific evidence" and would raise costs for families. Cassidy noted she was present when Trump called the MMR shot potentially quite lethal, and asked whether she would break with him as the country faces its worst measles outbreak in decades. Overton repeatedly declined to say Trump had been wrong on health matters. Democratic Sen. Ed Markey pointed out that the America First Policy Institute, where Overton once held a leadership role, had said she helped shape the executive order.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Aboulenein, Reuters

item.title: Delta Center renovations near finish line as Utah Mammoth home debut nears
item.description: Crews are working around the clock to finish the latest phase of the Delta Center's renovation before the Utah Mammoth play their first home preseason game there Oct. 1. Construction fencing still rings parts of the arena plaza, and concessions supervisor Nick Romrell said that two weeks ago he would have doubted it could be ready. The work is part of a three-phase plan that began in 2025 with the lower bowl, focuses this year on the north end of the upper bowl, and moves to the south end of the upper bowl in 2027. Mammoth President Chris Armstrong described 230,000 square feet of reimagined space in the north end, new sidelines, a premium club and gondolas in the building's upper reaches. Smith Entertainment Group CEO Ryan Smith said the redesign aimed at making every sightline work for both basketball and hockey.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Couple accused of hitting children with tree branches and withholding food as 'discipline'
item.description: A Sanpete County couple was booked into jail Wednesday for investigation of abusing their six children, ages 2 to 16. Andrew Leroy Skousen, 46, who serves on the Spring City Planning and Zoning Commission, and Michelle Beck Skousen, 42, each face 11 counts of child abuse. The Division of Child and Family Services referred the case about a week earlier to the North Valley Police Department rather than Spring City police, who had a conflict with the suspects, according to a booking affidavit. Investigators interviewed the children and reviewed photos showing significant bruising on one child's legs and arms. One child told police their father had them cut a tree branch he called a "switch" and then hit them on the legs with it, leaving welts, and said he would rather be hit with a belt because it hurt less; the affidavit also describes withholding food as punishment and emotional abuse.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Bear tranquilized, removed from Salt Lake City's Avenues neighborhood
item.description: Utah wildlife biologists tranquilized and removed a young bear from Salt Lake City's Avenues neighborhood Wednesday night after several days of sightings. The Division of Wildlife Resources began getting reports Tuesday about a bear moving through the Upper Avenues, where homes give way to the foothills. Resident Lydia Foreman said she and her husband spotted it from their window while setting up dinner, sitting near the base of some trees, and that although they regularly see deer and rabbits and occasionally cougars or bobcats, a bear in the city was startling. The animal was seen again around sunset Wednesday in a tree at Kay Rees Park, 535 E. 14th Ave., where biologists climbed a Salt Lake City fire truck ladder to tranquilize it about 9:30 p.m. and firefighters helped bring it down. DWR spokeswoman Faith Jolley said the bear was still being assessed Thursday morning as officials decided whether to relocate or euthanize it.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Neighborhood bombarded by roofing and repair companies after hail storm
item.description: A Kaysville neighborhood battered by Friday's hail and tornado-force winds is now fielding a wave of solicitations from roofing and repair companies. Resident Rich Baron said the sky turned green and garbage cans flew down the street as ping-pong-ball-sized hail damaged his roof, solar panels, vinyl fence and vehicles, leaving some panels cracked or no longer working. The calls began about an hour after the hail stopped, with one caller offering to add him to a repair list and explaining that his number came from a database. Baron said roughly a dozen companies have since called, knocked on his door or lingered near his house, all insisting they were not storm chasers. He plans to hire a company a friend recommended instead, finding that more trustworthy.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Powerful Hurricane Polo drenches Mexico's coast from offshore as Nolo nears Hawaii
item.description: Hurricane Polo pushed bands of heavy rain across Mexico's Pacific coast on Thursday while Tropical Storm Nolo bore down on Hawaii. Forecasters expected Polo to hold Category 5 strength as it skirts the Mexican coastline over several days; the National Hurricane Center in Miami warned that even with the eye and strongest winds staying offshore, the rain could bring life-threatening flooding and landslides. Nolo was churning about 295 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, forecast to reach hurricane strength Thursday night and approach the Big Island as early as Friday, prompting a hurricane watch for all of Hawaii County. Gov. Josh Green's office closed Big Island public schools and state and county offices Thursday and Friday, with Maui County closing Friday; forecasters projected up to 20 inches of rain on Maui and up to 35 inches on the Big Island. Mexican authorities were preparing shelters and clearing beaches, and the storms come as El Niño tends to suppress Atlantic activity while energizing Pacific cyclones.
item.dc:creator: Megan Janetsky and Gabriela Aoun, Associated Press

item.title: 6-year-old girl dies in West Haven after vehicle collision
item.description: A 6-year-old girl died Thursday morning after being hit by a vehicle the previous evening in West Haven, the Weber County Sheriff's Office said. Deputies were called about 6:45 p.m. Wednesday to a report of a vehicle striking a pedestrian on 2550 South near 2700 West. A sheriff's deputy was nearby when she was hit and performed CPR before she was taken to a hospital in critical condition. She died early the next morning. The driver remained at the scene and cooperated with investigators, and the crash was still under investigation Thursday morning.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Charges filed against alleged gunman who 'wasn't going to let that slide'
item.description: Carl Devon Hardy, 30, of Sandy, was charged Wednesday in 3rd District Court with six felonies after prosecutors said he shot at two strangers during a verbal dispute, wounding one. The counts include shooting a gun and causing serious injury, a first-degree felony; aggravated assault resulting in serious injury and being a restricted person in possession of a firearm, both second-degree felonies; and aggravated assault plus two counts of illegal discharge of a gun, third-degree felonies. Police responded Sept. 17 to reports of gunshots near 8372 S. Bellingham Drive and found two scenes, one in a grocery store parking lot and one at a nearby apartment complex, recovering three shell casings. Two men in their 20s said Hardy emerged from an apartment wanting to fight and that two other men calmed him down, but that he came back out shooting when they returned to the lot a short time later. One victim was hospitalized with a gunshot wound to the foot; the pair jumped into a canal and hid behind vehicles at a dealership, where officers found them.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Habitual sex offender convicted in Festival of Trees incident faces new charges
item.description: Christopher Joseph Rebstock, 51, of Salt Lake City, was charged Wednesday in 3rd District Court with ten counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, second-degree felonies that each carry a habitual sex offender sentencing enhancement. The case began in March when the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a cyber tip that an account had uploaded several dozen files depicting minors in sexually explicit conduct; Utah's Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force traced the account to Rebstock. Prosecutors note he was still on parole at the time from a 2013 conviction for attempted aggravated sexual abuse of a child, for which he received three years to life. That case stemmed from the 2012 Festival of Trees in Sandy, where witnesses saw him grab an 11-year-old girl who had just performed with her dance troupe and chased him down until officers arrived. He was already a registered sex offender then, having pleaded guilty in 2001 to an amended charge of attempted aggravated sex abuse of a child.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Professional football coming to Utah as UFL announces expansion
item.description: The United Football League announced Tuesday that Utah will get a franchise in 2028, part of a four-market expansion that grows the spring league to 10 teams. The new team will play home games at America First Field in Sandy. Rhode Island and Colorado Springs are set to join in 2027, with Utah and Oklahoma City following in 2028. UFL President and CEO Russ Brandon told KSL that Salt Lake stood out as a growing market with a strong football culture, describing the league as a football entertainment company. KSL Sports' Jeremiah Jensen and Steven Sylvester said Utah fans have consistently backed new franchises and expect the same here, though Jensen noted the league's own viability is a separate question.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Local teen inspired by childhood care hopes to use ASL to help deaf patients
item.description: Marking the International Day of Sign Languages, KSL profiled 19-year-old Phoenix Small, who is turning his own medical history into a career plan. Small was born with severe clubfeet, and doctors warned his family he might end up in a wheelchair or face amputation. He was treated at Shriners Children's Salt Lake City through multiple surgeries and stretches in casts, relearning to walk each time, and described walking on his own without casts for the first time as freeing. In high school he enrolled in American Sign Language to satisfy a graduation requirement and fell in love with it, though he said it took about a year and a half to get the hang of it. He now hopes to work as a medical interpreter and eventually help deaf patients at the same hospital that treated him.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Tiny worms may help doctors treat human brain disease
item.description: A flatworm called a planarian, capable of regenerating portions of its own brain, is the focus of research that may eventually pay off in human medicine. A University of Georgia team pinpointed close to a dozen genes behind that regenerative capacity, and the neurons the worms rebuild have counterparts in people. Figuring out how those genes operate, the researchers suggest, might someday open paths toward therapies for Alzheimer's, Parkinson's or traumatic brain injury.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Weather service confirms last week's storms produced a second Utah tornado
item.description: The National Weather Service has confirmed that last week's severe thunderstorm system spawned a second Utah tornado, this one near the Colorado border. In a preliminary report issued Tuesday, the agency's Grand Junction office said a brief and weak tornado touched down about 5 p.m. Friday between Jensen and Dinosaur, Colorado, lasting a few minutes and causing no damage. It was rated EF-U on the Enhanced Fujita Scale, meaning its peak winds, path length and other characteristics could not be determined. The office had issued severe thunderstorm and flash flood warnings for the area that evening but no tornado warning. The touchdown came roughly three hours after a far larger tornado formed in the mountains east of Fruit Heights, cutting a path 100 to 200 yards wide and well over a mile long; KSL meteorologists who toured the site estimate winds of 100 mph or more, which would rate at least EF-1.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: IOC President Kirsty Coventry visits Utah kids as excitement builds for 2034 Winter Games
item.description: International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry spent part of her first Utah visit in the job on Wednesday with children, as the state builds toward the 2034 Winter Games. She joined an assembly at Washington Elementary School in Salt Lake City, where students carried banners they had made and Olympians, Paralympians and community leaders greeted them as champions. Later she visited young players with the Utah Lady Grizzlies, an all-girls hockey organization drawing from across Utah and the Mountain West. The school stop was part of Champion Schools 34, an education initiative launched earlier this month in more than 70 elementary schools across seven Utah districts, building on the IOC's Olympic Values Education Program and pairing values like excellence, respect and friendship with reading and academics. Washington Elementary was the eighth school to hold an Olympic-style opening ceremony; organizers say the aim is to give Utah children a sense of ownership of the Games well before they arrive.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: University of Utah awards $250K climate prize to Houston-based Solidec
item.description: Houston-based Solidec won the $250,000 Wilkes Climate Innovation Prize on Wednesday, chosen from more than 500 submissions and a field of nine finalists. The University of Utah's Wilkes Center for Climate Science and Policy awards the prize each year to climate solutions with real potential that face uncertainty over funding or adoption. This year's announcement was made live from the Explorer's Club in New York City as part of Climate Week NYC. Solidec co-founder and chief technology officer Yang Xia said the company began with the premise that chemicals shouldn't come on trucks, and it builds autonomous on-site generators that produce essential chemicals from air, water and electricity — cutting transportation, storage, waste and emissions. University President Taylor Randall said the center's guiding principle is moving ideas out of the lab and into practical use.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Utah ranks No. 1 for lowest student loan debt burden, new study says
item.description: A WalletHub study released this month ranks Utah first in the country for the lowest overall student loan debt burden, weighing both how much debt students carry and what share of them carry it. Craig Whyte, executive director of Utah State University's financial aid office, attributed the result partly to Utah's comparatively low cost of higher education, which he credited in part to state Legislature efforts. He said his office works to identify money students never have to repay — scholarships, grants and similar resources — before discussing loans, and that the last thing they want is to tell a student to cover a gap with a large loan and deal with it later. USU senior Marinn Cahoon, who took out no loans, said students should work out how they will pay for college before they arrive on campus.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Qualcomm secures extension to global patent licensing pact with Apple
item.description: Qualcomm said Thursday that Apple has extended their global patent-licensing agreement, though the chip designer gave no timeline for the new terms. The existing deal runs through March 31, 2027, with an option to extend two more years; neither company responded to requests for comment. The extension keeps Apple tied to part of Qualcomm's patent portfolio even as the iPhone maker works to reduce its reliance on Qualcomm modem chips, and Qualcomm said in July that revenue from Apple products would fall faster than expected. Licensing accounted for roughly 15% of Qualcomm's revenue in the June quarter, and the company is counting on data center growth to offset the 2027 shortfall. The relationship traces to a 2019 settlement that ended a two-year global fight over wireless-patent royalties and modem supply, under which Apple made an undisclosed payment and the two agreed to a six-year licensing deal. Reuters corrected the story's headline to reflect that the agreement covers patent licensing rather than chip licensing.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Salt Lake City's contentious housing options proposal receives key endorsement
item.description: Salt Lake City's Planning Commission voted unanimously Wednesday night to recommend the city's proposed "expanding housing options" zoning text amendment, sending it on to the City Council, which holds the final vote. The measure would rework six primary residential zones — R-1, R-2, SR-1 and SR-1A plus two subsections — covering roughly 33,000 properties and about three-quarters of the city's residentially zoned land. Landowners could build small single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and four-unit townhomes on smaller lots, with maximum heights rising a few feet but staying at or under 30 feet. The vote followed another heated public hearing that left residents sharply divided, and Commissioner Richard Leverett said beforehand that the outcome would be largely trial and error. Supporters watching from the chambers applauded when it passed.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Prosecutors no longer seeking death penalty against Douglas Carter, citing new DNA evidence
item.description: Utah County Attorney Jeffrey Gray filed a motion Wednesday withdrawing the state's notice of intent to seek the death penalty against Douglas Carter, citing a DNA report prosecutors received the day before. Gray wrote that while the results do not exonerate Carter, DNA from blood on a doorknob and on the handle of the knife used in the killing excluded him, and that the finding warrants re-examining both the prosecution and Carter's custody status. Carter, 70, is charged with aggravated murder in the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen at her Provo home. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton said he got no advance notice of the report and had not yet been able to tell his client, adding that Carter has maintained his innocence for 41 years and that the actual killer remains unidentified. The Utah Supreme Court affirmed a new trial for Carter in May 2025, upholding Judge Derek Pullan's finding of intentional misconduct by police and a prosecutor.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Peruvian teacher with expiring visa focus of campaign to keep him at Vernal school
item.description: Backers of Jose Mendoza, a Peruvian teacher in Uintah High School's dual-language Spanish immersion program in Vernal, have launched a fundraising campaign to pay for an H-1B visa so he can stay. Mendoza teaches on a J-1 visa that expires at the end of the 2026-2027 school year, leaving his future in Utah uncertain. Supporters point to his results: the spring before he arrived, three students qualified for a college-level Spanish class, a figure that now stands at 48. Genica Donaldson, who leads the drive and has a student in his class, said the community wants continuity and teachers invested in the area. Colleague James McKay, who teaches German, Spanish and ESL at the school, said Mendoza has worked tirelessly to build the program.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Uintah School District studying middle school closure amid declining enrollment, safety concerns
item.description: The Uintah School District board of education voted 4-1 on Monday to begin studying whether to close Uintah Middle School after the 2026-2027 school year, with board member Robin McClellan casting the lone opposing vote. Superintendent Rick Woodford said enrollment has fallen by 1,000 students over the past decade and is expected to keep dropping over the next eight years, noting the district let go of 17 full-time employees last year. He framed the decision as a hard choice needed now for future financial viability. Woodford also said the middle school sits on the state's list of unreinforced masonry buildings, making it more vulnerable in an earthquake. Utah code requires at least 90 days' notice for public input before a closure vote, and Monday's action started that clock; the district's situation mirrors a statewide trend, with Utah K-12 enrollment declining in 2025 for a third straight year after two decades of growth.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: As police probe 2 Ole Miss student deaths, they urge people to avoid herbal extract kratom
item.description: Authorities investigating the deaths of two University of Mississippi students are urging people to avoid kratom, an herbal extract with opioid- and stimulant-like effects, after finding packaged kratom in both cases. Lafayette County Metro Narcotics, a multiagency unit, said the product came from a retail store, though there is no confirmed link between the two deaths and no confirmation that kratom or any other substance contributed. The students were found dead Monday at their homes, one on campus and one off, following a weekend centered on a major football rivalry; autopsies are being scheduled, according to the county coroner as reported by CNN affiliate WAPT. Officials asked the public to avoid any medication or substance not prescribed to them or obtained from a trusted, regulated source. Dr. Shawnboda Mead, the university's vice chancellor for student affairs, said the school is heartbroken and noted the coroner has confirmed only two student deaths despite considerable unverified claims circulating on social media.
item.dc:creator: Cindy Von Quednow, CNN

item.title: Curtis hasn't heard from White House since calling for investigation of Trump Jr.
item.description: Utah Sen. John Curtis said Wednesday he has heard nothing from the Trump administration since asking the Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden as part of a look at presidential relatives' business and personal dealings. Speaking to Utah reporters over Zoom, Curtis said colleagues from both parties have privately thanked him for saying what they were thinking. His letter followed his criticism of a Bahamas wedding after-party for Trump Jr. that ProPublica reported was paid for by a Russian oligarch; the president did not attend and later said his son repaid the money. Curtis said his concern goes beyond that event to Trump Jr.'s involvement in prediction markets and a cryptocurrency venture, calling the conflicts "deep" rather than accidental. Elected to the Senate in 2024 and not up again until 2030, Curtis is drawing criticism from some fellow Republicans.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL; Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Anthropic says Claude AI helped discover novel enzyme system
item.description: Anthropic said Wednesday that its Claude model helped identify a previously undescribed enzyme system with features reminiscent of the gene-editing tool CRISPR, the first result from the company's biology research push. According to Anthropic, Claude analyzed large DNA databases and surfaced an unusual arrangement centered on a reverse transcriptase, the enzyme class that copies RNA into DNA. The company named the system array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ART, and said it contains repeating DNA sequences resembling CRISPR patterns. Anthropic noted the underlying reverse transcriptase had appeared in earlier studies but said Claude was apparently first to recognize the broader system, including an array of non-coding sequences and an extra protein of unknown function. The announcement follows Reuters reporting that Anthropic had quietly set up a wet lab in the San Francisco Bay Area.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Rivian recalls about 100,700 vehicles over rearview camera display issue
item.description: Rivian Automotive said Wednesday it is recalling roughly 100,700 vehicles — most of what it has built to date — over a software flaw that can block the rearview camera display. The recall covers certain 2022-2026 R1T pickups, 2022-2027 R1S SUVs and 2027 R2 models, and involves non-compliance with U.S. and Canadian rear-visibility safety standards. The company told Reuters that in rare cases where stability control is switched off, a prompt asking the driver to re-enable it can overlap the camera view when shifting into reverse until the vehicle starts moving. Rivian said more than 95% of affected vehicles have already received a software fix. All vehicles built after Aug. 10 ship with the corrected software.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Judge says Trump's White House media ban may not comply with legal precedents
item.description: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly said Wednesday that President Donald Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House appears not to comply with binding appellate precedent, though he did not rule immediately. The outlets, which sued Monday, sought a temporary restraining order restoring their access, arguing the ban violated First Amendment protections and their due process rights. Kelly, a Trump appointee, pointed to two D.C. Circuit decisions establishing that journalists are entitled to due process before press passes are revoked, and said the process those cases laid out was not followed. He noted the government argued those rulings were wrongly decided but said that as a district judge he must apply them. Attorney Theodore Boutrous, for the news organizations, called the bans an unprecedented and severe punishment imposed without a semblance of due process; Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik argued the administration's side.
item.dc:creator: Jan Wolfe and Jack Queen, Reuters

item.title: Utah mother accused of rubbing hot spices on daughter
item.description: A 49-year-old Hurricane woman was charged Wednesday with aggravated child abuse, a first-degree felony, after her teenage daughter told police she was beaten and burned as punishment. Police say the mother picked the girl up from school Monday after she got in trouble, then turned the home's music up loud and struck her with a belt over roughly two hours. The girl reported that her mother rubbed a seeded spice on her face, mouth and throat, which burned and made her vomit, and threatened her with a knife. Investigators say the mother also forced the girl into the shower, hit her there and cut her hair with scissors. Officers documented large bruises consistent with belt strikes and arrested her Tuesday; KSL is withholding her name to protect the victim's identity.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: McDonald's expects inflation to keep traffic flat, shares dip after $8.5 billion capex plan
item.description: McDonald's told investors Wednesday that industrywide customer traffic in its key markets will likely stay flat while inflation remains high, sending its shares down as much as 6.5% to a near four-year low of $234.03. The chain simultaneously announced an $8.5 billion, decade-long support package for franchisees bearing costs under its "NEXT" strategy, plus targets for restaurant productivity and operating margins in the low- to mid-50% range by 2030. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the winners will be companies that create more demand and deliver it more efficiently. New U.S. business head Skye Anderson acknowledged the company had fallen short on consistent execution and must improve restaurant operations. The warning follows a second quarter in which McDonald's missed U.S. sales growth estimates and blamed missteps in winning back lower-income diners; its stock is down about 22% this year.
item.dc:creator: Anuja Bharat Mistry and Waylon Cunningham, Reuters

item.title: FBI investigating hackers' claim of stolen sensitive employee data, compromised jobs website
item.description: The FBI said Wednesday it is investigating claims by the hacking group ShinyHunters that it stole sensitive data on thousands of agents and job applicants and compromised the FBIJobs.gov portal. The bureau said the point of breach remains undetermined and that it is working with third-party providers supporting the site to limit risk; the portal was still offline Wednesday afternoon. A message circulating online and addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel and cyber division chief Brett Leatherman claimed the group holds data on nearly all FBI agents and applicants. The claims could not be independently verified, and an email to an address linked to the group went unanswered. ShinyHunters also demanded the bureau retract or correct a May public advisory describing it as a criminal group specializing in large-scale breaches and extortion.
item.dc:creator: Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Disney to raise prices on Disney+, Hulu subscriptions, Bloomberg News reports
item.description: Disney will raise prices across several streaming plans, Bloomberg News reported Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The ad-free Disney+ tier is set to climb $2.50, or 13%, to $21.49 a month, and ad-free Hulu rises by the same amount, while the ad-free Disney+ and Hulu bundle goes up $2 to $21.99. Standalone ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu plans each increase 50 cents to $12.49, though the ad-supported bundle stays at $12.99. Customers were expected to be notified of the changes as early as Wednesday, and Disney did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The move follows a broader industry pattern of raising prices and leaning on ad-supported tiers, and comes a week after Disney named Karandeep Anand its first chief technology officer and promoted Adam Smith to lead streaming.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj, Reuters

item.title: Idaho high school is victim of alleged 'swatting' hoax, deputies say
item.description: The Bonneville County Sheriff's Office says Bonneville High School near Idaho Falls was targeted by a swatting hoax Wednesday after a reported threat near the campus around 11 a.m. Swatting involves false emergency reports designed to draw a heavy law enforcement response, creating chaos and risk of injury, according to the FBI. Bonneville School District 93 alerted parents that the school had entered a hall check over a possible weapon on campus and asked people to stay away while officers investigated. A hall check keeps students and staff inside classrooms while instruction continues, one of four emergency procedures alongside evacuation, reverse evacuation and lockdown. Deputies checked the area as a precaution, found no violence or actual threat, and lifted the hall check after roughly 45 minutes.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Hart, EastIdahoNews.com

item.title: 'How else am I supposed to discipline them?' man accused of choking child asks police
item.description: Jason James Quigley, 36, of Santaquin, was charged Wednesday in 4th District Court with four counts of aggravated child abuse, a first-degree felony, plus obstruction of justice and public intoxication. Police were called Sunday after a 9-year-old ran to a neighbor's home reporting that Quigley was choking a 5-year-old at the residence. When officers questioned him, Quigley asked what else he was supposed to do to discipline the children and admitted drinking heavily, according to a booking affidavit; the younger child was found hiding under a bed. Both children told investigators Quigley believed they had stolen a cellphone. Prosecutors also allege he drove them up Goshen Canyon and held each over the river while threatening to drop them, saying he was testing them.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: McDonald's to create tiered loyalty program to lure repeat visitors
item.description: McDonald's will restructure its loyalty program into tiers, chief marketing officer Morgan Flatley said at the chain's investor day Wednesday, aiming to distinguish frequent customers from occasional ones. Flatley did not give a launch date or the number of tiers, but described three groups: about 220 million members worldwide who visit monthly or at least every 90 days, and roughly 150 million who have not eaten there in months. Frequent visitors could get faster points, early access to limited-time menu items and invitations to launch events, while mid-tier members may see game-like online challenges; lapsed members would be targeted with perks such as a birthday bonus. U.S. members can expect Uber ride credits and Disney+ subscriptions this year. CEO Chris Kempczinski said loyalty members account for about 30% of sales, and the shift follows a broader restaurant-industry move away from broad discounting that Starbucks made in January.
item.dc:creator: Waylon Cunningham, Reuters

item.title: Utah group to hold vigil honoring state's 2026 murder victims
item.description: Utah Homicide Survivors will hold a candlelight vigil at the State Capitol on Friday at 7 p.m. to mark the National Day of Remembrance for Homicide Victims. The service is set to include a memory garden, speeches and live music honoring Utahns killed and supporting their families. Among the scheduled speakers is a sister of Summer Roney, who was found slain in the back seat of her ex-boyfriend's car nearly two years ago. State officials and the FBI generally publish annual murder figures at year's end. Prominent 2026 cases include three people killed in Wayne County in March and two found dead in a Kearns home in April in what was later described as a domestic dispute.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Construction on SR 224 in Park City nears end, UDOT says
item.description: The Utah Department of Transportation and High Valley Transit say two major projects along state Route 224 in Park City are wrapping up after months of work. Crews are finishing new turning lanes at Deer Valley Drive and Park Avenue, with additional work concluding near Kimball Junction. High Valley Transit said one more paving job is scheduled for next week and that most construction should be done by the end of October. The work supports a larger bus rapid transit project linking Kimball Junction and Old Town. Bus service on that line is expected to begin in 2028.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Spanish Fork City Council approves changes to city code for data centers
item.description: The Spanish Fork City Council voted to amend city code, clearing a path for a proposed data center to move forward. Mayor Mike Mendenhall said the council weighed residents' concerns, particularly over water use, noting the city meters its water and could halt supply if needed. Jeff Chavez, CEO of Volition, the company behind the project, said its closed-loop cooling system uses roughly as much water as one or two Utah households. Council members also capped the city at a single data center unless a future vote changes that limit.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Utah hits new record for price of diesel fuel
item.description: Diesel in Utah reached a record $6.58 per gallon on Wednesday, according to AAA — two cents above Tuesday, 44 cents above a week earlier and $2.85 higher than a year ago. GasBuddy's head of petroleum analysis, Patrick De Haan, told KSL the increase traces largely to geopolitics, citing Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and disruption at the Strait of Hormuz tied to the U.S. and Israeli conflict with Iran. He said the refinery attacks became more damaging once the strait was closed, leaving Middle East refining capacity bottled up. GasBuddy pegged Salt Lake City diesel at $6.61, with regular unleaded just under $5. De Haan said the U.S. faces a tight diesel market rather than an outright shortage, and cautioned that a diesel export ban under consideration by the Trump administration would bring complications.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Zelenskyy, at UN, urges leaders to keep choking Russia's revenues and impede its war efforts
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday that Russia's revenues must remain a target, arguing that trade with Moscow buys the war more time. Speaking in English, he cast doubt on Putin's willingness to end the fighting, calling him "Patient Zero" from whom war keeps spreading. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the Security Council the same day that Moscow is willing to negotiate a lasting peace but will not accept a mere pause, which he said would let Ukraine and its backers rearm. Russia is scheduled to address the assembly Saturday, with Lavrov again standing in for Putin, who has not attended in years. Western analysts estimate more than 500,000 Russian troops killed and over 500,000 Ukrainian military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths, in a war now past four and a half years with front lines largely static.
item.dc:creator: Edith M. Lederer and Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press

item.title: World's largest copper mine halts operations after worker death
item.description: BHP suspended all operations Wednesday at Escondida in Chile, the world's largest copper mine, after a worker was killed in an accident during maintenance work. The union representing the site told Reuters the accident involved a front-end loader of a type commonly used in the industry. BHP gave no timeline for restarting; under Chilean practice, mines typically resume after a fatality only once inspectors confirm conditions are safe. Escondida sits in the Atacama Desert and is operated by BHP, with Rio Tinto holding a 30% stake and Japan's JECO Corp 12.5%. The company had projected output of up to 1.28 million metric tons of copper at the site this year.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Food insecurity up by 100K, Utah Food Bank reports. Here's a way to help
item.description: The Utah Food Bank reports that nearly 100,000 more Utahns are facing food insecurity than a year ago, bringing the state's total closer to 600,000 people. Demand typically climbs in fall and winter as household expenses rise and children spend more time out of school. America First Credit Union is collecting nonperishable food and cash donations at its branches, and director of public relations Dave Nellis said the contributions are distributed to six food pantries and organizations statewide. Donors do not need to be credit union members to participate. Nellis said small contributions add up, describing the goal as feeding neighbors and strengthening the community.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Fired IT employee accused of hacking Utah city emails, posting on Facebook
item.description: Wesley Fullenwider, 31, of Vineyard, was charged Wednesday in 4th District Court with unlawful computer access gaining confidential information, a third-degree felony, plus two misdemeanor counts of unlawful computer access. Prosecutors say the former contract IT technician kept getting into Vineyard city email accounts after the city asked in January that he be removed from its account. Fullenwider worked for Onward Technology, which provided IT support to Vineyard; the firm says technicians could reach client email but were not authorized to read it, and it fired him on May 11 after finding unauthorized access. Vineyard Mayor Zack Stratton told investigators that Fullenwider posted city emails to Facebook, including confidential attorney-client correspondence between the City Council and the city attorney. The Utah Attorney General's Office took up the case in May, and investigators say he accessed more than 700 emails.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump Gaza board pitches $2.45B Gaza plan, implementation uncertain
item.description: President Donald Trump's Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion plan Wednesday to begin rebuilding Gaza, presenting 66 programs to rehabilitate infrastructure and the economy at an event tied to the U.N. General Assembly. Officials conceded the plan's future is uncertain, with Israel and Hamas still at odds over terms of the U.S.-backed ceasefire announced nearly a year ago. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a long-term project that at least offers people hope. Jared Kushner, who devised the plan, acknowledged delays and said the effort was still sharpening the axe ahead of action. Reconstruction has yet to start as negotiators fail to agree on Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawal, leaving more than 2 million residents confined to about a third of the territory, and Israeli strikes continued Wednesday, killing four people including a Hamas official.
item.dc:creator: Nidal al-Mughrabi, Reuters

item.title: Mapleton bear removed from neighborhood
item.description: Utah wildlife officers trapped and removed a bear that had been raiding trash and feed in a Mapleton neighborhood for several weeks. Resident Cherise Rodman first saw the animal cross her driveway and get into garbage she had left out, and it returned the next day for a bag of chicken feed on her porch. Rodman keeps chickens and her neighbors have horses and other livestock, which she said made it lucky the bear never went after any animals. Neighbors kept storing cans in their garages, but the bear struck again Sunday night when the cans were left out, prompting the Utah Department of Wildlife to set a trap. The trap sprang Wednesday morning, and officers hauled the bear off without saying whether it would be killed or relocated.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: New Justice Court judge appointed; first new position in more than two decades
item.description: Nick Stiles has been appointed to the Salt Lake City Justice Court, filling a newly created sixth judgeship that is the court's first added position in more than 20 years. Mayor Erin Mendenhall selected Stiles from five forwarded candidates, and the City Council confirmed the choice Tuesday evening. Mendenhall said the court needed capacity to give cases proper attention and cited Stiles' range of experience across Utah's justice system. The court handles class B and C misdemeanors, infractions, traffic citations and small claims arising in Salt Lake City. Stiles currently administers the Utah Supreme Court and Court of Appeals, and previously worked as a city prosecutor, managed the Utah Judiciary's Domestic Violence Program and directed the Utah State Bar's Access to Justice Office.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Meta expected to unveil smart glasses without camera as privacy concerns grow
item.description: Meta was expected to introduce new smart glasses at its Connect conference Wednesday, including a camera-free pair, as scrutiny grows over AI devices that can record people without consent. The Information reported the camera-less models would come in two styles, Clubmaster and Burbank, alongside an expected refresh of the camera-equipped Meta Ray-Ban line and thinner augmented-reality glasses reportedly code-named Phoenix. Meta leads the category, with sales of the glasses it co-developed with EssilorLuxottica topping 7 million last year against mainly Chinese rivals such as RayNeo and Xiaomi. The devices have drawn restrictions at U.K. restaurants, pubs and theaters, plus a proposed California class action alleging Meta misled users about privacy and that human annotators reviewed footage of private moments; the company disputes the claims. Some analysts doubt dropping cameras resolves privacy worries, since the glasses can still capture audio.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Reuters

item.title: Provocative ad for bed sale leads to solicitation arrest
item.description: Miles Andrew Anderson, 22, of Salt Lake City, was arrested Tuesday and booked into the Salt Lake County Jail for investigation of 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor and obstruction of justice. The case began in June when a tipster reported a Craigslist listing that advertised a platform bed for $200 but included several photos of a girl, apparently about 12, posed on it in a nightgown. Salt Lake City police said the ad's wording and images were suspicious enough to open an investigation and obtain a warrant for the email address behind the post. Detectives traced the listing to Anderson and questioned him at his home. According to a booking affidavit, he initially claimed he had come across child sexual abuse material and bulk-downloaded it to make a predator-poaching post before deleting most of the files.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Award-winning author, creative writing teacher named Salt Lake City's first poet laureate
item.description: Poet and educator Joel Long has been named Salt Lake City's inaugural poet laureate by the city's Arts Council and Mayor's Office. Long, who lives in Sugar House, has taught English and creative writing at Rowland Hall since 2004 and has published seven books, five of them poetry collections. His honors include a White Pine Press Poetry Prize and a 2009 Salt Lake City Mayor's Award for Literary Arts. Mayor Erin Mendenhall said Long would help carry poetry beyond the page into daily city life while establishing the program's foundation. The three-year post, which drew 16 applicants after the search opened in April, carries a $5,000 annual honorarium and asks the laureate to write civic poems, run neighborhood readings and workshops, and develop a signature community project.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Space investment more than doubled to $23 billion in year to June, report says
item.description: Private investment in space companies worldwide more than doubled to $23 billion in the year through June, according to a report released Wednesday by British investment firm Seraphim and Relm Insurance. The firms attribute the surge partly to SpaceX's June IPO, which reshaped the funding landscape and drew investors hunting for the next comparable payoff. Relm said the sector is moving from hype to commercial reality, with capital flowing toward Earth observation, in-orbit manufacturing and satellite supply chains. Relm product development VP Andrew Bonwick said Earth observation's real value lies in analytics, since customers buy answers about ships, crops, refineries or wildfire risk rather than space services. The report found investors growing more selective toward Earth observation firms with visible revenue, while in-orbit manufacturing remains early-stage and satellite suppliers bring more production in-house to control costs.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram, Reuters

item.title: Lowe's employees give back to their community on Red Vest Day
item.description: Utah's Family Support Center was chosen earlier this year as one of 100 organizations nationwide to receive a Lowe's Community Impact Grant. On Tuesday, Lowe's Red Vest associates spent the morning at LifeStart Village in Midvale putting the $10,000 grant toward improvement projects for resident families. Kurt Baker, who manages a Lowe's in Layton, said employees live in the community and were glad for the chance to give back. LifeStart Village houses dozens of single-parent families working toward independence after domestic violence and homelessness. Staff say demand far outstrips capacity, with more than 400 families currently on the waiting list.
item.dc:creator: Allison Stuart, KSL

item.title: Polo off Mexican coast is among 'the strongest storms ever' as Odalys becomes a hurricane
item.description: Hurricane Polo, which the National Hurricane Center has called an extremely dangerous storm, was churning about 165 miles south of Zihuatanejo on Wednesday with maximum sustained winds of 150 mph after briefly reaching Category 5 strength. Forecasters expected it to turn sharply northwest and then west-northwest over several days, sparing land, though tropical storm conditions were anticipated in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima through Thursday. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts did not expect the storm to make landfall, but hurricane-force winds extended 40 miles from the center and tropical-storm winds up to 105 miles. Polo became the Pacific season's third Category 5 on Tuesday after Genevieve and Lowell. A second system, Odalys, strengthened Wednesday into a Category 1 hurricane roughly 1,295 miles off the southern tip of Baja California with no threat to land.
item.dc:creator: Megan Janetsky and Desiree Brooks, Associated Press

item.title: Actress, DNA expert to keynote next year's RootsTech. Tickets available now
item.description: RootsTech 2027 will run March 4-6 at the Salt Palace in downtown Salt Lake City under the theme "Celebrate!" — chosen to echo the Salt Lake Temple Celebration beginning a month after the conference. Organizers announced Wednesday that actress Jane Seymour and genetic genealogist CeCe Moore will deliver keynotes, with Moore speaking March 4 and Seymour March 5. Registration opened Wednesday at early bird pricing; online attendance, the expo hall and Family Discovery Day events remain free, while classes require paid registration. FamilySearch International, the family history arm of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, has hosted the conference for 16 years and drew participants from more than 200 countries in 2026 across events in 24 languages. FamilySearch events director Jonathan Wing said attendees are being invited to treat family history as a living celebration spanning past, present and future.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah cancer survivor completes Wasatch 100 with two of his sons
item.description: Cory Larrabee, 50, of Draper, finished this month's Wasatch 100 Endurance Run alongside his sons Keaton, 22, and McKay, 23. McKay said he stopped at mile 93 doubting he could beat the cutoff and asked his uncle for a blessing, which he credits as a major reason he finished. His father and brother had crossed hours earlier, and Cory was waiting at the line to embrace him. Cory first ran the race in 2002 with his own father, a year after finishing chemotherapy for cancer that cost him two of his four quadriceps muscles during his senior year as a track and cross-country athlete at Southern Utah University. He described that 2002 run as proof he could do hard things and the start of a new chapter, coming when Keaton was only a few months old.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Eagle Mountain rezoning for possible data center draws little opposition
item.description: A rezoning request that could eventually allow another data center in Eagle Mountain drew only two public comments at a planning commission hearing Tuesday night, a contrast to the heated debates such projects have triggered elsewhere in Utah. The proposal comes from property owner Reagan Peck, who holds 41 acres next to the existing Meta and QTS sites south of the city. Peck told the commission the request only changes zoning and does not guarantee a data center will be built. Meta has run its Eagle Mountain facility for about five years with roughly 1,200 employees, and the QTS campus due to finish in coming months is projected to add about 2,000 jobs. Economic Development Director Abby Ivory said residents have grown familiar with the technology and that the land has little other development potential, crediting the city's outreach for public trust.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Sandy among Utah communities set to celebrate 'Dolly Day'
item.description: Sandy will host a free outdoor screening of "Steel Magnolias" on Friday at Sandy City Hall in memory of Dolly Parton, who died Aug. 25 at 80. The date, dubbed "Dolly Day," nods to her 1980 hit "9 to 5," and Tremonton, Farmington, Park City and Cedar City are planning observances of their own. Mayor Monica Zoltanski said the singer had a knack for showing up in ways that mattered to people and fits Sandy's identity as a certified kindness city. Attendees are asked to bring a new children's book for the Canyons School District #CSDReads literacy campaign. Pinkbox Doughnuts is sponsoring the event, offering gift cards to the first 50 donors and a year of doughnuts to one.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake restaurant Monarca recognized by Mexican Consulate for quality, authenticity
item.description: The Mexican Consulate in Salt Lake City awarded downtown restaurant Monarca the Sello M, or M Seal, on Tuesday, making it the first Utah restaurant to earn the designation. Owners Alfonso and Claudia Brito opened the upscale restaurant in 2021 after building up from a taco cart to a food truck to their two Santo Taco taquerias in downtown and Rose Park. Acting general consul Antonio Cruz Diaz said the seal requires a rigorous evaluation showing a restaurant uses Mexican recipes, traditional ingredients and techniques, and cooks trained in authentic Mexican cuisine. He singled out Monarca's nixtamalization process for its tortillas, its Oaxacan corn, and its use of Utah-sourced products, saying the kitchen honors its roots while still innovating. The seal is part of a Mexican Foreign Ministry initiative that has recognized 38 other U.S. restaurants, including 17 around Los Angeles.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Friendly rivalry takes center stage at Salt Lake County Senior Decathlon
item.description: Nearly 100 older adults gathered Tuesday at the Magna Kennecott Senior Center for Salt Lake County's annual Senior Decathlon. Participants from senior centers across the county competed in 10 games and activities alongside live music and food. Reigning champion Sherry Mousley, who says she once won three gold medals at a single decathlon, sat out the competition this year. Instead she volunteered, running the Boggle station, and joked that she already had enough medals. Mousley said the senior center remains a central part of her life regardless of whether she is competing.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake City close to fully replacing 200 North Temple trees lost in 2024 mishap
item.description: Salt Lake City is roughly halfway through replacing the hundreds of trees a city worker accidentally killed along the North Temple corridor in 2024 by spraying them with herbicide. Public Lands crews began planting 100 new trees in August and are repairing irrigation and soil for another 100 that have waited in planters since the mishap, with completion expected by the end of November, according to deputy director Tyler Murdock. Another 30 to 40 trees are slated for 1000 West in Fairpark this year through a partnership with the Utah State Fairpark, part of some 270 additional trees planned near the corridor along with hundreds of rose bushes. The original plantings dated to UTA's green line TRAX construction, which opened in 2013. Fairpark Community Council chairman Jeffery Olson said neighbors were distraught as the trees died off.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: 'You will not receive forgiveness from me,' sister of DUI victim tells former Layton officer
item.description: Samuel Andrew Rockwell, a former Layton police officer, appeared before the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole on Tuesday for the first time since his conviction in the 2021 crash that killed 23-year-old Emily Worley. Rockwell was off duty but already suspended and facing termination when he crashed on Bangerter Highway at an estimated 116 mph; he pleaded guilty in 2023 to automobile homicide while driving under the influence and drew a one-to-15-year sentence. Worley's sister, Kaitlin Krulisky, told the board she would not forgive him, saying he had sworn an oath to protect lives. Her father, Richard Krulisky, argued two years was too little and objected that Rockwell has served his time in county jails rather than state prison. The family also took issue with his law enforcement and military service having been raised at sentencing as grounds for leniency.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah Youth Sports Giving Day close to $4 million in overall donations
item.description: Utah Youth Sports Giving Day has drawn nearly $2.4 million in donations less than two weeks after launching, and matching gifts from Utah businesses and foundations push the campaign's total impact toward $4 million. The first-year effort targets cost, which organizers call one of the biggest barriers keeping Utah children out of sports. Jenny Teemsma of Miller Sports + Entertainment said the state calls itself the state of sport and wants young families to have access to it. Utah Crew head coach Victoria Rojo said rowing carries high operating costs and that the money lets her program expand scholarships and cut dues. The campaign, led by Miller Sports + Entertainment with the Larry H. & Gail Miller Family Foundation and the Daniels Fund, opened Sept. 12 at a Salt Lake Bees game and passed its $1 million public goal in under 10 minutes.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
item.description: Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials announced Tuesday plans to strip 760,000 people from Affordable Care Act exchanges, alleging the enrollments were fraudulent or tied to people who do not exist. Vance, who leads a government anti-fraud task force, said canceling roughly 315,000 enrollments covering those 760,000 individuals would save $2.2 billion, and he faulted the government for not verifying eligibility. He appeared alongside CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz and said another 419,000 enrollments face additional eligibility checks. The administration also imposed a six-month freeze on new agents and brokers signing up enrollees, saying that group accounts for a disproportionate share of the fraud identified. About 19.2 million Americans were enrolled in ACA marketplace plans as of early 2026, a figure that grew during the pandemic under enhanced subsidies from laws signed by former President Joe Biden.
item.dc:creator: Fatima Hussein & Michelle Price, Associated Press

item.title: 2 outdoor hockey rinks now open for public use in St. George
item.description: St. George has opened two outdoor rinks at JC Snow Park near downtown, built not for ice but for ball hockey, and they are free for public use as park amenities. Cory Henwood, who heads Red Rock Hockey, said the sport has grown fast locally and his organization offered the city both money and labor to improve and expand the space. The league began in 2023 with 50 players practicing in a school parking lot, then moved to an outdoor futsal field at the same park while hauling in its own boards. Growth to several hundred participants drove the push for a purpose-built venue. Henwood said Red Rock Hockey helped channel donations well into the six figures toward building the new rink and refurbishing the existing one.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Meta, Utah Valley University partnering to build observatory in Eagle Mountain
item.description: Meta has given Utah Valley University $450,000 toward building the Walden Park Observatory in Eagle Mountain, raising the company's total contribution to the project to $700,000. UVU, Utah County and the city of Eagle Mountain have also chipped in, and the site sits at Walden Park on North Frontier Street. UVU physics professor Joe Jensen stressed that the facility is meant for public access rather than research, deliberately sited in town instead of on a remote dark-sky peak. Jensen said the building will also host lectures for UVU students and faculty, and its design departs from the domed shape most people picture because a conventional dome would not have suited the surrounding neighborhood.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Utah History Summit brings historians together to expand the state's story
item.description: Historians, museum staff and community organizations from around Utah are meeting at the Museum of Utah for the first Utah History Summit. The gathering focuses on how state history gets preserved and shared, and on widening which communities are represented in that record. Eliza Carr, public programming manager for the Utah Historical Society, said organizers want to spotlight history work happening across Utah. One effort highlighted is the Peoples of Utah Revisited Project, which builds on a 1976 bicentennial book in which each chapter examined a different Utah demographic that had not previously been researched.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: False bomb threat causes road closures in West Haven
item.description: A reported bomb threat in West Haven on Tuesday turned out to be false after an extended police response that shut down part of 1900 West. Weber County Sheriff's Lt. Sean Endsley said the report came in around 9 a.m. and that both northbound and southbound lanes between 2550 South and 2100 South were closed while crews worked. Nearby businesses were evacuated as a bomb squad and K-9 units from Davis County swept the area. Nothing was found, but Endsley said investigators will follow up on the origin of the threat.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Exclusive-Meta testing a 'human concierge' for its new personal AI agent, Muse
item.description: Internal company posts reviewed by Reuters show Meta has been piloting a “human concierge” arrangement in which contractors quietly take over some phone calls placed by its new AI assistant, Muse. Meta told employees about the test last week, shortly after publicly launching Muse's calling feature. Muse, which has led U.S. app download charts since debuting two weeks ago, is built to carry out tasks on a user's behalf such as sending email, shopping and booking travel, and the calling feature lets it phone U.S. businesses to book appointments, check stock or gather contractor quotes. According to the posts, some employees objected on privacy grounds, warning that routing calls through call-center contractors could expose sensitive user information unintentionally.
item.dc:creator: Katie Paul, Reuters

item.title: Italian police find $3.6 million in cash hidden in apartment's walls, floors and furniture
item.description: Italian anti-mafia officers recovered $3.6 million in cash concealed in the walls, floors and furniture of an apartment in Caivano, near Naples, during a dawn raid Monday that produced 34 arrests. The Naples Carabinieri told CNN the money was in bundles of 50-euro notes wrapped in cellophane and stacked beneath floor and wall tiles and inside hidden wardrobe drawers, and officers hauled it out in plastic mop buckets to an armored vehicle. Police also seized 11 Rolex watches along with weapons and drug-dealing paraphernalia. Anti-mafia prosecutor Nicola Gratteri, who led the months-long operation, said investigators wiretapped cellphones that relatives had smuggled to incarcerated mobsters. Gratteri told reporters that a single home yielded 3.2 million euros in cash plus the valuable watches.
item.dc:creator: Barbie Latza Nadeau, CNN

item.title: Category 5 Hurricane Polo is an 'extremely dangerous' storm off the coast of Mexico
item.description: Hurricane Polo strengthened into a Category 5 storm off Mexico's southwestern coast on Tuesday and was expected to intensify further, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Forecasters described it as extremely dangerous with maximum sustained winds of 165 mph, centered about 205 miles south of Zihuatanejo and stationary over the Pacific at midday, and said an aircraft would be flown into the storm to gather data. Mexican authorities suspended classes in several coastal areas as the system brushed the shoreline. Forecasters warned of flash flooding and mudslides, with 3 to 6 inches of rain expected in Guerrero and Michoacán and lesser amounts along coastal Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco. Guerrero and Oaxaca have been hit by several powerful hurricanes in recent years and some communities are still recovering.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Semitruck driver accused of driving on I-15 shoulder without valid license
item.description: Irune Alonso Heredia, 35, of Des Plaines, Illinois, was arrested Monday and charged Tuesday in 4th District Court after allegedly driving a semitruck erratically on I-15. Prosecutors filed reckless endangerment, a third-degree felony carrying a road rage enhancement, along with a class C misdemeanor for operating a commercial vehicle without a commercial driver's license. The Utah Highway Patrol said it received reports of a semi weaving across the road around 4:50 p.m., with at least three drivers calling in, and charging documents say the truck passed a vehicle on the right shoulder. A trooper stopped the semi near Nephi and noted the trailer was still resting on the white line. According to the arrest affidavit, the driver angrily questioned why she had been pulled over before the trooper could speak.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah firefighters begin prescribed burns as preventative measure
item.description: Crews have started prescribed burning in the Heber-Kamas Ranger District, concentrating on the Castle Peak area. Firefighters are also working in the Pitt and Page area, where smoke will likely be visible to nearby residents. Dispatchers asked the public not to call in reports of smoke from these planned operations. Crews burned roughly 1,300 slash piles over the weekend, each pile being a gathered stack of forest debris that firefighters ignite in a single controlled spot.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI
item.description: The extortion group ShinyHunters claims it breached the FBI and stole data on thousands of bureau employees. In a statement on its dark-web site and in an online chat with Reuters, the group said it targeted the FBI in retaliation for a May 2026 bureau announcement that described ShinyHunters' techniques and urged targets not to pay. The group provided what it said was a screenshot of a defaced FBI job site plus a sample of stolen data; Reuters could not verify the screenshot, though a notice on the FBI job site Tuesday said it and the Special Agent Applicant Portal were unavailable. Reuters partially corroborated some of the personnel information by checking names and addresses against credit bureau records and previously breached data held by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs.
