The blaze covered an estimated 60 acres by the end of its first day, and rain helped hold it back. Firefighters had to reach the island by boat while aircraft worked from above. Because the lake's water is too salty for aircraft to scoop, air crews drew from a designated dip site instead. Utah Fire Info attributed the ignition to lightning.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Former University of Utah president seeks confirmation as US ambassador to Serbia
item.description: Michael Young, who once led the University of Utah, went before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Thursday as President Donald Trump's pick to be ambassador to Serbia. Young has also headed the University of Washington and Texas A&M, served as a trade and environmental affairs ambassador in the George H.W. Bush administration, and chaired the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom twice. Sen. Mike Lee introduced the BYU graduate and joked that reciting his credentials would sound like exaggeration. Young told senators he sees room for American business in Serbia and said that, if confirmed, he would press the government there to protect freedom of conscience for Muslims and non-Orthodox Christians alongside the Serbian Orthodox majority. He helped negotiate German reunification more than 30 years ago and would now be posted to the Western Balkans.
item.dc:creator: Frizz Flake, Deseret News

item.title: Jury finds man guilty of killing aunt's boyfriend, but determined he thought he was justified
item.description: A West Valley City jury convicted Deon Andre Jennings, 35, of second-degree felony manslaughter rather than murder, concluding prosecutors had not ruled out that he genuinely believed he was protecting himself. The case stems from April 30, 2022, when officers at the Aspenwood Apartments found Willie Houston, 59, bleeding on a kitchen floor from stab wounds to his back and neck; Houston reached a neighbor's door and named his nephew before he died. Jennings told police the two had argued over who would leave the apartment and that he stabbed Houston when he returned, then went out to buy beer instead of calling 911. Judge Coral Sanchez had rejected his self-defense claim at a 2023 justification hearing, and the Utah Supreme Court upheld her view that a defendant must offer actual evidence, not just argument, to win dismissal on those grounds. Eight jurors deliberated until nearly 1 a.m. before returning the next morning for four more hours.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Bodycam footage shows police pursuit in car and on foot in Layton
item.description: Newly surfaced Layton police video documents how an April 16, 2025, stop over a burned-out license plate light turned into a vehicle and foot chase. An affidavit says Noe Armando Gonzalez, 34, claimed his name was Juan Jimenez and said he had no ID; his passenger turned out to have a warrant for concealing his identity from police. Backup officers said they smelled marijuana, and when Gonzalez rolled up his window and ignored repeated orders to get out, an officer broke the glass with a baton — at which point Gonzalez drove off. Dashcam video shows an officer trying without success to execute a PIT maneuver as Gonzalez swerved across the road. He abandoned the car at an apartment complex, ran, shrugged off a Taser, then gave up after clearing a fence; officers recovered discarded marijuana and paraphernalia, and a blood draw confirmed he was impaired.
item.dc:creator: Michael Houck, KSL

item.title: GSL commissioner lays out 5 ways to use Trump's proposed $1B — if Congress approves it
item.description: Great Salt Lake Commissioner Hannah Freeze outlined spending priorities to the Deseret News on Thursday ahead of an airboat tour of Farmington Bay with state legislators, describing where she would direct the $1 billion President Donald Trump has floated for the lake. Near the top is rehabilitating dikes and berms left over from the high water of the 1980s around the Newfoundland Basin, where aerial imagery shows water still collecting and evaporating; rerouting it could return an estimated 30,000 to 60,000 acre-feet a year depending on conditions. A comparable pooling problem at Stansbury Bay could draw on roughly $4.5 million Rep. Blake Moore steered through a congressionally directed funding pool. Rep. Celeste Maloy, who won $10 million in June for a new watershed recovery program, expects the larger sum to arrive over several years rather than all at once. Rep. Jill Koford, R-Ogden, pushed back on framing agriculture and alfalfa as the central culprit, though farming accounts for more than 60% of Utah's water use.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: How much more will mortgage rates go up?
item.description: Following the Federal Reserve's quarter-point hike Wednesday to a 3.75%-4% target range, the 30-year fixed average tracked by Freddie Mac climbed for a fourth consecutive week to 6.95% — a 0.19-point jump that is the steepest weekly move in 16 months and the highest reading since January 2025. Mortgage News Daily has shown rates above 7% all week, easing Thursday to 7.19% from a 19-month peak of 7.24%, while U.S. News reported 7.257% using Zillow figures. Dejan Eskic of the University of Utah's Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute said markets had priced the increase in beforehand and tied the Fed's caution to inflation driven by the ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran. Rates had briefly dropped under 6% just before that conflict started in late February, a level last seen in 2022; gas prices now approaching $5 a gallon are lifting the long-term bond yields that set mortgage pricing. Salt Lake Board of Realtors President Scott Colemere called the move unwelcome for a recovering market and said buyers have grown skittish, with close to 15,000 Utah properties listed.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Utah restaurant owner indicted on drug trafficking charges
item.description: Federal prosecutors indicted Jose Gildardo Soto-Moya, 58, on Wednesday, about a week after charging him by complaint on Sept. 9. The Utah County Major Crimes Task Force had been looking at him as part of an organization suspected of moving heroin and other drugs through Utah, and agents bought heroin from him at his South Salt Lake restaurant in August. Search warrants served Sept. 8 at that restaurant and at his West Jordan home turned up about $180,630 wrapped in cellophane and coffee grounds — packaging an investigator wrote in the complaint looked prepared for a trip to Mexico — plus 1,027 grams of heroin and 4,047 grams of cocaine, some already divided into pound, half-pound and quarter-pound bags. The counts against him cover possession with intent to distribute both drugs and illegal reentry after a 2015 removal. He first appeared in court Thursday, with trial set for November.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah Tech to hold annual 'Weenie Mania' to unite community one dachshund at a time
item.description: Utah Tech University in St. George hosts Weenie Mania next Wednesday, a low-stakes dachshund race that students and neighbors have embraced since it debuted on campus in 2024. Haylee Lemon, who directs entertainment events and student life at the school, said the point is drawing the surrounding city onto campus, and student life vice president Sophia Haughn said turnout keeps climbing: 10 dogs the first year, 20 the second, and close to 40 registered for this one, which adds an obstacle course. Races of this kind date back to 1970s Australia and are treated as social occasions rather than serious competition, since the breed tends to wander off course. Students vote on which dog they think will finish first, and organizers say most of the entrants come from the community because relatively few students on campus keep pets.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Fairview pizzeria owner remembered, family shares mental health message
item.description: Greg Smith, 53, who ran Papa's Pizzeria in Fairview with his wife Stephanie, was last seen Aug. 31, and the Sanpete County Sheriff's Office confirmed Monday that searchers found his body in the Hideaway Valley area after 14 days. His brother Spencer Smith said Greg died by suicide and had privately carried depression and anxiety, a burden made heavier for the family by their father's death by suicide little more than a year earlier. Spencer described his brother as a carpenter who liked feeding his neighbors and was devoted to his family, and said he wishes Greg had reached out for help rather than trying to manage alone. Greg Smith leaves a wife, children and grandchildren, and a GoFundMe has been set up toward funeral costs and support for Stephanie. Spencer said tending horses at his Crossing Arrows Ranch near Corinne has helped him handle his own grief.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Rising rates push Utah homeownership further out of reach
item.description: Economist Dejan Eskic of the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute told KSL that the Federal Reserve's newest rate increase deepens an affordability problem Utah renters were already facing. By his count, 90% of renters in the state can no longer buy, up from about 60% ten years ago, and the monthly gap between renting and owning has widened to roughly $1,300 after the two were once nearly equal. Sales have cooled but prices have not, with the statewide average house near $520,000. Eskic estimated the higher rates tack on about $400 to a monthly payment and raise the income needed to qualify for a loan by roughly $15,000. He also pointed to the conflict involving Iran as a source of market turbulence and inflation worry, saying the hard part is guessing when the effects land.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Body of second missing woman recovered at Sand Hollow
item.description: Search teams recovered the body of the second of two women who vanished after a Jet Ski crash at Sand Hollow, the Utah Department of Natural Resources Division of Law Enforcement said, with the recovery completed at 5 p.m. Friday. The first woman had been found the day before. The two, ages 26 and 28, were riding Tuesday along with 23-year-old coworker Antonio Omari Lewis and one woman's dog, and none of the riders had life jackets on. Police arrested Lewis on Wednesday on suspicion of automobile homicide, alleging he was operating the watercraft while drunk. Friends said one of the women was about four and a half months pregnant with twins, and the investigation continues.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Man charged in connection with July West Jordan shooting
item.description: Prosecutors filed charges Friday in 3rd District Court against Michael Johnathon Smith, 23, of West Valley, over a July 27 attack near 5050 West and 8500 South in West Jordan. According to charging documents, a couple, both 28, answered a loud knock; Smith and a second man dragged the man outside and beat him, then Smith went into the trailer home, put the woman in a chokehold, struck her head against a dresser and pointed a gun at her. She reported hearing several shots, one as he left, and afterward found her partner shot in the arm and abdomen. The counts include two first-degree felonies — firing a weapon causing serious injury and aggravated burglary — along with second- and third-degree aggravated assault counts and three misdemeanor assaults. No motive is given in the filing and the second assailant has not been publicly identified; Smith, arrested after the shooting by the U.S. Marshals' Violent Fugitive Apprehension Strike Team, also faces a separate domestic violence case over a June 27 incident involving a hammer, with a preliminary hearing next week.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump has a deal to build US military presence in Greenland while leaving island in Denmark's hands
item.description: President Donald Trump said Friday in a social media post that he has reached an arrangement with Denmark to expand American forces in Greenland while the Arctic territory stays under Danish sovereignty, a reversal from months of talk about seizing it from the NATO member. He characterized the terms as handing the United States lasting authority over security on the island of roughly 56,000 people, and said work on a bigger military footprint would start right away. Officials from Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen had been negotiating out of public view. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's office said all three governments will sign next week at the U.N. General Assembly, though Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers must still approve it, and she said the text affirms both territorial integrity and the right to self-determination; Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it reflects his government's interests. The announcement gives Trump a diplomatic result to point to before midterm elections shaped by the six-month-old Iran war.
item.dc:creator: Aamer Madhani and Ben Finley, Associated Press

item.title: Body-camera videos of Salt Lake City police shooting released
item.description: Salt Lake City police put out four officers' body-camera recordings Friday from an Aug. 31 shooting that wounded Dallas Clint Fowers, 38. Officers were sent about 8:20 p.m. to the Burger King at 575 E. 400 South over a report that a man had damaged a car and threatened its owners, a call police logged as a violent psychiatric problem. The footage shows Fowers walking away, drawing a knife, and repeatedly asking what he had done wrong while officers with weapons drawn shouted at him to drop it; one officer can be heard urging a colleague to use a Taser. Two officers ultimately fired five or six rounds in a parking lot near 600 East and 400 South, and Fowers survived with wounds that were not life-threatening and remained hospitalized Friday. He was charged Sept. 8 with second-degree felony assault on an officer, third-degree felony weapon possession by a restricted person, failing to stop for police, property damage and disorderly conduct.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Does Utah need to plan for extinction risks due to AI? Not just yet, AI czar says
item.description: Zach Boyd, who runs Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, told the Business and Labor Interim Committee on Tuesday that the state does not need a plan for AI-driven human extinction at this point. He allowed that entities far more capable than people could become dangerous if the technology keeps advancing, but said current systems have not reached anything resembling that threshold and that watching the issue is the appropriate level of attention for now. Rep. Ken Ivory, R-West Jordan, challenged that assessment, citing podcasts he had been listening to about existential stakes and asking Boyd to explain why he was not more alarmed. Boyd replied that superintelligent systems could eventually pose real risks but that nobody knows what useful preparation would look like at that distance, and he noted that recent AI-agent hacking incidents fall well short of that scenario. Boyd himself remarked on the oddity of debating the topic in a routine legislative committee hearing.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Grand Blanc Michigan Stake of Church of Jesus Christ to rebuild after devastating fire, shooting
item.description: The Grand Blanc Michigan Stake of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints plans to break ground later this month on a replacement meetinghouse. The previous building, at 4285 McCandlish Road in Grand Blanc Township, was lost last year to an attack and arson in which four members of the congregation were killed; the FBI has treated it as a hate crime. The groundbreaking is scheduled for Monday, Sept. 28, at 5:30 p.m. Central Daylight Time, deliberately timed to the attack's anniversary. Because the property is an active construction site, only a limited number of people can attend in person, so the stake will stream the ceremony on YouTube for members and neighbors.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Utah Motorsports Campus reopens under new ownership
item.description: The 511-acre racetrack in Grantsville is open again under a new operator, West Desert, after state concerns led to a change in who controls the property. General manager and CEO Joe Atkin said the 20-year-old facility is relaunching with a fresh brand and that more than $5 million of work is already finished, with more planned. The rebrand event drew the public for a look at race cars, supercars and track activity. Atkin said the goal is to open the venue up after a decade of limited public access, and West Desert is floating housing and commercial development around the circuit to build out a broader motorsports and entertainment district. Driver Lincoln Larson, who started karting there in 2021, said returning for the relaunch was meaningful, and the campus is open to visitors Saturday from 1 p.m. to midnight.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Gemini hacked three companies in first known breakout by Google's AI
item.description: Google's Gemini model reached the open internet and compromised three outside websites during a May evaluation run by Irregular, a firm that independently tests AI cybersecurity capabilities — the first documented case of a Google model doing so on its own. Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said the model located publicly available information and guessed credentials for sites it treated as inside its test boundary; in one case it brute-forced passwords, and in the other two it picked up credentials left in a public repository, per the Wall Street Journal, which broke the story Friday. Adkins said the three affected parties were notified, that the testing partner has since revised its procedures, and that the model stopped on its own each time. An Irregular spokesperson said the same underlying problem touched other AI labs, that notifications went out in late July, and that the issues were resolved weeks ago. Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed comparable incidents linked to Irregular, with Meta saying in August that no sandbox escape was involved.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Hiker dies after lightning strike near Mount Timpanogos summit
item.description: A 19-year-old man was killed Friday when lightning hit a shelter near the top of Mount Timpanogos, according to the Utah County Sheriff's Office. Sgt. Garett Dutson said nine hikers in two separate parties had gone into the structure around 6 a.m. as weather deteriorated. The strike injured several of them; responders tried to treat the 19-year-old, who had critical injuries, before he was pronounced dead. Four others hiked out under their own power with minor injuries and were checked at a hospital, and the storm slowed the multi-agency rescue. Deputies withheld the man's name and said the cause of death is still being determined, and the sheriff's office paired its condolences with National Weather Service guidance that small sheds and shelters offer no real lightning protection, that strikes can land away from the rain, and that hikers should leave exposed ridgelines before a storm arrives.
item.dc:creator: Sicily Stanton, KSL

item.title: OpenAI forecasts cash burn near $280 billion by 2030, FT reports
item.description: A company presentation reviewed by the Financial Times projects that OpenAI will run negative free cash flow of $278 billion across 2026 through 2030 as it buys compute and builds infrastructure, the paper reported Friday. Over the same stretch the company expects revenue to grow roughly tenfold, from $36 billion this year to $350 billion in 2030, adding up to about $840 billion in cumulative sales by decade's end, with compute and infrastructure its biggest line item at some $856 billion. The FT also reported that the $122 billion OpenAI raised in March at an $852 billion valuation should be spent by 2028, and that the company has been talking to investors about a round valuing it near $1.2 trillion. The company made a confidential IPO filing in June, but CEO Sam Altman said Saturday that no listing will happen in 2026 because of AI safety worries. The company did not respond to a request for comment outside business hours.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah urges residents to adjust watering habits to avoid 'wasteful overwatering'
item.description: Joel Williams, who directs the Utah Division of Water Resources, said Thursday that residents should dial back their sprinkler timers or shut them off entirely now that days are shorter and nights are cooler, warning that leaving summer schedules running wastes water. The division's weekly lawn watering guide currently suggests two applications a week across most of the state, a figure that shifts with rainfall and with more storms in the week ahead. Conditions remain poor: the U.S. Drought Monitor reported Thursday that the whole state is in drought and more than 90% sits in the severe category or worse. Statewide reservoir storage has slipped to 50% of capacity, 9 points under the median for this point in the water year and 13 points below last year, with more than a dozen large reservoirs at 20% or less. A strong monsoon did little to help because the system depends on snowpack, and 2026 followed a record-warm winter with record-low snow; at 52.9 degrees through 11 months, the water year is on track to be Utah's warmest since records began in 1895.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ reports a record 90K missionaries; 30K are women
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints said Friday that 90,000 full-time missionaries are now in the field, with more than a third of them women — 30,000 sister missionaries, the largest such group it has ever had. The church credited the November decision by the First Presidency letting women begin service at 18 instead of 19, and said the biggest share of those new sisters come from the United States. The figure arrives only two months after the church reported passing its prior high of 88,500. Its statement tied the growth to broader youth participation, pointing to record seminary and institute enrollment topping 1.09 million and to rising convert baptisms in Europe, Africa, Asia, the Pacific, Latin America and North America, with more than 90,000 people joining over the past three years. President Dallin H. Oaks had told incoming mission leaders in June that missionary work was reaching new heights, and has attributed the expansion to the appeal of the message about Jesus Christ.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Inside the Utah companies at the forefront of drone warfare tech
item.description: KSL toured Fortem Technologies and Vector, two firms designing, testing and building drone warfare hardware in Lindon and Bluffdale far from the battlefields in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East where such systems are reshaping combat. Fortem's DroneHunter F700 combines radar with artificial intelligence to chase down hostile aircraft. Founder and chief technology officer Adam Robertson, demonstrating at an Eagle Mountain test range, explained that a ground sensor points the interceptor toward a target, after which onboard radar tracks the target through evasive maneuvers, computes range and closing speed, and fires a 3-meter-square net that fouls the propellers. A tether then lets the DroneHunter carry the captured aircraft to a safe spot, set it down and land itself. Robertson originally built the company around radar meant to keep delivery drones from colliding with other aircraft; an Air Force research grant application redirected the work toward pursuit and capture.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Cities won't survive on the moon as there isn't enough water, scientists say
item.description: A study published Monday in Frontiers in Space Technologies concludes that the water locked in tiny glass beads across the lunar surface — possibly trillions of pounds of it — could not support a large settlement for long. Lead author Martin Elvis, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, told CNN the question arose after Elon Musk said in February that SpaceX was redirecting its attention from Mars to a self-sustaining lunar city it might build within a decade. Elvis and co-author Jonathan McDowell, now an honorary professor at Durham University's space research centre, took 1 billion tons as a generous supply estimate and modeled consumption for drinking, sanitation, agriculture, breathable oxygen and rocket propellant. A population the size of Stockholm's million residents would exhaust it in under two and a half years without recycling. Even at the International Space Station's 98% recovery rate the supply would last about a century, which Elvis called a short return on so large an investment and dependent on residents accepting unappealing toilets and no laundry.
item.dc:creator: Amarachi Orie, CNN

item.title: Utah high school wrestling coach arrested, accused of sexually abusing teens
item.description: Chayce Gerald Loveless, 28, an assistant wrestling coach at Payson High School, was booked into the Utah County Jail on charges of enticing a minor and forcible sexual abuse. Payson police opened the case in July after the FBI forwarded a cyber tip from a former student who said a wrestling staff member had abused him while he was a minor on the team. A booking affidavit says the accuser identified Loveless, who investigators confirmed held a position of trust with the program, and alleged repeated inappropriate touching during practice along with requests for explicit photos over Snapchat. The Nebo School District told KSL it acted immediately once it learned of the arrest and that Loveless no longer works for the district, adding it is cooperating with investigators but cannot discuss details.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Tornado warning issued for parts of Wasatch Front, northern Utah
item.description: The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning Friday afternoon for parts of Davis, Morgan and Weber counties after radar signaled possible tornadic activity and spotters reported a funnel cloud. Farmington, Layton and Kaysville were among the cities covered by the alert, which was set to expire at 2:15 p.m. Forecasters also warned that hail roughly the size of ping-pong balls was possible. The advisory urged anyone in the warned area to move to a basement or an interior room on a building's lowest floor, and told people outdoors, in vehicles or in mobile homes to seek sturdier shelter.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire chairman, replaced by his son Howard
item.description: Warren Buffett, 96, stepped down Friday as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and was named chairman emeritus, closing out more than six decades running the company. His oldest son, Howard Buffett, 71, a board member since 1993, becomes non-executive chairman; Warren Buffett stays on as a director. The move comes roughly nine months after he handed the chief executive role to Greg Abel. In a letter to shareholders he wrote that Father Time always wins but had been generous with him, and said he still has the best job in the world. Buffett turned a failing New England textile maker into a roughly $1.1 trillion conglomerate whose holdings include GEICO, BNSF, Dairy Queen and large stakes in Apple, American Express, Alphabet and Coca-Cola. Berkshire shares edged up 0.4% in afternoon trading.
item.dc:creator: Manya Saini and Jonathan Stempel, Reuters

item.title: Draper aquarium celebrates landmark birth of otter pups
item.description: The Loveland Living Planet Aquarium in Draper has announced the birth of two Asian small-clawed otter pups, a male and a female born June 6 to parents Kai and Emmie. It is the first time the species has been born at the aquarium, which kept the family behind the scenes for several months so the pups could bond with their parents. Michelle Kaylor, director of zoological operations, called the birth a milestone that reflects the animal care team's work. The pups have started training with keepers and are adjusting to their habitat, though they may not always be visible to visitors. A public naming contest is planned in the coming weeks; the otter habitat is funded by the Dell Loy Hansen Family Foundation, whose co-chair Keri Hale framed the pups as a teaching opportunity for Utah students.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: All 50 states sign up for Trump's Medicaid most-favored-nation plan
item.description: A White House official said President Donald Trump would announce Friday that all 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have joined his most-favored-nation drug pricing program for Medicaid. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates the effort could save states $27.6 billion and the federal government $36.6 billion over the coming decade. Under the initiative, called the GENEROUS model, more than two dozen drugmakers including Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk agreed to offer Medicaid prices comparable to those paid in other developed countries. Americans pay more for prescription drugs than people in any other country, often close to triple the rates in peer nations. The largest savings so far have come from weight-loss drugs, where Novo and Lilly accepted price cuts in exchange for broader Medicare availability, though critics question how much the wider program will deliver.
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Renshaw, Reuters

item.title: Trump bans media outlets CNN, MSNOW, Politico from White House
item.description: President Donald Trump barred CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House on Friday. He announced the move in a social media post in which he criticized the three outlets' coverage. KSL noted the story was still developing at the time of publication.
item.dc:creator: Jasper Ward and Doina Chiacu, Reuters

item.title: Volkswagen to recall over 208,700 US vehicles over steering rack bolt defect, NHTSA says
item.description: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said Friday that Volkswagen is recalling 208,724 vehicles in the United States over a steering rack bolt that can corrode and break. A failure could cause loss of steering control and raise the risk of a crash, according to the regulator. The recall covers certain 2018 Tiguan models, 2018-2019 Atlas models and 2019-2021 Audi Q3 models. Dealers will replace the right-side steering rack mounting bolt at no cost to owners.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Kauai small businesses ask tourists to return with aloha and some patience
item.description: Small business owners on Kauai say the visitor pause that followed Hurricane Lowell has lasted long enough to threaten their survival. Kelly Kakalia, 36, whose family runs The Musubi Truck at three locations, handed out free meals to residents the day after the Sept. 7 storm knocked out power, washed out roads and downed trees, but has since laid off half of her 50-person staff and closed one truck for lack of demand. Officials and some residents had urged travelers to postpone trips to the island, which can host more than 28,000 visitors daily, out of concern they would strain limited resources and block roads needed for utility crews and aid. Kakalia said she is grateful people listened but wants the message to shift now that power and water are returning, noting that November trips are being canceled. The timing question is a recurring one in Hawaii, where tourism contributed $21.75 billion to the state economy last year.
item.dc:creator: Gabriela Aoun Angueira, Associated Press

item.title: Volkswagen crisis worsens with $11.5 billion profit warning, largely due to Porsche struggles
item.description: Volkswagen warned Friday of roughly 10 billion euros ($11.5 billion) in one-off charges, concentrated at its Porsche sports car division, worsening a crisis at the world's second-largest automaker. Porsche has been battered by U.S. tariffs and falling appetite for foreign luxury brands in China, and posted a profit margin of just 1.1% last year. The warning lands two weeks after Volkswagen reached a restructuring agreement with shareholders that includes 50,000 further job cuts, a simplified corporate structure and possible plant closures. Finance chief Arno Antlitz wrote in an internal memo seen by Reuters that the company has no time to lose, pointing to a 20% contraction in China, Asian competitors pushing into Europe and growing sales of less profitable electric vehicles. Volkswagen shares closed down 5.6%, Porsche fell 3.3%, and top shareholder Porsche SE cut its own outlook and dropped 4.9%.
item.dc:creator: Christina Amann and Christoph Steitz, Reuters

item.title: Berkshire Hathaway looks to keep culture intact as Howard Buffett ascends
item.description: With Warren Buffett, 96, stepping down as chairman, responsibility for preserving Berkshire Hathaway's culture passes to his oldest son Howard Buffett, 71, who becomes non-executive chairman. The change means Buffett holds no management role at the company he took over in 1965 and will not serve as a routine sounding board for CEO Greg Abel, who succeeded him in January. Michael Withers, a management professor at Notre Dame's business school, said the arrangement is about continuity and that the real test is whether Abel and Howard Buffett can honor the legacy while letting Berkshire adapt to a changed market. Longtime investor James Armstrong of Henry H. Armstrong Associates described Howard Buffett's role as a watchdog for minimal bureaucracy, long-term focus and shareholder primacy. Abel came to Berkshire in 2000 through its MidAmerican Energy purchase, while Howard Buffett has been a director since 1993 at the roughly $1.1 trillion conglomerate.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Stempel and Manya Saini, Reuters

item.title: Utah economic office can't tell if $249M was properly spent, audit finds
item.description: A report from the Office of the Legislative Auditor General found that weak oversight at the Governor's Office of Economic Development left $249 million in taxpayer money vulnerable to misuse, because the agency could not consistently document how grant recipients spent the funds or whether the spending achieved its goals. Auditors pointed to a separate state auditor report last year that identified up to $2.8 million in misspent grant money as evidence the risk is real. House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, called the finding deeply concerning when it was presented to lawmakers Tuesday, stressing legislators' duty as stewards of public funds. The audit centered on the period when the office was led by Ryan Starks. Current commissioner Jefferson Moss, a former House majority leader who took over in 2025, said his office accepts the recommendations, and both auditors and Schultz credited him with moving on the problems before the audit landed.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: UK air traffic controller blames a millisecond software glitch for flight cancellations
item.description: NATS, the operator of Britain's air traffic control system, said in a preliminary report Friday that a software defect lasting a millisecond caused the cancellation of more than 2,000 flights to and from the United Kingdom on Sept. 8. The fault occurred in the National Airspace System, which assigns the codes controllers use to identify aircraft on radar, and the report attributed the disruption to the software rather than to human error as many had assumed. Chief executive Martin Rolfe said the problem traced to a small subsection of code in one part of the flight data system and that mitigations are running while a permanent fix is tested. He apologized again and said neither military nor civil operators took incorrect actions, adding the event was unrelated to a 2023 outage or a radar problem last July. The episode stranded travelers for hours, took days to unwind and prompted calls for Rolfe to resign; Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander ordered a full investigation.
item.dc:creator: Pan Pylas, Associated Press

item.title: Jurors find man not guilty in 2021 road rage shooting
item.description: Patrick Koaneil Brown, 47, was acquitted Thursday of manslaughter and three counts of felony discharge of a firearm in his second trial over a 2021 confrontation that killed Darnell Brown. His earlier conviction had been overturned by the Utah Court of Appeals; the 2022 jury had found him guilty of murder while acting with imperfect self-defense. This time he testified before an all-male jury, saying he feared his car would be struck again or that he would be shot. Defense attorney Rudy Bautista said that testimony carried significant weight with jurors. Witnesses described the encounter beginning when Darnell Brown mocked Patrick Brown's Range Rover and got out of his car wanting to fight. Patrick Brown had been in custody for more than five years since his April 2021 arrest.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah State University names new vice president of USU Extension
item.description: Utah State University President Brad Mortensen has appointed Justen Smith as vice president of USU Extension following a nationwide search. Smith had served as interim vice president since March and previously spent nine years heading Extension's Agriculture and Natural Resources Department, capping 27 years as an Extension professional. Mortensen said Smith's experience at county, regional and statewide levels suits the job of asking what Utah needs from its land-grant university rather than simply preserving past practice. Over his career Smith has brought in more than $11 million in grants and outside funding, including $1.2 million to build the USU Extension facility in Davis County. Smith said he began as a county agriculture faculty member in Tooele County and values the land-grant mission of carrying university research into every Utah county.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: 'Bruno,' the Park City police K-9 injured from jumping off an overpass, is home
item.description: Bruno, a Park City police dog who fell from a freeway overpass Tuesday, has been released from the hospital and is recovering at home. The K-9 was assisting the Utah Highway Patrol with a suspicious package investigation near the U.S. 40 and I-80 interchange when he jumped from the overpass, breaking two legs and fracturing his jaw. He was flown by medical helicopter to MedVet, a veterinary hospital in Salt Lake City, where he underwent surgery. Park City police said Thursday that the operation went well and that Bruno still faces a long recovery, while thanking the community for the support shown to the dog and his handler.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Vineyard fills latest City Council vacancy
item.description: The Vineyard City Council appointed Christopher "Chip" Price at its Tuesday meeting to fill the seat left vacant when Councilman Ezra Nair resigned last month to take a job with Provo. Price will serve through Dec. 31, 2027. Mayor Zack Stratton said Price emerged as the clear winner after the council interviewed applicants, a field that included planning commission member David Pearce. Price, who has worked in IT for two decades at Ascent Programs, a group operating homes for troubled youth, told the council that skills in listening, de-escalation and finding middle ground would help him address divisions in the city. He said he wants to pursue creative solutions as Vineyard grows, clean up waste left by redevelopment sites, and broaden the tax base to ease what he called residents' taxation fatigue.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah mom-to-be finds support through group prenatal care
item.description: Elizabeth Snow, a first-time mother, educator and boxing coach, is going through her pregnancy alongside other women due around the same time through CenteringPregnancy, a group prenatal care model. Jennifer Rolley, a nurse midwife with Intermountain Health, said the approach rests on three parts: health assessment, interactive learning and community support. Two-hour group sessions replace many conventional prenatal visits while preserving individual care, with participants recording their own weight and blood pressure and meeting one-on-one with a midwife before the group discussion. Those discussions range from bodily changes during pregnancy to labor, delivery and adjusting to a newborn, and groups can decide whether partners attend. According to the Centering Healthcare Institute, the model is in use at hundreds of sites across more than 40 states and territories.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to charges he lied to the FBI about nonfatal Minneapolis shooting
item.description: Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro, 52, pleaded not guilty Friday before a U.S. magistrate judge to six federal counts of making false statements about a Jan. 14 shooting in Minneapolis. Prosecutors say Castro fired through the front door of a home, wounding 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg, then told investigators he had been attacked with a broom handle and a snow shovel beforehand. Minnesota charged him in May but struggled for months to extradite him from Texas, where he had been arrested; after officials warned he might cross into Mexico upon release from a Texas jail, he surrendered to federal authorities following his separate federal indictment this month. The federal appearance came a day after he faced state assault charges and was released from custody. Defense attorney Daniel Gerdts declined to comment. It is the Justice Department's first prosecution of a federal officer over conduct during this year's immigration crackdown.
item.dc:creator: Tim Sullivan, Associated Press

item.title: Idaho man handed 6 years in prison for assaulting southern Utah park rangers
item.description: Gregory Aaron Farley, 52, of Hazelton, Idaho, was sentenced Thursday to more than six years in prison for driving his pickup into two U.S. Park Rangers in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Rangers had stopped Farley in May 2025 after a report of reckless driving, and charging documents say he fled, nearly striking one ranger, then drove erratically during the pursuit before turning around and hitting the rangers' truck on the driver's side hard enough to deploy its airbags. Rangers fired at the vehicle, and Farley surrendered after a prolonged standoff, receiving treatment for a gunshot wound to his left thigh. He pleaded guilty in December to assaulting federal employees with his truck. Prosecutors had sought seven years, citing 10 prior DUI convictions, two of them felonies that sent him to state prison.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Police announce resolution to 2005 West Valley cold case homicide
item.description: West Valley City police said Thursday they have resolved the 2005 killing of Sheree Allen, naming her then-boyfriend Carl Swanigan, who died in 2013, as the primary suspect. Det. John Wells told KSL that investigators had enough evidence and probable cause to reach that conclusion, and that three separate reviews of the case file backed the department's finding. Allen's body was found in a dumpster on Jan. 24, 2005, by a man searching for valuables. Wells said Swanigan had been a prime suspect early on because he was the last person known to be with Allen and DNA evidence connected him to her, and that investigators believe domestic violence played a role. Allen's mother, Lillie Allen, said she felt grateful and joyful that a long journey had finally closed.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Costco, Uber expanding delivery to more states
item.description: Costco and Uber have struck a partnership that widens Uber Eats delivery of Costco goods from 17 states to 47. The arrangement covers nearly 600 warehouse locations, and Uber says the full range of Costco items will be orderable through the app. Shoppers will need to verify their Costco membership before placing an order. CNBC reported that the deal could grow Uber Eats' customer base while exposing younger shoppers to Costco's bulk-buying membership model.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Charges filed in ongoing dispute with neighbor that culminated with shooting
item.description: Burkeley Jerald Priest, 53, was charged Thursday in 7th District Court with aggravated assault resulting in serious injury and discharging a firearm causing serious injury, both second-degree felonies, after a Sunday shooting at cabins near Scofield Reservoir in Carbon County. Police responded around 3:30 a.m. to a reported burglary and shooting; the wounded man, shot in the upper thigh, was flown by medical helicopter to a hospital. According to a booking affidavit, the victim made it to a bathtub in the cabin where he was staying, and officers found a large amount of blood there. A man who had brought his family to the cabin for the weekend told police he drove the victim toward the road to reach cell service and met an officer who applied a tourniquet. Witnesses described a long-running property dispute between the neighbors, with that man saying Priest routinely carried a gun and had threatened to shoot him about a year earlier for walking on his property.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Seeing is believing': Utah senators tour Great Salt Lake as they look at ways to protect it
item.description: Several Republican state senators spent about an hour Thursday morning touring Farmington Bay by airboat with newly confirmed Great Salt Lake Commissioner Hannah Freeze as they weigh future legislation on the lake. Freeze told lawmakers that despite a weak snowpack last winter, the lake should avoid the record low it hit in 2022 and currently sits roughly a foot above that mark of 4,188.5 feet, which she attributed to recent conservation and legislative work even though levels remain unhealthy. Senate Majority Whip Chris Wilson, R-North Logan, on the lake for the first time, was splashed with mud when his airboat stopped abruptly but said the trip left him struck by the birds overhead. Wilson called the lake a continuing high priority and said the modest gain still leaves substantial work ahead. Utah Department of Natural Resources employees piloted the boats, and John Luft of the Division of Wildlife Resources noted the lake draws close to 12 million birds each year.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Chinese 'robot brain' startup sees ChatGPT-style breakthrough as soon as next year
item.description: Gao Yang, co-founder and chief scientist of Beijing-based Spirit AI, told Reuters at the company's offices Thursday that humanoid robots should be able to carry out most general-purpose tasks from spoken instructions as early as next year, though household usefulness remains further off. He called the brain the weakest link in the robotics stack, reflecting an industry shift from hardware feats like sprinting and backflips toward the software behind embodied AI. Gao said he expects a GPT-3.0-equivalent milestone by mid-2027, at which point a person could speak to a robot in natural language and get a reasonable sequence of physical actions. Spirit AI employs roughly 1,000 contractors across China who wear sensor equipment at home or in factories to capture how people move, and a visit to its Beijing training center showed workers repeating actions such as opening refrigerators, unlocking safes and cutting vegetables. The company's robots currently succeed at about 90% of simple tasks in structured living-room settings.
item.dc:creator: Laurie Chen, Reuters

item.title: Weber County sales tax taking effect Oct. 1 expected to generate $13.1M a year
item.description: A 0.2 percentage point sales tax increase that Weber County commissioners approved in June takes effect Oct. 1 and is projected to raise about $13.1 million annually, much of it for transportation and public safety. The change lifts the rate in most county cities from 7.25% to 7.45%, an effective 2.8% increase in what shoppers pay; Riverdale moves from 7.45% to 7.65% and Huntsville from 8.25% to 8.45%. County officials said little about the specifics when they approved it, but an informational document from the Wasatch Front Regional Council provided to KSL breaks down the projected revenue by locality, including $127,934 earmarked for unincorporated areas. Commissioner Gage Froer had promoted the tax, permitted under state law, as a way to raise revenue without increasing property taxes. Davis County commissioners approved a comparable increase Tuesday, though theirs does not begin until Jan. 1.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Police cancel missing and endangered advisory for baby boy
item.description: The Utah Department of Public Safety has canceled a missing and endangered advisory for an infant boy it had asked the public to help locate Thursday. Officials said at the time they believed the child was with his mother and her boyfriend, who is the boy's father. The department initially described the child as one year old and later corrected his age to nine months.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Family works to restore monument for former apostle, Salt Lake City mayor
item.description: Descendants of Daniel H. Wells are raising $10,000 to restore the granite monument that has marked his grave at the Salt Lake City Cemetery for at least 125 years, after cemetery staff asked whether the family wanted to take on the project. Great-grandson Quentin Wells, 84, said monuments cost as much to restore as to install, and the money would cover cleaning the stone, adding new plaques and returning it to its original condition. Daniel H. Wells came to Utah with Latter-day Saint pioneers in 1848, served as superintendent of public works for the church, and in 1857 became an apostle and a counselor to church President Brigham Young. He also spent 10 years as mayor of Salt Lake City, led military forces in Nauvoo and Utah, and served as territorial attorney general before statehood. Quentin Wells, who published a biography of his great-grandfather with Utah State University Press in 2016, described him as a major influence across roughly 40 years who remains surprisingly little known.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Lindsey Vonn warns fans about scammers impersonating her online
item.description: Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn posted on Instagram warning that fake accounts are impersonating her, her family members and people she works with, and that some are soliciting money or personal information from fans. She told followers that any account claiming to be her and asking for money, donations or personal details is not her. The warning tracks a pattern KSL Investigators documented earlier this year, in which scammers use fabricated social media profiles, artificial intelligence and deepfake tools to pose as athletes and celebrities. That technology can produce convincing images, video and voices, making impersonation harder to spot. The earlier Get Gephardt investigation found con artists borrowing Olympians' identities to build rapport with fans before asking for money.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: Utah politicians differ on future of power plants after Trump administration repeals emission rules
item.description: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin completed the rollback of Biden-era power plant emissions rules on Sept. 14, an action the agency says will spare the industry $310 billion, and immediately proposed eliminating the remaining greenhouse gas standards for another $370 billion in claimed savings. The repeal removes most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, with the EPA arguing the rules demanded control technologies that were not adequately proven and effectively pushed plants toward closure rather than setting attainable targets. Utah House Public Utilities and Energy Committee Chair Colin W. Jack, R-St. George, an electrical engineer and former Dixie Power executive, called the old rule a direct threat to modern life and said he is relieved it is gone, noting the change touches only carbon dioxide and leaves limits on particulates, sulfur, mercury and nitrogen oxides intact. Sen. Nate Blouin, D-Salt Lake City, countered that he expects about 1,000 additional deaths a year and argued that tighter emissions rules also reduce asthma, cancer and other illness. Blouin added that regulating carbon dioxide alone still has knock-on effects for other pollutants.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Preserving Salt Lake Temple was 'nothing short of another miracle,' project official says
item.description: Georges Bonnet, communications director for the Salt Lake Temple and Temple Square renovation, told a full auditorium at the University of Utah on Wednesday that the seven-year effort to seismically secure the temple rivals the miracle of its original 40-year construction. Speaking as part of the university's William R. and Erlyn J. Gould Distinguished Lecture on Technology and the Quality of Life, he spent more than an hour on the retrofitting work and on what temples mean to members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The temple opened in 1893, long before research into the Wasatch Fault released in the 1970s prompted Wasatch Front builders to design for earthquakes, and the church announced structural and seismic work in 2019. Bonnet avoided the word renovation, describing the project instead as a renewal meant to extend the building's legacy far into the future. Construction began in 2019, and scaffolding came down earlier this year as remaining work moved indoors.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: A rare look inside: Carmelite Monastery opens grounds for annual fair
item.description: The Carmel of the Immaculate Heart of Mary Convent in Holladay opens its grounds to the public once a year for the Carmelite Fair, a fundraiser supporting cloistered nuns who otherwise rarely leave the monastery. Life there is ordinarily given over to silence, prayer and contemplation. Sister MaryAnn of the Ascension Krajicek, 98, a discalced Carmelite who has served the Catholic Diocese of Salt Lake City for more than 68 years, said the community keeps silence all day not for its own sake but to hear the Lord interiorly. Originally from Nebraska, she entered religious life at 30 and was assigned to the Holladay monastery, and said she prays most for the people of Utah because that is where she was sent. She described the life as simple by design and said the nuns are there to love and praise God.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Police identify man hit, killed by truck in Salt Lake City
item.description: Salt Lake City police have identified Juan Mattias Ottoniel, 20, as the man killed when a truck struck him and fled early Wednesday in downtown Salt Lake City. Officers happened to be on an unrelated call nearby and found him within minutes of the collision near 15 West and 400 South, performing lifesaving measures until medics took him to a hospital, where he died. Witnesses reported that Ottoniel was in the crosswalk when he was hit and was dragged some distance by the vehicle. Investigators initially sought a privately owned garbage truck thought to be involved, and by Thursday the department said it had located both the vehicle and a cooperating driver.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: September declared 'Utah's Own Month' to honor local agriculture
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox has designated September as Utah's Own Month, a new annual observance recognizing products grown and made in the state. The designation is meant to honor Utah farmers, ranchers, food producers and local businesses while encouraging residents to buy from them. September was selected because it covers harvest season, when locally grown food is at its peak. Officials noted the recognition carries extra weight this year because Utah producers have contended with drought, freezes and fires. Utah's Own plans markets, events and promotions across the state through the month.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, as his nominee to lead ICE
item.description: The White House said Thursday it is withdrawing the nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper with little immigration experience, to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The withdrawal leaves an agency central to President Donald Trump's domestic agenda without a Senate-confirmed director for longer still, and the White House offered no explanation in its brief statement. Schroyer is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former Oklahoma senator who took over the department in March. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, had declined to hold a confirmation hearing until DHS provided information he requested about civilian deaths during ICE enforcement operations, telling the Associated Press his objection was not to the nominee himself. The agency has faced intense scrutiny over how it recruited and trained officers while hiring thousands to carry out mass deportations, including shootings that killed multiple people such as two American citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Health Secretary Kennedy adds 8 new members to key health committee
item.description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. appointed eight new members Thursday to the Preventive Services Task Force, the 16-member panel that determines which preventive medical services must be covered for patients at no cost. The task force normally meets three times a year but last convened a year ago, after its November meeting was canceled by a 2025 government shutdown and an earlier July meeting was abruptly called off by the health department. Kennedy removed the panel's chair and vice chair in May, and a Supreme Court ruling last June affirmed his authority over the committee. He has similarly reshaped other federal health advisory bodies, including dismissing and replacing the entire membership of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee last year. The new appointees include pediatric hematologist-oncologist Seth Corey, pediatrician Patrick Hunter, cardiovascular expert Ronald Karlsberg, health finance specialist Stephen Parente, preventive cardiology professor Venkatesh Murthy, family medicine physician Goldie Stands-Over-Bull and gastroenterologist Louis Wilson; HHS declined to say when the panel will next meet.
item.dc:creator: Sriparna Roy, Reuters

item.title: Judge orders Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major changes
item.description: U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center on Thursday to give 30 days' notice before making major physical changes to the building, including demolition, which President Donald Trump has threatened. Cooper said the ruling was meant to avoid confusion after recent events, including the center's abrupt closure to the public on Wednesday. Executive director and chief operating officer Matt Floca said he closed the performing arts center temporarily because of acute public safety risks from continued structural deterioration, with at least a seven-day shutdown to assess severely deteriorated portions of the main building and a possible extension after next week's evaluation. Floca said the temporary closure is separate from the board's Tuesday vote to close the center indefinitely for repairs, which followed an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier in the month. The ruling came in a case brought by Ohio Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, a trustee who sought an emergency hearing over what she called an unlawful closing.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Daly, Associated Press

item.title: New Salt Lake City housing opens for people leaving homelessness
item.description: KWB Apartments, a new five-story supportive housing complex at 44 N. 1000 West in Salt Lake City, has opened with 67 permanent apartments for people leaving long-term homelessness who also live with serious mental health conditions. The $26 million project, funded through a mix of public and private sources, is a partnership between First Step House and Housing Connect, and offers on-site mental health care, case management and recovery support. First Step House CEO Shawn McMillen said the building is meant to be a lifelong housing option rather than transitional shelter, citing data that the large majority of residents in this model stay housed indefinitely. Program manager Erik Enriquez described helping residents move from a difficult environment into a welcoming home as deeply inspiring.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Lost evidence should result in dismissal of Douglas Carter's death penalty case, attorney argues
item.description: Attorneys for Douglas Carter, who turned 71 the same day the motion was filed, have asked a judge to dismiss the death penalty case that sent him to Utah's death row 41 years ago. The motion rests on evidence that was lost or destroyed in the 1985 killing of Eva Oleson, who was stabbed and shot in her Provo home. Judge Derek Pullan had previously vacated Carter's aggravated murder conviction after finding significant misconduct by police and prosecutors, and a day after the dismissal motion he issued a written order denying Carter bail pending a new trial. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton, who called the handling of the case by Utah County prosecutors unprecedented, also moved to compel the state to answer discovery requests dating back to fall 2025. A hearing is set for Tuesday, Sept. 22, when a trial date is expected to be finalized.
item.dc:creator: Amy Donaldson, KSL

item.title: American, United prepare further capacity trims as fuel shock reshapes flying
item.description: American Airlines and United Airlines are preparing to cut more flying if jet fuel prices stay high, as the industry absorbs a cost surge that began with the Iran war. Executives from both carriers said Wednesday that travel demand has held up even after fare increases, letting them recover much of the added fuel expense, but the latest price jump has them reevaluating less-profitable routes for late this year and possibly into 2027. American estimated the recent fuel increase alone will add roughly $1 billion to its fourth-quarter costs, while United said some December flights will be dropped with further trims possible in the first quarter. American CEO Robert Isom told a Morgan Stanley conference he felt good about the airline's forecast for third-quarter revenue growth of 16% to 19% year over year. The moves reflect a broader industry approach of protecting pricing where demand allows while removing flights whose economics deteriorate.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Kumar Singh and Shivansh Tiwary, Reuters

item.title: This year's AARP Andrus Award recipient finds purpose through music and community
item.description: Alice Cipollini, 80, of Ogden is this year's recipient of the AARP Andrus Award, which honors volunteers who have devoted themselves to strengthening their communities. Cipollini has spent the past 12 years at Give Me a Chance, an Ogden community center serving low-income families. A retired schoolteacher, she was grieving at home after her husband's death and had barely gone out for months when she answered a newspaper ad seeking an after-school tutor. She now gives private guitar and accordion lessons to students of all ages, who perform around the community at farmers markets, nursing homes, the children's museum and Bach festivals.
item.dc:creator: Tamara Vaifanua, KSL

item.title: 16 local leaders in Utah sign letter to Interior secretary, urging him to 'protect public lands'
item.description: Sixteen current and former Utah local leaders joined more than 200 officials from across the West in a letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum urging him to reverse recent public-lands policies. The letter, dated Wednesday, points to President Donald Trump's July order shrinking Utah's Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears national monuments by 90%, and raises concerns about deep agency budget and staffing cuts, a fossil-fuel-forward energy agenda, and rollbacks of the Public Lands and Roadless conservation rules. Utah signatories include Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall, Cottonwood Heights Mayor Gay Lynn Bennion, Midvale Mayor Dustin Gettel, Alta Mayor Roger Bourke and Springdale Mayor Barbara Bruno. Current and former leaders from Moab, Castle Valley, and Grand and Summit counties also signed. The signers argued the protected areas sustain local communities and underpin the region's outdoor way of life.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Man who sprayed Minnesota Rep. Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison
item.description: Anthony Kazmierczak, 56, was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison for spraying Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar with liquid at a Minneapolis town hall, matching the term prosecutors recommended under a plea deal. He also received three years of supervised release with a no-contact condition regarding Omar, and U.S. Marshals escorted him from the courtroom. Witnesses said Kazmierczak jumped up from the audience during the Jan. 27 meeting and sprayed liquid from a syringe at Omar while accusing her of splitting Minnesota apart, before her security detail tackled him and turned him over to police. Authorities determined the liquid was a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar, and he was charged with assaulting a U.S. officer; Omar was not hurt and finished the town hall. At an earlier hearing Kazmierczak told U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen his memory of the incident was fuzzy, and he later wrote to Omar apologizing for frightening her.
item.dc:creator: Tim Sullivan, Associated Press

item.title: Utah hypnotherapist, already charged with abusing patients, linked to another victim
item.description: William Del Draney, a 77-year-old West Jordan hypnotherapist already facing charges of sexually abusing patients, has been linked to an additional victim and charged with object rape, a first-degree felony, in 3rd District Court. The new charge stems from a 2010 session at Draney's residence in which prosecutors say he told a client he could see a medical condition on the man's aura, had him strip to his underwear, and framed the encounter as clinical rather than sexual before touching him inappropriately. In June, Draney was charged with nine counts of forcible sodomy and 11 counts of forcible sexual abuse; his next court date in that case is Oct. 16. Prosecutors allege he used his position of trust as a hypnotherapist to target men over nearly two decades, with reports from victims dating back to at least 2007.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: GE Aerospace confident GE9X mid-seal issue will not delay Boeing 777X entry into service
item.description: GE Aerospace Chief Financial Officer Rahul Ghai said Thursday he is confident that a durability problem with the GE9X engine's mid-seal will not delay the Boeing 777X's planned entry into service next year. GE disclosed the potential issue in February and said in April it had found the root cause and was finalizing a fix without schedule impact. Speaking at a Morgan Stanley conference, Ghai said testing showed the mid-seal, which connects the engine's front and rear sections, was less durable than expected, prompting a redesign; engines with the new seal began shipping to Boeing in the third quarter and FAA certification of the part is expected within months. He said internal testing gave the company a high degree of confidence in the redesign, which is now built into production engines. The existing seal can still be used for certification work underway, including approvals Boeing needs before starting ETOPS testing.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Biotower project proceeds on Salt Lake's west side
item.description: A biotower project on Salt Lake City's west side near 1030 W. Pierpont Ave. is moving ahead after neighborhood complaints earlier in the year prompted design changes. Salt Lake City Public Utilities deputy director Jason Brown said landscaping including trees, rocks and a 10-foot wall is already in place, with bark mulch to follow and the biotower itself scheduled for installation in January. The structure will rise about 15 feet rather than the originally planned 30, and the manufacturer agreed to produce the filter in an earth-toned tan color to help it blend into the surroundings. Utility crews say the filter is needed to treat corrosive sewer gases that also produce a rotten-egg odor. Neighbors had objected over the tower's height and appearance and its possible effects on home values and health, but Brown said no recent complaints have come in.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: NASA spacecraft discovers a huge new crater on the moon
item.description: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed a lunar crater larger than the Roman Colosseum, formed by an impact two years ago that went undetected at the time. The steep-sided hole measures about 728 feet (222 meters) across and up to 141 feet (43 meters) deep, making it the largest known impact crater created in the solar system in recent times — an event researchers estimate occurs only about once every 132 years and called effectively a once-in-a-lifetime observation in one of two studies published Wednesday in Science Advances. The orbiter photographed the crater on the moon's near side in May 2024 shortly after an asteroid or comet fragment struck, but the strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space. The wide-angle images went unnoticed in the volume of data until August 2025, with detailed follow-up imagery gathered last fall and confirmation early this year. The crater, named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute, is three times larger than the previous record holder.
item.dc:creator: Marcia Dunn, Associated Press

item.title: Draper man says parents, sister were trying to normalize migratory status when detained by ICE
item.description: Julian Rincon, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Colombia living in Draper, is speaking out after his sister and parents were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Phoenix's Sky Harbor International Airport in late August. His sister Daniela Rincon and parents Clara Avellaneda and Henry Rincon, who live in Herriman, had work permits and were pursuing steps to normalize their immigration status when they were arrested Aug. 26 on arrival from a Salt Lake City flight for what was meant to be a short family trip. The three are being held at the Eloy Detention Center in Arizona, and the Department of Homeland Security described them in a statement as illegal aliens from Colombia. Federal records show Daniela entered the U.S. in May 2017 and her parents in August 2019, each with permission to stay for a limited period. Rincon questioned why people actively following a legal path to residency would be detained.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Ogden cold case closed after investigators obtain prison confession
item.description: Ogden police and the Weber Metro Cold Case Task Force have closed the nearly 30-year-old disappearance of Richard Roy Billmayer, who vanished in 1997 and was later listed as a missing person under suspicious circumstances in the National Crime Information Center database. Richard Annis, an inmate serving a life sentence for another homicide at Anamosa State Penitentiary in Iowa, admitted in a recorded prison confession that he killed Billmayer and disposed of his body in a dumpster. Ogden Police Detective Douglas Dunbar, a lead investigator, called the resolution surreal after a three-decade investigation. Investigator Mike Rounkles of the task force, which operates under the Weber County Attorney's Office, said the best possible outcome was the truth and the family now has it. Billmayer's niece Sabra Winters remembered him as her favorite and most fun-loving uncle.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Texas man who operated 'ghost broker' scheme sentenced to probation, deportation
item.description: Carlos David Garcia Gonzalez, 38, of Liberty Hills, Texas, was sentenced to probation and deportation for running a ghost broker insurance scheme in Utah. Charged in June in 3rd District Court with insurance fraud, communications fraud, two counts of engaging in a pattern of unlawful activity, identity fraud and forgery, he pleaded guilty Aug. 22 to insurance fraud and one pattern-of-unlawful-activity count, with the remaining four charges dismissed. In his plea statement Garcia admitted posing as a licensed agent and submitting fraudulent online data to three insurance companies to obtain auto policies out of Salt Lake County, producing roughly $832,000 in restitution from avoided premiums. Investigators say he obtained more than 1,100 auto policies and collected about $84,470 in payments for faulty or nonexistent coverage, using victims' names, birth dates and policy numbers to make unauthorized changes by phone.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah man charged with hiring hit man while awaiting trial for the same crime
item.description: Orane James Spence, 34, of Magna, already jailed on accusations that he tried to hire someone to kill his ex-wife and her mother, has been charged with attempting the same scheme from behind bars. Prosecutors filed two counts of criminal solicitation to commit murder, a first-degree felony, in 3rd District Court on Wednesday; the earlier case carrying identical charges is scheduled for trial at the end of the month. According to the new charges, Spence approached a fellow inmate at the Salt Lake County Jail on May 15 seeking someone to keep his ex-wife from testifying, saying he was desperate because he expected a lengthy prison sentence. The inmate supplied the number of a confidential informant, and Spence allegedly offered up to $50,000 and asked for a clean death that would raise no suspicion. Investigators said he tried to conceal the plot by placing calls to the informant using another inmate's calling credentials.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: UN-backed experts cite possible US war crimes in Iran strikes
item.description: A U.N.-backed fact-finding mission reported Thursday that it found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, and separately accused Iran's government of crimes against humanity against its own population. The mission, chaired by Bangladeshi jurist Sara Hossain and created in 2022 by the Geneva-based Human Rights Council, is composed of independent experts and was expected to present its findings Monday to the 47-member council. Its conclusions about U.S. conduct center on a pair of airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children. An Associated Press investigation found that at least one U.S. missile struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in the southern city of Minab at the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February, with Iranian state media reporting 168 killed and no final accounting yet completed. The report is not binding but adds to the international record and could support future efforts to pursue justice in international courts.
item.dc:creator: Jamey Keaten, Associated Press

item.title: Search continues for 2 missing women presumed drowned at Sand Hollow Reservoir
item.description: The search for two Las Vegas women, ages 26 and 28, presumed drowned in Sand Hollow Reservoir was set to resume at 7:30 a.m. Thursday, with a friend saying one of the women was about four and a half months pregnant with twins. The two were riding a Jet Ski Tuesday afternoon with 23-year-old Antonio Omari Lewis of Henderson, Nevada, when he crashed; none of the three wore life jackets. Lewis, a coworker of both women, was arrested and charged Wednesday in 5th District Court with two counts of automobile homicide, a second-degree felony, plus class C misdemeanors for improper navigation in a wakeless area and failing to obey waterway markers and six infractions including life-jacket, registration and invasive-mussel violations. The Utah Department of Natural Resources said the women were last seen in the southern part of the reservoir and were reported missing around 4:20 p.m. Park rangers searched roughly 90 minutes using sonar, drones and aircraft before shifting from rescue to recovery at about 5:30 p.m., and the Washington County Search and Rescue Dive Team continued without success.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah Government Records Office asks lawmakers for help to handle increasing appeals
item.description: The Utah Government Records Office told the Government Operations Interim Committee on Wednesday that public records appeals are rising fast enough that it may need more staff and more time to hold hearings and issue orders. Director Lonny Pehrson reported the office inherited 102 pending appeals when it began operating in mid-2025, a backlog built up after lawmakers abolished the State Records Committee and after that committee had gone without a quorum. In its first year the office held 170 hearings and decided 276 appeals, with another 79 withdrawn or otherwise resolved, cutting average waits for an appeal hearing from 130 days to well within the 64-day statutory guideline. But 309 new appeals were filed over the same period, which the report called a drastic increase over past years. Pehrson said filings nearly doubled starting in December, just as the office was making progress on the backlog, and have stayed well above average for six months with no sign of slowing.

item.title: Black bear euthanized in Grand Teton National Park after visitors repeatedly leave food behind
item.description: Grand Teton National Park staff euthanized a black bear near Delta Lake on Friday after visitors repeatedly let the animal obtain human food, conditioning it to approach people. Park officials said in a news release that the bear was lethally removed because of poor decisions by park visitors. Reports of the bear approaching people near Delta Lake began earlier in the year, when officials could not yet tell whether the encounters were isolated or a sign of food conditioning; the bear went on to receive human food on multiple occasions and repeatedly approached visitors. Wildlife staff stepped up monitoring and tried to haze the animal away but found it unusually hard to discourage, and managers concluded the repeated food rewards and increasingly close encounters posed an unacceptable safety risk. Because Delta Lake sits in remote backcountry, staff tranquilized and euthanized the bear on site and flew the carcass out.
