item.title: NASA says new Roman telescope's lifespan could more than double, to 22 years
item.description: NASA says the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope may be able to operate for up to 22 years, more than double the lifespan announced before its launch. The agency had previously described a five-year primary mission plus a five-year extension, supported by a 10-year fuel budget. NASA credits the longer outlook to the precision of the telescope's first mid-course correction, anticipated results from a second correction and orbital insertion still ahead, and extra fuel loaded before liftoff. Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote in an agency blog post that exquisite planning by the orbital dynamics team, execution by operations staff and a precise SpaceX launch left Roman with fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations. The observatory launched Aug. 30 from Cape Canaveral aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket and is traveling toward Lagrange Point 2 to study major questions in astrophysics and cosmology.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: Emigration Canyon residents concerned over proposed Sinclair fuel pipeline expansion
item.description: Emigration Canyon homeowners are raising concerns about HF Sinclair's proposed Westline Connect project, which could route a new refined petroleum pipeline through the area. Company representatives presented the plan to the Emigration Canyon City Council this week, and the proposal remains in early planning with no final route chosen. The project would expand the Pioneer Pipeline, which carries refined fuels into Utah from Wyoming, and the UNEV Pipeline, which moves refined products from the Salt Lake City area to Las Vegas. A company representative said the Pioneer Pipeline's existing capacity of 60,000 barrels a day would grow by another 35,000. HF Sinclair argued in a statement that fuel demand across the Mountain West has outpaced the existing pipeline network, leaving producers dependent on trucking, and that the project would steady supply and remove truck traffic from highways in four states.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Fossil tooth analysis confirms Tyrannosaurus rex was warm-blooded
item.description: A study published Wednesday in Science Advances offers the first direct estimate of Tyrannosaurus rex's body temperature, putting it at roughly 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 Celsius) — about the same as humans. Researchers reached the figure by analyzing chemical signatures preserved in fossilized teeth, a technique that co-author Robert Eagle, a geobiologist and associate professor at UCLA, described as the most direct constraint on T. rex body temperature achieved so far. Scientists have suspected for nearly 60 years that the predator was warm-blooded, and a T. rex footprint found in Alaska in 2022 bolstered the case by showing the animals thrived in frigid settings where cold-blooded reptiles could not. The finding supports the view that T. rex maintained an active metabolism even in cold climates. Researchers say knowing the temperature sharpens understanding of the dinosaur's behavior, physiology and interactions with other species between about 69 million and 66 million years ago.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Nicioli, CNN

item.title: Understand needs, forge solutions, President Oaks invites at Washington National Cathedral
item.description: President Dallin H. Oaks of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints spoke at the Washington National Cathedral on Wednesday, on the eve of Constitution Day, calling for common ground in preserving religious freedom. He told the audience he speaks for no political party or pressure group but for the Constitution itself, which he described as a model allowing a diverse people to govern themselves. Oaks brought seven decades of constitutional study to the address: he clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice Earl Warren, taught law for 15 years, and served more than three years on the Utah Supreme Court before his 1984 call to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He has served as an apostle for 42 years and was sustained as church president in October 2025. In his remarks he recounted early church members' expulsion from Missouri in the 1830s and their move west beyond U.S. borders in the 1840s, describing those pioneers as refugees.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Jensen, Deseret News

item.title: Salt Lake City, UDOT crafting emergency plan for flooded west side residents
item.description: Salt Lake City and the Utah Department of Transportation disagree over who is responsible for an August water main break that flooded more than a dozen Poplar Grove homes, but both are moving to help residents still displaced a month later. The Salt Lake City Council informally voted Tuesday to include a new emergency household stabilization fund of up to $50,000 in an upcoming budget amendment, authorizing staff to prepare as though the money is already allocated. Mayor Erin Mendenhall said UDOT has signaled willingness to match whatever the city contributes. The money is intended to help displaced residents secure temporary housing and cover other pressing costs. Councilman Alejandro Puy, whose district covers Poplar Grove, proposed the item and said there is an immediate need for stabilization; the discussion came a day after KSL interviewed homeowners still unable to return home.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams and Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Great Salt Lake dust expensive to manage, study finds
item.description: A University of Utah study from the Wilkes Center for Climate Science and Policy finds that dust blowing off the Great Salt Lake's exposed bed is both a growing health hazard and an expensive problem to manage. John C. Lin, the center's scientific director and an atmospheric sciences professor, said researchers used a high-resolution computer model of dust sources and wind patterns and overlaid it with population data, finding Tooele County faces the highest average exposure, followed by Salt Lake County. The study puts the collective health costs to Utahns of continued lake decline at roughly $115 million a year, with Lin noting documented cases of exposure causing missed school and work. Mitigation options the team examined ranged from engineering solutions to periodically flooding the playa and growing vegetation or installing structures to slow the wind, but costs could reach into the billions if pursued over decades. A follow-up study will examine which pollutants appear in different parts of the lakebed and at what concentrations.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Utah drivers change habits as gas prices climb
item.description: Utah drivers are paying roughly $1.50 more per gallon than a year ago, with the state average near $4.80, and new survey data suggests the prices are reshaping driving habits. LendingTree data shared with the KSL Investigators found 81% of drivers said transportation costs have changed their behavior: 31% are driving less, 38% are combining errands into fewer trips, 29% have started carpooling and 28% shop around for cheaper fuel before filling up. Drivers interviewed at Utah pumps described the prices as out of hand and brutal. The report reiterated familiar savings measures such as maintaining proper tire pressure and using gas apps to compare prices. LendingTree also suggested that drivers who have sharply cut their mileage ask their insurer whether lower annual mileage qualifies them for a reduced premium.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt and Sloan Schrage, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist hospitalized after Sandy crash
item.description: A teenage boy was critically injured Wednesday night in a collision between a motorcycle and a car in Sandy. Sandy police said the crash happened at 8 p.m. as the teen rode a motorcycle on 9000 South and collided with a car at 470 East. The motorcyclist was taken to a hospital with critical injuries. The far-right lane at 9000 South and 470 East was closed as a result. Police said the crash remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Dr. Nicole Saphier, Trump's 3rd surgeon general pick, grilled over vaccine stance
item.description: Dr. Nicole Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News contributor who is President Donald Trump's third nominee for surgeon general, faced sharp questioning about childhood vaccines at her Senate confirmation hearing Wednesday. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy pressed her to say whether she believed vaccines cause autism — a link scientific consensus rejects but which the administration has repeatedly sought to revisit — and Saphier replied that she does not believe childhood vaccines cause autism. Asked whether parents should give children the measles, mumps and rubella shot, she called the MMR vaccine the greatest tool for combating measles; the president recently urged spacing the shots out. Saphier described vaccines as a critical tool for preventing infection while saying she appreciated the administration's efforts to address concerns among vaccine-hesitant people. Cassidy countered that those efforts were only creating more confusion and pushed her to answer with greater clarity.
item.dc:creator: Fatima Hussein and Ali Swenson, Associated Press

item.title: Holocaust survivor shares her story of trauma, healing and faith
item.description: Sora Vigorito, the youngest known survivor of Josef Mengele's twin experiments at Auschwitz, spoke at the University of Utah to one of the largest audiences she has ever addressed. Rabbi Moshe Nigri, who first reached out to her, said roughly 1,500 people had signed up before reservations closed for lack of space; about 900 attended in person in the Student Union building and another 200 to 300 joined remotely. The program opened with prelude music from a quartet of LDS Institute of Religion musicians, followed by remarks from Nigri, his wife, University Interfaith Initiatives executive director Charlie Freedman, and Ethan Smith, president of Chabad on Campus at the university. Vigorito, who was nearly killed before she turned four, told the audience she has no memory of her mother, who disappeared with her older sister while begging for food and was likely seized by the Nazis. She survived in hiding with her grandmother.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Park City synagogue vandalized; hate-crime enhancement considered
item.description: Temple Har Shalom in Park City is rebuilding its sign after vandals damaged it over Labor Day weekend, days before the Jewish community observed Rosh Hashanah. Letters were torn off and the Star of David was damaged. Rabbi Jeff Dreifus said the attack was surprising given how long Jews have been part of the fabric of life in Park City, and that it left congregants feeling deliberately targeted and unsafe practicing Judaism in what they consider their Jewish home in the mountains. The Summit County Sheriff's Office is investigating the case as criminal mischief, which covers intentional damage to another person's property, and is weighing whether a victim-targeting or hate-crime enhancement applies; the Summit County Attorney's Office would make the final charging decision. Dreifus said it is the first public display of antisemitism against the congregation he can recall.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL
